speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, June 18, consideration of Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs; and Motions Nos. 10, 16, 20, 25, 26, 28 and 35 (Mr. Robinson (Burnaby)).
Is the House ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak in support of the motion to delete Clause 3 from Bill C-9. Clause 3, Mr. Speaker, is the proposed Section setting out the establishment of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. I have indicated in earlier remarks that I accept the fact that Canada, like every other country, needs a security service. It needs a security service which will protect the interests of Canada. I am not very concerned whether that security service should be a civilian security service or a part of the RCMP.
I recognize the fact that, for many years, and even today, the RCMP had and has an excellent reputation. It has earned the respect of most Canadians. Therefore I am not too worried about the question of where the new security service should be lodged, either as a civilian service or as part of the RCMP. What I am concerned about is that its mandate should be crystal clear. It should know what its job is, and what its responsibilities are. It should know what it can do and what it cannot do in order to fulfil its mandate.
[DOT]	(mo)
For many years most people in Canada knew very little about the work of the security service. There were people in trade union movements, universities, student and church organizations who had a feeling that the security service was keeping an eye on them, infiltrating their organizations, even though they believed that the things that they were doing were quite legitimate and did not need to be spied upon. But they
had no real evidence that this was happening until a few years ago.
I was a Member of this House when stories began to circulate about some of the activities in which the security service had been involved. I remember that, as each story came out, the then Solicitor General, first the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), and later the present Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), assured Members of this House, the media, and the general public that these were isolated cases. Well, either they had not been told what was going on or they did not want to know. The McDonald Commission looked into all these questions, and in fact they did not know what was going on.
Eventually we had the prosecution of a former RCMP officer, Mr. Samson, which, along with other things, led to the establishment of the McDonald Commission. It spent several years, heard hundreds of witnesses in public and in secret, and made a report which ought to have caused a great deal of hard thinking and anguish on the part of all Canadians. The situation was in fact very, very serious. The report said that the security service had been involved in the theft of membership lists of a legitimate political Party, involved in burning barns, and in the theft of dynamite, and wire tapping. Those are just a few of the activities in which the Security Service had been involved.
Eventually the McDonald Commission made a number of recommendations calling for legislation to set up a new security service to make clear what its job and responsibilities were, what its officers could and could not do, and what they should be able to do in order to fulfil their mandate. We have had at least two Bills from the Government supposedly dealing with the problems, and making proposals on how to deal with the recommendations. The first Bill died because there was so much opposition to it. It was clear that the Bill and the proposals were deficient.
[DOT] (U15)
Now we have this second Bill which was referred to the Senate and had a number of changes made to it, based on the recommendations of the Senate. The Minister has said repeatedly that it is only a small group of malcontents who are opposing that Bill for political reasons, or because they do not understand it. But the Bill is still being opposed by very important non partisan groups in the community. I will list them very briefly. They are the Canadian Conference of Churches, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, the provincial Attorneys General, and organizations such as the Canadian Jewish Congress. Such organizations appeared before the committee and made very detailed critiques of the

Security Intelligence Service
Bill, which included a number of very specific recommendations on how the Bill should be amended to meet the standards of fairness which are required. Virtually all of their recommendations have been ignored.
I remind Members of the House that the Canadian Jewish Congress was very active in an earlier major debate which we had in Parliament on the question of the Constitution and the Charter of Rights. Its presentation was made at that time by its then president, Professor Irwin Cotier, a professor of law at McGill University. He is a leading spokesman on human and civil rights, and is legal counsel to Anatoly Shcharansky, the famous Soviet dissident.
Mr. Cotier was an assistant to the new Leader of the Liberal Party, Mr. Turner, when Mr. Turner was the Minister of Justice. A long article in yesterday's Globe and Mail said that Professor Cotier was one of the people Mr. Turner recruited when he became the Minister of Justice. Mr. Turner wanted small 1 liberals, progressive thinking people who were interested in questions such as civil rights. Professor Cotier was one of Mr. Turner's assistants. The article in the Globe and Mail reads:
Prof. Cotier says at first he mistrusted his boss, figuring that he was not serious about the issues, such as civil liberties or poverty, he said he wanted to address.
Mr. Cotier says his mind was changed when he watched Mr. Turner deliver a hard-hitting speech calling for justice to the poor-
I wonder what Mr. Cotier would think about the Bill we are discussing now. I wonder what the new Leader of the Liberal Party would think about this Bill. Mr. Cotier has not spoken on this Bill, but the organization of which he was the president until about a year ago, has spoken.
I will quote a few of the recommendations of the Canadian Jewish Congress which the Solicitor General has ignored completely. Dealing with threats to the security of Canada they proposed the following amendment to what is now in the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who preceded me was asking rhetorically what Mr. Turner or Mr. Cotier, the eminent lawyer on civil rights, would think of this Bill. What does it matter? It does not matter what Mr. Turner thinks. There is nothing new about Mr. Turner. It is not a new deal, it is the old deal writ large.
Mr. Turner is now the leader of the Liberal Party. We saw the unseemly haste with which all the sycophantic members of the Trudeau Cabinet jumped on his bandwagon early in the game, because they knew that the fix was in. The establishment was going to put him in office.
When the Hon. Member asks what would Mr. Turner think, I say that it does not matter what Mr. Turner thinks. What
matters is is whether the public would buy a used Government from that man.
Alan Borovoy is not a kook, lunatic, or nut; he is one of the most sensible and intelligent critics on the question of civil liberties in Canada. He has said that this Bill in its present form is the most dangerous attack on civil liberties since Confederation.
When one talks of Mr. Turner, and reform, and the new Liberal Party, it is all a lot of garbage. The first thing that happened in this House after Mr. Turner became the Leader of the Liberal Party was the implementation of notice of closure on a Bill that is absolutely essential and integral to the civil rights of Canadians. What we listened to last weekend was absolute claptrap. There is nothing new. It is not the new deal. I said, it is the old deal, writ large.
The disgrace about this Bill is that the Government said at second reading stage that we could make suggestions at committee. That was a fraud. It was dishonest and was not intended. The Government has not made a significant acceptance of suggestions made by Hon. Members in committee or by those who came to the committee at great expense to the Canadian taxpayer.
All that we are listening to on the Government side is sanctimonious nonsense. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is reported in today's Canadian Press as saying that this is all a filibuster, and even a child could understand that Hon. Members are just playing games. Are we playing games with Clause 2, subparagraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d) which define what are threats to the security of Canada, and trigger what a secret group can do secretly, in the dark, to other Canadians?
Some day someone will ask why some of us MPs did not say something. The fact of the matter is that we have been saying a lot, but because the media have been running around writing inane stories about an inane bunch of people, nobody has been reporting what we have been saying. One of these days the same reporters, the same graduates of the same crummy journalism schools, will be writing sanctimonious, pious editorials asking how did all of this happen in the House of Commons of Canada. When that happens, I hope some of them have their noses rubbed in some of the speeches that have been made here.
I am fed up to the teeth with the hypocritical claptrap of the Liberal Members. We are not even allowed to put most of the amendments in the House that would force them to vote. Even the Liberal Party's former Solicitor General does not agree with this Bill. They will not even listen to him. He is the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand). Unfortunately he is away, and I had to move his amendments yesterday. He was probably sent away.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who is an eminent Member of the House and has been here for many years, asks the rhetorical question: what would John Turner think of this Bill? John Turner knows all about the Bill and has thought about it. He said to get it out of the House as fast as possible because he does not want to be embarrassed by
June 19, 1984

it. Therefore yesterday the Solicitor General, who has been wandering around with a John Turner button on his lapel for weeks, if not months, said that he will move notice to cut off debate. I would not mind their cutting off debate if they would accept some amendments that would make this Bill safer for Canadians.
I practised law in courts for 17 years before I was elected in 1972. I worked in a logging camp and lived in a bunkhouse when I was 15. I do not come from a silver spoon background, and I have been about. I got out of law school and I went to the Yukon, and paid my debts by running a string of pack-horses. I have served in the Canadian army. There is not much I haven't done or haven't seen.
I do not come to this debate with some kind of ingenuous, rosy hued notion and fantasy out of the classroom. Of course I am a civil rights lawyer. Any lawyer who knows the common law has to be a civil rights lawyer. Common law is our pride and our tradition, because lawyers who went to court had the guts to get up and say some of the things that were not the conventional clap-trap wisdom and herd mentality of either the media or the cocktail party set. That is what this debate is about, Mr. Speaker.
The Government could accept some amendments to this Bill if it had any conscience or any sense. But the Government has dug in. The Liberals have been told by a group of so-called experts that that is what they have to have. The other people who come representing traditions and values that determine and guarantee our freedom have not been listened to. Those of us who talk about civil rights are looked upon by the Government as some kind of left-wing kook fringe.
I am ashamed at what is happening in this House. I am ashamed also that across the country the people who are supposed to be watching this debate, and supposed to be finding out what the issue really is, cannot seem to figure it out. I do not know what we have journalism schools for. What about the people in the ivory towers of the media who prate, rant, and preach, and tell us, MPs, how we ought to behave every once in a while, give us lectures about the price of food in the parliamentary restaurant, tell us that we should never have an increase in pay, or get so righteous? While all of this has been going on, where have they been? Sitting in their ivory towers, in their executive suites, while their underpaid minions have been dazzled by a party show that has gone on in the last few weeks. As a consequence this vital issue, as Alan Borovoy said, the most important issue in civil rights since Confederation, has been ignored.
I am ashamed for this place, and I am ashamed of the Government.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: For debate, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson).

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this group of amendments is to deal with the question of the appointment of the Director of the proposed civilian security service. A number of questions were raised in that connection, including the proposed term of office of the Director, as well as the consultation which should be mandatory on the appointment of such an important individual and the powers which the Director of the service will hold.
I listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) with respect to the previous motion. I only wish that his fire and brimstone had been applied equally vigorously in committee. This legislation might not have seen the light of day in its present form had his colleagues in caucus been a little more vigorous in their opposition to this legislation instead of co-operating with the Government in expediting its passage.
The first motion is Motion No. 12 which would delete Clause 4. However, I should like to talk for a moment or two about Motion No. 14 in particular. That motion would require that the Minister appoint the Director of the service only following consultation by the Prime Minister with the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, as well as with the Leader of each Party having at least 12 Members in the House. This was one of the essential recommendations of the McDonald Commission, that in the appointment of such an important official whose powers are so sweeping under the terms of the legislation, there should at least be consultation if not a requirement for ratification of that appointment. Indeed, I believe a requirement for ratification would be preferable, but at least there should be consultation before appointment to such an important position.
What is the history on this question? Shortly after the report of the McDonald Commission was tabled, the Government announced that it intended to create a new civilian security service. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) went on to name the man he decided was to head the service. At that point it was Mr. Fred Gibson. There was no consultation whatsoever with either of the Opposition Parties, the Government having ignored that recommendation. Some time later Mr. Gibson was appointed to the position of Deputy Minister and yet another individual was named to be Director of the new civilian security service whenever it was created, Mr. Ted Finn from the Privy Council Office, a former crony of Michael Pitfield. There was no consultation whatsoever with the Opposition on the appointment of Mr. Finn, the new Director, despite the very clear direction on the part of the McDonald Commission that there should be consultation with the Opposition before the appointment of such an individual. The purpose of Motion No. 14 is simply to include in the Bill the requirement for that consultation. I cannot imagine how the Government could oppose such a reasonable suggestion.
I am sure we will hear from the Hon. Member for Vancouver South with respect to Motion No. 13 since that motion was moved in his name. However, with respect to Motion No. 12,
the motion to delete Clause 4,1 would note that it is one which deals with the question of the Director of the service and the powers of this new service. Those powers which will be granted to the new Director are sweeping and unprecedented in any democratic society. For the first time in Canadian history the Director of the new service will have the power to go before a court and seek a warrant to break into anyone's home, to remove anything-this is what some have called legalized theft-to break into an office or any other place, to instal bugs and to take away anything it wants to take away. In effect, we are seeing here the legalizing of what was documented as illegal by the McDonald Commission. If the security service breaks into the offices of the APLQ and steals documents, under this Bill that is now legal. If the security service breaks into the offices of the Parti Quebecois, a legal party, and steals computer tapes with its membership records-and the McDonald Commission said that that was illegal-under the provisions of the Bill that is now legal.
The McDonald Commission documented a series of breaches of federal and provincial law. In virtually every instance the response of the Government has been to change the law to make what was illegal then legal now. Surely in a democratic society that cannot be acceptable.
The Director appointed under the provisions of Clause 4 will have the power to appear before a Federal Court judge and seek a judicial warrant, after having consulted with the Minister, to break into any place, to remove any thing or to open first-class mail. That power has never before been granted for any purpose to any police agency in the history of the country. The Government comes before Parliament and says that it is a power which it needs, despite the fact that the McDonald Commission clearly argued against extending the power to open first-class mail of Canadians suspected of so-called domestic subversion. The Director can seek the power to open the first-class mail of all Canadians. The Director can go before the courts and seek a warrant to invade the confidential medical records and confidential psychiatric records of Canadians, a power which is not in existence at the present time.
For the first time in the history of our country, the Director of the service will be able to go before the courts of this land and seek a warrant to access confidential income tax records which, once again, have never in the history of this country been made legally accessible to any police force or security service. The McDonald Commission documented the fact that the security service illegally had access to income tax records. The response of this Government is that while it may have been illegal then, we are telling Parliament that we are going to make it legal today. That is the power that is contained in this Bill and which is conferred on the Director under Clause 4. It is for that reason that we are seeking the deletion of Clause 4. Nowhere, in no other western other country in the world, whether it be the United States, West Germany, the United Kingdom, New Zealand or Australia, are the kinds of powers being sought in this legislation conferred.
June 19, 1984

What is so special about the threats to Canada? I suggest these motions should be supported. These draconian powers which are granted to this new super spy must be curtailed. On that basis, I urge the House to adopt Motions Nos. 12, 13 and 14.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two about Motions Nos. 12, 13 and 14 which deal with Clause 4 of the Bill. In the original statute this clause was different. After having heard the witnesses, the Government agreed that it would accept an amendment. It prompts the comment that on many occasions the Government was prepared to accept the evidence of the Senate committee, the McDonald Commission and our own committee, yet in other clauses that were equally reasonable and upon which Government Members themselves could see the logic of the change, Cabinet has decided not to accept it. I think it is fair comment that if the thinking of the McDonald Commission was proper on several of these issues, surely it is just as proper on other issues. I do not understand why the Cabinet accepted some and not others. Likewise the Senate. I would like the Minister to comment on that. It is not this clause in particular but some of the others as well. I would like him to think about it. Maybe he could give us the benefit of his thinking as to what occurred within Cabinet that some of the McDonald Commission recommendations were accepted and some were not, in terms of judicial warrants and so on.
Why do you accept some and reject some?
My acceptances and rejections are based on evidence that we heard in committee.
So are ours.

We have a disagreement then as to the weight that should be attached to the evidence we heard. The Minister will agree that some of his own Members felt in their questioning of the Minister that a change would be acceptable if the Minister did not. Is that because he and the Cabinet have vastly superior access to information, even though they did not hear the witnesses? This is a general comment I have about the whole process which has broken down in Parliament.
We have second reading of the Bill. In a sense, second reading is premature. It is only after you hear the witnesses that you get the broad scope of the Bill. I agree with those who believe that after the Bill is introduced for first reading it should go directly to committee. We could then hear the experts from the various fields. The committee could then recommend changes. At that point the Bill could come back at second reading and be discussed on principle. It would be easier for the Government to accept amendments at that stage, before we have second reading debate and it has been passed in principle. The Government at second reading of this Bill stood and defended the principle of it. It then went to committee. When faced with the many changes suggested by the experts, the Government will not accept them. The Government and its caucus are convinced that the Bill has been approved in principle and therefore cannot accept any changes.

Clause 4 dealing with the Director originally stated that the Director shall be appointed to hold office during good behaviour for a term not exceeding five years. We immediately picked up on the fact that the Director could not be dismissed by the Government if the Director did something politically improper or improper for reasons other than conduct. We therefore proposed the motion that the Director hold office at pleasure. That makes him much more accountable and responsive to the government of the day. That was a good amendment and I commend the Minister for accepting it. I wish he would accept some of our other amendments at the same time.
The Director at the expiration of his first term of five years can be reappointed for a further five years and no person shall hold office as Director for terms exceeding ten years in the aggregate. That is good. We should learn from the United States situation when Mr. Edgar Hoover was director of the CIA. He was in office so long that he collected dossiers on all people in public life. He was able to block appointments of people to public office, promotion of officials within the hierarchy of the United States administration and actually perverted the political scene in the United States because of the power he had built up in the office. We do not want that to happen. I am glad that the Director, as good as he or she may be, will have to leave at the end of ten years. If I had my way, that same rule would apply with respect to the Prime Minister, the Premiers and indeed to all of us in public life. After ten years such a person would have to drop out for at least one term.
There is no doubt that the Hill is an unreal place. There is the very real possibility of losing touch with what those at the grassroots feel about issues. We would be much more responsive if we had to stand down for a term after ten years in office.
Motion No. 12, which is an attempt by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) to have the whole clause struck out, is pursuant to his strategy that if he cannot have his changes, the whole Bill should be knocked out. I disagree heartily with his comments vis-a-vis the comments of my colleague from Vancouver South who presented his case in committee in a rational and logical way. If it would not have been for the Hon. Member for Burnaby, I feel the Government would have been more inclined to accept amendments. I think the strategy and tactics of the Hon. Member for Burnaby in committee so early on inflamed the Government and it took extraordinary remedies. The actions of the Hon. Member for Burnaby have been deleterious to the parliamentary process in dealing with this Bill. I know from talking with some of my colleagues on the Government side privately and off the record that they may have been inclined to accept more of these amendments had it not been for the actions of the NDP and the Hon. Member for Burnaby.
As I look at the further sections of the Bill dealing with the Director, I note that the Director has absolutely enormous

Security Intelligence Service
powers regarding the appointment and management of the employees of the service. The relevant clause states:
The Director ... has the control and management of the Service and all matters connected therewith.
The clause dealing with appointments relates back to Clause 4. Clause 8 reads:
Notwithstanding the Financial Administration Act and the Public Service Employment Act, the Director has exclusive authority to appoint employees-
That is a very broad power. This Director is being given an enormous power over his own employees. If this Director were to have unlimited tenure, that power could very easily be used against the employees of the service.
I have one more minute left, Mr. Speaker. That is a part of my argument regarding why there should be a limit of ten years on the tenure of the Director. He has exclusive authority to appoint employees and, in relation to the personnel management of employees, to provide for terms and conditions of their employment. That is a very dramatic power and I think we would not want to have anyone with that kind of power hold an office for more than ten years.

Mr. Speaker, very briefly, I am supporting the amendments that have been put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), and particularly the motion to amend the clause that requires consultation with leaders of other Parties. In a case like this, it is of absolute importance that there be no veto power by other political Parties. That would be wrong and unwise.
The Bill gives this agency wide and sweeping powers. It gives it powers far in excess of those suggested by the McDonald Commission and far in excess of and much more sweeping than those suggested by virtually every major group that appeared before the committee. Therefore, there should at least be some consultation between the leaders of the Parties in this House of Commons, Parties which have received a substantial degree of support from the Canadian electorate.
I believe that the people of Canada have a right to the knowledge that the director of any agency that has the right by law to interfere in many aspects of Canadian life that have hitherto been considered well protected if not inviolate has been subject to a Parliamentary review. They have the right to the knowledge that the experience and character of such a person has been subject to a review by those people Canadians have chosen to represent their various legitimate interests in the House of Commons. I am not suggesting that the Government is not acting with the best intentions. We all have our own various ways of achieving what we think is good for society. However, I cannot understand why the Government and the Minister would have an objection to this kind of consultative process.
It has often been said that justice must not only be done but must be seen to be done. Nowhere must it be seen to be done more than in the choosing of a director and the setting up of an administration that is responsible for the very broad and sweeping powers for which this legislation provides. Even at
this late date I would hope that the Minister, if he will not support the motion put forward by my colleague, will at least consider consulting with his other colleagues and perhaps returning to the House with Government amendments which would provide that what is seen to be done when setting up the administration of this service is beyond reproach and that every step is taken to ensure the consideration of all valid and legitimate expressions of political opinion in Canada. This is the very least that should be done when setting up an agency which has a mandate, as I have said many times before, that gives it very wide and sweeping powers.

One of the things that has bothered me is that this legislation raises some serious questions about the protection of Canadians from unauthorized snooping and spying by an agency of the Government, the function of which is the collecting of files on individuals and the compiling of portfolios on people in Canada-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point of these amendments which are before us is either to amend the position of the Director of this service that is proposed by this legislation or indeed to remove the provisions respecting the appointment of a Director. It seems to me that that is one way of manifesting our objection to the way in which the Government has dealt with this legislation. There has been a lack of sensitivity to the suggestions that we have made about the accountability of people who will be involved in this service and particularly about the person who will be primarily involved in the operation of the new security service, the Director. This person will play a pivotal role in carrying out the functions of the new security agency. Therefore, naturally we are concerned about what precisely will be the parameters of the powers of the Director.
Are we getting ourselves into the same situation which was subject to much criticism with respect to the operations and the arbitrary nature-according to all press reports-of the director of the FBI, J. Edgar Hoover, in the United States? We know through freedom of information sources in the United States about certain things which transpired because of the fact that the director of the FBI had limited accountability. The director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation deemed it appropriate to obtain the goods on certain people within the United States for purposes which he felt were justified. However, in the cold light of historic perspective, they turned out to be very much self-serving endeavours on the part of the director of that agency. We must guard against the availability of unlimited discretionary powers for the director of any agency in this country.
This agency will not be involved in the prosecution of criminals. It will not be involved directly in law enforcement as such. It is an agency which collects and deciphers information on people and on organizations. Its sole purpose is to garner information with respect to activities going on within Canada and outside of Canada. The question may be asked: If they are not in a position, as a police force is, to prosecute or lay informations, what difference does it make whether they collect information with respect to the citizens of Canada? There is a well-known axiom that knowledge is power. If certain groups in a free and democratic society have the function of advising government in terms of security matters and are able to develop files on individuals across Canada, and this information is made known without accountability to political sources within our country, the information has the possibility, indeed the probability, of being used for political purposes to the detriment of people in Canada.
I do not want to rehash old news, but I am still scandalized by the actions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) at the time of the election of our new Leader, the Hon. Member for
Security Intelligence Service
Central Nova (Mr. Mulroney). The Minister of Finance instructed officials in his Department to go through files and to seek out information which might cause embarrassment to the Leader of the Opposition. People say that this could not happen in Canada. However, the Minister of Finance was forced to stand in his place and admit that that was precisely what happened.
Knowledge is power. The danger with this organization is that if it is able to obtain information with respect to individuals in our country through surveillance, authorized wire taps, investigation of income tax returns, investigation of medical records, information which may be embarrassing or damaging to the reputations of individual Canadians, think of the potential that that information could be put to by a government that is inclined to use that information for its own purposes.
When we talk about the appointment of this Director-and these motions precisely deal with that-do we not have the responsibility as a Loyal Opposition to indicate that we have many, many concerns about the accountability and the review process which is generally contained in the legislation? Our many concerns have been expressed and manifested in different ways-through motions, at second reading debate and also within committee-about the mandate which has been given to this agency. We are concerned about the scope, the breadth and the fact that there is a high element of discretion involved with respect to activities which could be carried out by this agency.
In conclusion, are we not entitled to look at the powers and the accountability which the Director of this new service should be given? I am in support of the amendments which are in this particular grouping because I think the Government has, with the weight of its majority, decided to ram this legislation through. It is insensitive to the representations which have been made, insensitive to the feelings of the people of Canada and insensitive to the whole concept of freedom in a democratic society.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the motions with which we are now dealing relate to two very important clauses of the Bill, Clause No. 6 and Clause No. 8, which essentially set out the functions, duties and responsibilities of the management of the Director of the service as well as the relationship between the Minister responsible, that is, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), and the Director. These clauses as well permit the
Director to establish unilaterally terms and conditions of employment for employees of the new service.
There are four or five motions before the House, Mr. Speaker. These motions deal with a number of subjects because of the way in which the Speaker has chosen to group them. In ten minutes it is very difficult to explain adequately the full purpose of the amendments.
The first grouping of amendments is of those which deal with Clause No. 6, that is, Motion No. 17, which refers to the deletion of Clause No. 6, as well as Clause No. 19 and Clause No. 20. Speaking first, Mr. Speaker, to Motion No. 19, as Clause No. 6 is now worded, the Minister at his or her discretion may issue written directions to the Director of the service and, after those written directions are issued, shall forward a copy to the review committee. Nowhere in this Bill, however, is there any obligation on the part of the Minister to issue such written directions when dealing with important questions of policy. Therefore, the review process, which has already been effectively gutted by the provision in the legislation which would deny access to any documents which are referred to as Cabinet documents, is further weakened by the possibility that the Minister may not in fact pass on written directives to the review committee. The first purpose of this amendment is to require that directives be in writing when dealing with the broad, general operational policies of the service.
As well, Mr. Speaker, this Bill at the present time is totally silent on a number of very important policy questions which I believe must be addressed in the context of the legislation and, more importantly, must be addressed by the Minister and the review committee. These are set out in Motion No. 19. First, Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 19 requires that the Minister establish clear policies with respect to the use of undercover operatives-informers, if you will-by the service.
The placement of an informer can be one of the most intrusive and invasive technique which is available to a security service. It is far more intrusive in a number of instances, Mr. Speaker, and far more chilling in its impact on an organization, than even the placing of a telephone bug or the opening of mail. In a number of instances, as we know all too well, informers have been used not just to collect information, but to attempt to shape the decisions of the groups which they infiltrate. Yet, Mr. Speaker, this Bill is totally silent on the question of the role of informers. Indeed, there is not even a requirement that a warrant be obtained, the minimal requirement of a judicial warrant before an informer is placed in an organization by the security service.
The Keable Commission, which was established in the Government of Quebec, very strongly argued that there must be provision for judicial review before the use of undercover spies and informers in a democratic society. Yet, Mr. Speaker, not only is there no requirement for judicial warrant, but this Bill does not even address the issue of informers and the placement of informers.
Once again, we do not have to look very far; we do not have to look beyond the report of the McDonald Commission to see
June 19, 1984

the historic abuse of the placement of informers into groups which broke no laws whatsoever. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, right here in Ottawa Hon. Members will recall that the security service placed an informer, Andrew Moxley, into that subversive group which was attempting to persuade Canada not to test the Cruise missile. As well, informers have been placed into groups which are attempting to support liberation movements in Central America. This Bill, which purports to establish a statutory mandate for the security service, says not a word on this fundamental question.
My amendment would as well, Mr. Speaker, require that policies be established with respect to the use of physical surveillance by the service. Once again, there is no reference to that whatsoever in the Bill as it now stands. My amendment would require policies to be established with respect to the training of employees in order to ensure they are a little more sensitive to civil liberties.
It would, finally, Mr. Speaker, require that policies establishing minimization procedures for warrants issued under this Act be set out, and set out clearly. This Bill goes far beyond comparable American legislation in terms of the nature of warrants and the extent to which warrants can be used. Minimization procedures, Mr. Speaker, would require that if a tap is placed and it subsequently become known that the tap should not have been placed, then it would be removed immediately and any information collected would be destroyed. That minimal safeguard is totally lacking in this legislation.
As well, Mr. Speaker, there is a requirement-this is something which was proposed by many witnesses-that the Director must keep the Minister fully and currently informed of all operations of the service in order to avoid any suggestion of blindness, so that a Minister cannot suggest that he or she did not know what was going on in the service. This would require that the Director be fully and currently informed and thus could not use the excuse of wilful blindness.
As well, Mr. Speaker, there is a reference in this motion to the terms and conditions of employment, and a specific prohibition of discrimination of employment in the service, a discrimination on the grounds which are set out in the Canadian Human Rights Act, as well as on the basis of political belief or sexual orientation. Hon. Members will again recall that in appearing before the justice committee, the present Commissioner of the RCMP security service stated that "the security service at this time will not in fact hire individuals who may be gay or lesbian". That was indicated, Mr. Speaker, despite the fact that he admitted openly that there was no threat to security whatsoever in the case of individuals who are quite open about their orientation, but he said that other members of the service do not feel comfortable with these people around.
What kind of absurd rationale is that in a democratic society? It is the same rationale, Mr. Speaker, that we heard with respect to blacks and women not so long ago, with respect to Jews and other minorities, that they do not feel comfortable around them. Yet this Minister, Mr. Speaker, stands by and
Security Intelligence Service
permits that kind of discrimination to take place. He should be ashamed of himself, Mr. Speaker, as a member of a minority himself, that that kind of discrimination would be tolerated in this society. This amendment, Mr. Speaker, would ensure that that kind of discrimination would not be permitted in the new civilian security service.
Indeed, the proposed Director, Mr. Finn, has said before the committee that he would not allow such discrimination and this amendment, Mr. Speaker, would ensure, in statutory form, there would be a bar on that discrimination which is not tolerable in today's society or, indeed, in any society.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the amendment would require that the terms and conditions of employment of members of the service not deny them collective bargaining rights. As it stands now, the legislation would deny the fundamental freedom of association-a freedom which is supposedly contained in the Charter of Rights-to members of the new service. This amendment in Motion No. 24 would ensure collective bargaining rights for all members of the service. I want to commend the association of 17 Division of the RCMP for attempting to secure collective bargaining rights for all members of the force. Not the right to strike but the right to bargain collectively on terms and conditions of employment, a right which is denied even possibly to employees of this House.
I want to reiterate that the thrust of the amendments is clearly to establish the responsibility of the Minister to set out policies with respect to the use and placement of informers by the new security service, informers who can have such a chilling impact in a free and democratic society; policies with respect to training and minimization procedures for warrants. Secondly, it would prohibit discrimination in establishing terms and conditions of employment on the grounds set out in the Canadian Human Rights Act as well as on the basis of political belief or sexual orientation. Finally, it would deny the service the right to infringe on freedom of association and full collective bargaining rights. I strongly urge Members of this House to adopt these motions which would strengthen the service and bring the terms and conditions of employment in the service into the 20th century.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about Clause 6 of this Bill pursuant to these five motions grouped for debate. Clause 6, dealing with management of the service, states that:
The Director, under the direction of the Minister, has the control and management of the Service and all matters connected therewith.
You will see instantly that the issue we have to deal with is whether the Minister is responsible politically for the actions of the Director, or whether he can somehow slip out of the noose, so to speak, if the service does something improper, as the RCMP did back in the 1970s. We had quite a debate in committee as to whether that was so. As I recall, the Minister felt that because the Director is under the direction of the Minister, the Minister would be on the hook for that type of wrongdoing. That may well be so. Clause 6(2) provides that:
4784

June 19, 1984

In providing the direction referred to in subsection (1), the Minister may issue to the Director written directions with respect to the Service and a copy of any such directions shall, forthwith after it is issued, be given to the Review Committee.
My concern as a Member of Parliament is that if this section said the Minister "shall" issue to the Director written instructions which then have to be followed, it would be less easy for the Minister to somehow get out of the ultimate responsibility. All of this instructions would have to be in writing, copies would go to the review committee, and if the service did something outside of those written instructions then the Minister would be quite properly off the hook and the Director would be on the hook. We had quite a debate over whether the Minister "shall" issue directions, and if you review the minutes of the committee the Minister was saying that there are occasions when that is just totally inappropriate because he might be in Timbuktu or something like that and have to give telephone instructions. We accepted the Minister's point on that, but I think we would all agree that we want to have the Director responsible to the Minister, so that if anything goes wrong there is political accountability at the highest level for the actions of the Director.
Clause 6(3) goes on to say that the directions are not statutory instruments. That is in order to maintain secrecy other than through the established review mechanism, the Inspector General and the Review Committee. But it does raise an issue that Hon. Members should think about seriously. This review committee will be appointed by the Governor in Council and they will be Privy Councillors. At first we thought that would mean retired MPs and Senators, because the statute clearly states they cannot be active MPs or Senators. But we found in the evidence of the Minister that no, that was not necessarily the case and they may well pick someone off the street, appoint them Privy Councillor and then put them on the review committee. That completely changes the sense of direction and accountability.
We believe, and the witnesses were clear, that people who have served in public life, in elected office, whether MPs or Senators who at one time served in the House, have a much greater understanding of what Canadians are feeling than someone who might be appointed from a university, the academic community, or some Liberal who has served the Party in a minor role. Therefore, I wish Government Members would take another look at that because I believe we should be closer to the United States situation where the review committee is composed of elected officials.
The U.S. has a much more sophisticated CIA operation. There is a review body of elected officials, one from the Senate and another from the House of Representatives. Why is it that in Canada we distrust having elected officials as a review committee? The U.S. has no trouble with this and they certainly have no more leaks, I suppose, than other countries I believe the Minister should rethink this question.
The witnesses also felt that the Minister should be politically responsible for the CSIC on a day to day basis. That is why we got into this argument about "shall" as opposed to "may".
The Canadian Jewish Congress proposed very extensive amendments to Clause 6(1). For example, they say:
The Director, under the direction of the Minister, has the control and management of the Service and all matters connected therewith, but the Director shall comply with directions issued by the Minister under subsection (2) and shall keep the Minister fully informed of the operations of the Service.
They have five other subsections of amendments, none of which was accepted by the Minister. I wish he would stand in the House and tell us why he did not feel disposed to accept the amendments of the Canadian Jewish Congress. They come at the problem with a very special and particular interest. They, more than anyone else, have been oppressed by secret service agencies in other countries, whether it be South America or Eastern Europe. Therefore we felt that their evidence had much more weight than that of myself, say, as a civilian having been born and raised on the western plains. I never have been exposed to any form of oppression, other than by the Grits here in Ottawa responding to central Canada, I suppose. I wish the Minister would stand and tell us why he was not disposed to accept the evidence of the Canadian Jewish Congress on this clause.
We are under time allocation and I wonder if the Minister should not respond on these major clauses particularly.
We are not there yet. I will as soon as we are.
Will you respond on Clause 6? I felt the Canadian Jewish Congress had done a very good job. Those are the only comments I have with respect to Clause 6, Mr. Speaker.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this group of motions deals with Clauses 12, 13, 15 and 16. These are the clauses which effectively establish the mandate of the new security service to deal with the so-called threats to the security of Canada, which we know have been drafted far too broadly, the mandate to provide security assessments, and the new and unprecedented mandate under Clause 16 of this Bill, the so-called foreign intelligence mandate, which would permit the new service to target foreign visitors to Canada who have broken no law whatsoever and pose no threat whatsoever to the security of the country.
In the 10 minutes available to me I will attempt to explain briefly the purpose of each of these amendments. My colleagues will deal more specifically with the threatening and unprecedented powers which are contained in Clause 16 of this Bill, which powers have been severely criticized by many witnesses appearing before our committee.
Motion No. 30 would delete Clause 12 and Motions Nos. 31 and 32 would amend Clause 12, failing deletion. Clause 12 is the clause which gives the service the power to "collect, by investigation or otherwise, to the extent that it is strictly necessary, and analyze and retain information and intelligence respecting activities that may on reasonable grounds be suspected of constituting threats to the security of Canada".
The purpose of this series of motions with respect to Clause 12 of this Bill is to ensure two things. Motion No. 31 would ensure that the service would only retain information which it is strictly necessary, in the pursuit of its mandate, to retain. The present RCMP security service has open files on over 800,000 Canadians. They have some 1.3 million files. Under the wording of this Bill as it is presently construed, it would not be a requirement that unnecessarily open files be closed.

June 19, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
This amendment would achieve that. The amendment would include the following:
(2) It shall not be a function of the service to carry out measures to enforce security.
This deals with the question of so-called disruptive measures which were clearly documented by the McDonald Commission, the countering and disruption of lawful political groups. A clause of this nature was strongly recommended for inclusion by the McDonald Commission and is contained in comparable legislation in New Zealand and Australia. Disruption of political groups has been well documented not just here in Canada but in other jurisdictions as well. That is why those other jurisdictions have seen fit to include a clause of this nature. Yet the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan) denies that such a clause should be included in this legislation.
There are many examples of the abuses of countering and disruptive techniques both before and after 1974. These include the so-called preventive security interviews or briefings which can jeopardize the employment of individuals, relations with the press when members of the service plant material in the press about events or persons, misinformation and smear campaigns, disruptive measures which mislead other Government officials, the abuse of double agents and informants. As well there is the conspicuous surveillance and technique of intimidation which is an attempt to discredit individuals and members of particular groups.
These are types of disruptive measures that the Solicitor General assures us will not be conducted by the new agency. Yet when he is put to the test and it is suggested that a clause be included which would specifically bar such disruptive measures, a clause which is contained in comparable legislation elsewhere and which was recommended by the McDonald Commission, the Solicitor General says that he will not do it.
Many of the witnesses who appeared before the committee have a real fear that such disruptive measures may indeed be permitted under the Bill. Indeed, Professor Peter Russell, Research Director for the McDonald Commission, said in a letter:
I strongly endorse your effort to persuade the government to adopt recommendation 33 of the McDonald Commission calling for a clause in the legislation establishing the security intelligence agency which 'expressly denies the agency any authority to carry out measures to enforce security'.
The Government snubs its nose at that kind of very sensible recommendation.
Clause 13 would permit the Government to exchange information, to use a euphemism, with intelligence agencies of other countries, the existence of which is not even acknowledged by a number of those countries according to the Solicitor General. What kind of banana republics are we sharing our information with? The new security agency would continue to share information with them under the terms of this legislation.
The proposed amendments to Clause 15 would deny the use of any of the so-called intrusive techniques for security assessment. Specifically, it would deny the right to plant an informer or the right to use physical surveillance in conducting security assessments. According to this Bill as it now stands, individuals who are applying for a job with the Government could be targeted by the service for purposes not dealing with a threat to the security of Canada but to determine whether or not they get a security clearance. Again, consider the chilling impact that that has in a free and democratic society.
The final series of amendments in this grouping deal with proposed Clause 16. I wish that I had more time to set out clearly the implications of Clause 16 because this is a new power which is not contained within any agency in Canada at the present time. The security service does not have the power to engage in foreign intelligence activities. The Department of External Affairs does not have this power. The Department of National Defence does not have this power. Nowhere in Canada today does such a power exist. Yet the Solicitor General comes before Parliament and says that the Government wants the power to be able to target visitors to this country, anyone who is not a Canadian citizen or landed immigrant. Why? It is not because they may be a threat to the security of Canada since that is covered elsewhere in the Bill. It is because the information they have might prove helpful to Canada in obtaining information about external affairs or national defence. This means that no foreign visitor to this country is immune from the use of the most intrusive techniques at the hands of the security service. Their hotel room can be broken into. Their phone can be tapped. Their office be broken into and documents seized. Their income tax records can be examined as well as their medical records, not because they are a threat to our security but because they might have information which is helpful to us.
A visiting businessman, a visiting delegation of American Congressmen or a visiting professor who is an expert on eastern Europe matters could be targeted by this new service. When I suggested to a witness from the United States who is an expert on intelligence policy that these powers were proposed for Canada, she could not believe that in a democratic society such as Canada the Government was seriously claiming that it wanted these powers. If a government in the United States came before Congress seeking this kind of power, there would be a national uproar. Nowhere in the western world, including the United States, do such powers exist. In the United States it is only in the case of a foreign power or an agent operating on behalf of that power that certain intrusive techniques can be used.
This Bill would indicate to anyone visiting this country from outside that they are fair game and can be targeted. I suggest that the implications of that kind of proposal not just on the academic community but on our reputation abroad are devastating.
In conclusion, I would urge the adoption of these motions which would tighten the mandate of the new service. They are motions which would deny the right to send information to repressive dictatorships about Canadians or refugees from those countries. They are motions which would deny the use of
June 19, 1984

intrusive techniques for security assessments and they would effectively exclude form the mandate of the service this very dangerous, unprecedented power to collect foreign intelligence against individuals who pose no threat whatsoever to the security of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this is the set of motions that deals with the heart and core of the Bill, namely the duties and functions of the service. For that reason the Government must accept some amendments in this area. Surely, when the evidence of the witnesses is so clear, including that of the Canadian Bar Association, the Government would feel compelled to accept these amendments. However, I suppose I am blowing in the wind because the Government did not accept them at committee stage.
The duty of Members of Parliament is to take the Bill as reported back from the committee, study the recommendations and look at the proposals and report stage amendments so as to form an opinion and make suggestions to the Minister. I urge my colleagues opposite to look at the proposed amendments to Clause 12 because they are reasonable.
Clause 12 states: "The Service shall collect, by investigation or otherwise. . What do those words "or otherwise" mean? We discovered from the evidence that they mean that the service can do virtually anything. It will be able to do to citizens of this country far more than the FBI can do in the United States, which is a world power and a world source of technology and inventiveness. There are far more spies in that country pursuing their industrial secrets and military secrets. Yet the FBI in that country will not have the intrusive powers that the Canadian Liberal Cabinet will foist and impose upon the citizens of Canada. There should be people rioting in the streets over the incredible power Cabinet is seeking to impose on them. It is simply wrong. I am not sure why we are so complacent. So many of our people seem to have this incredible trust in the Government. Clearly on the evidence it is not warranted.
When you look, Mr. Speaker, at the powers governments have taken in this country in the last ten or 15 years, what do you find? You find the imposition of Crown corporations to an incredible extent, taxes that are extracted directly through the income tax system, sales taxes and energy taxes, and then taxes indirectly on the people by way of the deficit and inflation. To my mind Canadians should be marching in the streets.
It all comes back to Clause 12 of this Bill which was agreed to by the Liberal Cabinet without adequate review by the Government's own back-benchers. If a Cabinet of which I was a back-bencher put some of these clauses in the Bill, I would be standing in this House pursuant to the mandate that I received from my constituents and I would say: "No way, I am going to vote against you. I do not care if you are the Cabinet. You are responsible to the House. As a back-bencher on the Government side, I have a duty to hold you accountable. If you do not, then I will vote against you and if it brings on an
Security Intelligence Service
election, so be it." I honestly believe that many of the Government Members on the back-benches are not performing their duty. I know if they sat with their uncles and aunts and went through this Bill, their uncles and aunts and other relatives would be saying to them: "That is too much power in the hands of a Cabinet. It is too much power in the hands of a director. You, as my Member of Parliament, should be diluting it."
Clause 12 reads:
The Service shall collect, by investigation or otherwise, to the extent that it is strictly necessary-
At that point our Motion No. 32 puts forth an amendment suggested by the Canadian Bar Association. The Canadian Bar Association consists of men and women who looked at Bill C-157, made their submission to the Senate committee and had some of their recommendations accepted. They then looked at Bill C-9 and again throughout the process consulted lawyers across the nation who deal with this matter daily. They came up with the proposed amendment which would have Clause 12 read, after the word "necessary":
-for the purpose of protecting the security of Canada, and analyse and retain.
Those words, Mr. Speaker, are a real check on the abuse of power by the service. Yet the Liberal Cabinet has rejected the suggested amendment by the Canadian Bar Association. This clause goes on to read:
-and analyse and retain information and intelligence respecting activities that may on reasonable grounds be suspected of constituting threats to the security of Canada-
We put forth the amendment at committee stage and it was rejected. We wanted the words "and probable" added. Within our common law jurisdiction we have jurisprudence built up around the words "reasonable and probable". They are in the Criminal Code. Lawyers have been using these words and judges have been making decisions on these words for hundreds of years throughout the common law tradition. The Government tells us that the words "reasonable and probable" are exactly the same as the individual word "reasonable". That is not so, Mr. Speaker. When judges look at a case, if the test is reasonable and probable grounds, that means something. If a new section says "reasonable grounds", that means the standard has been lowered and therefore people can be scrutinized for a much lower position by the Director and his agents than if the words were "reasonable and probable grounds". The Government itself should at least be maintaining the standards set under the Criminal Code of reasonable and probable grounds with which we have all lived for many hundreds of years.
Do you think that we could get the Liberals to accept this amendment, Mr. Speaker? No, because they got a statement from some lawyer, one of the 600 they canvassed in the department. Finally one gave them an opinion that "reasonable" was exactly the same as "reasonable and probable". All of us with common sense, let alone those who have some legal training, know that if instead of the words "reasonable and probable", which have been interpreted, as a conscious act of

June 19, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
Parliament, a new clause uses only the word "reasonable", it is a much lower test.
What are the consequences of a lower standard? Our citizens can be investigated using such means as opening first-class mail, entering cars and houses, installing bugs in cars and houses and intercepting communications with lawyers. This can be done even though in common law there is a solicitor-client privilege, which is not the privilege of the lawyer but the privilege of the client to be able to deal with a lawyer in confidence. Indeed, lawyers' offices can be broken into at night and documents removed without leaving copies. Agents can destroy a man. It is the same as when the President of the United States destroyed good people who were innocent by turning the IRS on them. That situation could happen here.
Suppose you went to your doctor, Sir, to have a test for some condition that you want kept confidential for business or personal reasons or whatever. Agents can go into your doctor's office, take documents away and use them against you. That is not the tradition of this country.
That is not what our ancestors came here for. They came here to get away from that kind of conduct, for God's sake! But here we have a Liberal Cabinet making that a real possibility. I just do not understand why each generation continually has to refight the battles of 1215 and 1776 to try and get freedom. Let me come to the entrenchment of constitutional rights. In spite of the fact that our ancestors fought and died for the right to own property, the Liberal Government would not entrench that as a right, and that issue the NDP has to take some heat. Members of the NDP are not standing up for the rights of people to own property. They are just as glad that they do not.
What about the Premiers? Of course, they are Tory Premiers.

We understand, but this is the Parliament that sets those rights. If the provincial Premiers of whatever political stripe are opposed, we should be standing up and saying that we speak for the people. We know that some of our people come from Eastern European countries. As I said yesterday, I have sat around the kitchen table with many Eastern Europeans, people with marks and tattoos on their arms. They tell me this Bill is dangerous, and I believe them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say something about a piece of legislation that strikes me as nothing short of treasonous. Regarding the duties and functions of this service, Canadians from coast to coast must wonder why not one single Liberal has stood up to support it. Not one single Liberal who is actually representing his or her constituents has got up even to make a comment on one of the most draconian unCanadian, treasonous pieces of legislation that has ever come before this House. As far as I am aware, it is endorsed only by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), who as I have said before will not be the Solicitor General for very long.
Let me deal quickly with Clauses Nos. 12, 13, 14 and 15. With only ten minutes I want to spend some time on Clause 16 and on why that particularly draconian measure should never see the light of day outside this Parliament.
Before I do that, I want to add to the words of other Members in this House today. It is peculiar that the press have somehow been muzzled in this country on a Bill that portends to change the face and nature of Canada totally in terms of freedoms which many of our forefathers fought very hard to gain. It seems very few Members of Parliament are prepared to stand up and fight for that today. I can say only one thing, Mr. Speaker. This Parliament is dying as a result of the way this kind of legislation is going through where no one on the Government side gets up to defend a piece of legislation. The Opposition are always in a position of having to educate themselves on every piece of legislation and of getting up and fighting to try and change legislation. We have an occasional loudmouth on the other side. They never have the guts to rise and say that they stand for these particular clauses and why they stand for them. Not even the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has the gumption to stand and explain why he supports a piece of legislation which is clearly treasonous in terms of Canadian history.
The duties and functions of the service in terms of collection, analysis and retention are improperly worded. The clause is far too broad. Clause 13 in terms of security assessments is far too broad. I would encourage Canadians, who have some interest in what is about to happen to their rights now that closure has been invoked and this legislation is to be jammed through, to take some time to read this. Only those who are watching television or listening to this debate on the radio will learn about it, because the press has never bothered to come in here to cover any of the ongoing debate. The press does not even understand that if it starts writing articles opposed to this sitting Government or to some Minister, it, above and beyond all others-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I hesitate to interrupt my hon. friend who is talking about the press not being here. The Canadian public should know that there is not a single member of the Press Gallery, numbering several hundred persons, in the Chamber at this time. Probably none of its members are watching this debate.

speechtext: Obviously that is a contribution to the debate. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) should continue his remarks.

Mr. Speaker, that was an important and timely point of order. As I said, I will focus my comments on Clause 16. With only 10 minutes left and with closure having been invoked, it is not possible for me to cover Clauses 12, 13 and 15. I do not think many Canadians recognize what we are
June 19, 1984

being asked to give up. We are gaining nothing with this guts part of the legislation that relates directly to spying techniques. Not only will it affect Canadians but, as my colleagues have pointed out, it will affect those tens of millions of foreigners who come to Canada every year. Very few Canadians realize that about 30 million Americans per year come to Canada and that there are literally tens of millions of others who travel through Canada either for the purpose of visiting relatives or for the purpose of carrying on some kind of business.
I should like to focus upon the wording of Clause 16. Very specifically it reads:
Subject to this section, the Service may, in relation to the defence of Canada or the conduct of the international affairs of Canada, assist the Minister of National Defence or the Secretary of State for External Affairs, within Canada, in the collection of information or intelligence relating to the capabilities, intentions or activities of
(a)	any foreign state or group of foreign states; or
(b)	any person other than
(i)	a Canadian citizen,
(ii)	a permanent resident within the meaning of the Immigration Act, 1976, or
(iii)	a corporation incorporated by or under an Act of Parliament or of the legislature of a province.
What is being proposed here is to allow spying, not only in relation to defence. At the very least this clause should be broken into two parts to remove the distortion so that those who would quickly read it will not think that it is only for the defence of Canada. This was designed by the Solicitor General. I suppose the Liberals opposite know that. I am no longer so sure because none of them will rise and speak. This is clearly intended to be a very broad-ranging power to allow spying on anyone who comes into Canada, whether they are coming here to visit a relative, for commercial purposes or for teaching.
I should like to deal very quickly with the teaching aspect. The Canadian Association of University Teachers made a very excellent presentation to the committee, which was scoffed at by Liberal Members. It was supported very broadly by those associated with universities and colleges in Canada. Referring to Clause 16, Mr. Donald Savage of CAUT wrote:
We find this section ... seems to say, for instance in he university context, that two Ministers of the Crown can sign a document which will allow the security forces to collect intelligence relating to the capabilities, intentions or activities of any visiting foreign professor or any foreign student at a Canadian university. It does not require that this be triggered by reasonable suspicions of involvement in terrorism, espionage or subversion. It need only be done pursuant to the conduct of international affairs of Canada. Nor does this section indicate how this intelligence will be gathered, but I assume that it would allow telephone tapping, mail opening and any other similar means to gather the information.
It is true that the section then goes on to say that such information will not be directed at Canadian citizens, permanent residents or corporations. However, no safeguards are provided for the foreign visitor. If our interpretation is correct, ... I suspect that some foreign academics may well have qualms about coming to our country as visiting professors if they can be subjected to intelligence operations in the casual manner suggested in section 16. We in Canada wish, of course, to have programs concerning other parts of the world of the highest possible quality. This necessarily involves invitations to distinguished foreign academics to come as visiting professors. By the nature of things, internationally respected foreign area programs must be able to attract such scholars.
Security Intelligence Service
We are not, of course, suggesting that such visiting scholars be immune from security legislation. They should be subject to investigation on charges of terrorism, espionage or subversion in exactly the same manner as other Canadians.
As I indicated, it was signed by Mr. Savage, Executive Secretary of CAUT. His suspicions and those of academics in Canada are absolutely correct. As a result of the desire of the Solicitor General to be able to spy on anyone anywhere at any time, to bug their telephones, to break into their homes, to break into their cars or do whatever he pleases, ultimately it comes down to base, crass politics. Certain people who are so taken by their own power demand that they be protected from any kind of forces of change. The ultimate reactionary conservative sits there as the present Solicitor General.
As I said several times in my speech, I consider these sections to be acts of treason against the people of Canada, nothing short of that. It changes what my family came here for 300 years ago and what they fought for in every war since then. That man and that Party intend to take it away. The press sits on its hands absolutely mute. Its members are sitting across the street drinking beer and drooling in their own froth. They do not have the guts to write a single editorial in the country to cover any of the debate here or to give the kind of round, sound condemnation which there should be of the Liberals over there. Those people are not fit to govern this country. In fact, they are not fit to live in this country. They should not be sitting in the House of Commons if they are not prepared to rise and tell us why they want these kinds of powers which can be put against anyone who comes into the country and which can be put against any foreign state. The Solicitor General should rise and explain. He should get one of jackals on his back-benches, who are only interested in their pay cheques and their pensions, to rise on this one piece of legislation and for once in the history of the country explain why they intend to take away all the rights for which I, my family and my forefathers have fought. I say that it is an act of treason and he should not be in this House of Commons.
And people call us arrogant!
