-with great respect I say he is wrong. The Hon. Member for Skeena is saying exactly what I said a couple of hours ago in this Chamber. The fact is that the media of the country are asleep at the switch on this Bill. They do not want to be told that. There is only one member of the several hundred person Press Gallery of Canada in the Press Gallery right now.
A couple of days ago this Bill was called by Alan Borovoy, general counsel to the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, hardly a left-wing twit or some kind of screwball nitwit, "one of the greatest threats to civil liberties Canada has seen for many years". That got reported; Lord knows how, but it got reported. The Hon. Member for Skeena is not in the same Party as I am, but he talked about his ancestors fighting for the liberties we have had for over 300 years. So did mine. We came here in 1759 with the Scottish Regiment that was forced to enlist because we were pushed out of our Highland home. All those years we were loyal to the flag and to the Crown of this country. My friend from Skeena is right when he talks about the traditions that are bound up in the principles of this Bill. I am fed up to the teeth with this limp-wristed, handwringing, sanctimonious lecturing and preaching we have been getting from the Government side and some kind of vacuous minded editorial writers.
What is all this talk about Bill C-9 being debated endlessly? They go back to the Mackenzie Commission in 1969, the 1977 revelation of wrongdoing in the late sixties and early seventies, the McDonald Commission, Bill C-157 and the Senate committee. They say it has all been settled.
Where are these twits who say it has all been settled? Who are these people who comment like that, who cannot understand that, under our system of government, when you pass a piece of legislation the words rule you? It is the words in front of us now in Bill C-9, not in Bill C-157, the McDonald report or the Mackenzie report. It is these words that rule us. When somebody like Alan Borovoy can say that this Bill is the greatest threat to civil liberties this country has ever seen, somebody in the country should know about it.
I am fed up with the fact that all the reporting has been about a filibuster in the committee or in the House. What is wrong that these people cannot understand why we are indignant? I will tell you why. This Bill could have been and should have been a better Bill. The Government absolutely refused to accept a single amendment. The only amendment we got through committee, which would give to the review committee the right to look at Cabinet documents relating to the security service, went through because the Chairman of the committee, a Liberal, the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), a damn good Member, voted with the Opposition. We got it through, and what does the Solicitor General do? He has an amendment, that he is going to present, wiping out the only thing we got in committee. That is what they are doing.
The media of this country, the several hundred people who sit around here and criticize us for the price of food in the
restaurant or the cost of the rug or MPs who did not pay their bills on time, all go to the restaurant. That is probably where half of them are right now instead of being here. I do not care whether every one of them campaigns against me in the next election. In the last couple of days on this issue the media have been a disgrace to a free country. As I said earlier, one day they will be writing editorials when something goes wrong because the proper amendments were not put in. It is absolutely appalling. I do not know how many deans of journalism there are, but this ought to be compulsory reading for every one of their students from now on. The media have absolutely copped out on this. I do not care whether they like me for saying it. The fact is that the Canadian public does not realize that the only time these guys and women come in here is during Question Period when you have the show. The rest of the time they do not cover this stuff. It is no good their coming now and saying "Well, we covered it months ago, we wrote some in-depth articles some months ago".
The issue is the fact that Canadians came to committee with suggestions for change, not suggestions to destroy the Bill, not suggestions to destroy the security service, not suggestions saying that we should not have lawful mandates that constrain, regulate and overview the security service. Canadians said the wording is faulty, it can be better. There are dangers in the loose wording that is there and in some of the concepts. What is appalling is that since the day we got into second reading debate, months ago, the Government has had no intention of accepting any amendments, nothing. That is what should be in the headlines of every paper.
As for John Turner and his reform Liberals, as I said earlier, it is not the old deal but it is the old deal writ large. I have to say one other thing about Mr. Turner, who is supposed to be a lawyer. This is the guy who has never told us why he brought in the War Measures Act. Once upon a time when I was 20 and Mr. Turner was in his mid-fifties I would have been impressed, but I am not anymore. I say in conclusion, knowing that nothing has changed, that everybody ought to be asked: Do you really want to buy a used government from this fellow?

Mr. Speaker, I am amazed by the remarks that were just made by the Minister. It was just yesterday that the Minister and his Government moved closure.

The Minister does not rise, not because he does not want to prolong the debate. He knows that the debate will end. The Minister does not rise because he knows that the

Let me read a portion of a letter which was received by the Chairman of the Standing Committee from the President of the Canadian Association of Slavists, Nicholas Zekulin. The letter reads in part:
We are, of course, aware that not all the activities of all visiting academics, professors or students, are legitimate, but this does not mean that some safeguards should not be built into the legislation specifying that there should be grounds for suspicion of activity inimical to Canada before the provisions of the act are invoked.
That seems to me to be a very reasonable proposal. As well, I have in my possession a letter addressed to the Chairman of the committee from Dr. Peter Bly, Professor of Spanish and President of the Canadian Association of Hispanists. He has written the following:
Obviously, we could not countenance the activities of foreign professors and students detrimental to Canada's security and would publicly support all attempts to prohibit the entry into Canada of such undesirable people. But we feel that indiscriminate surveillance and monitoring of bona fide visitors will adversely affect our attempts to establish links with Spanish-speaking academics as well as being a gross injustice to these individuals in question.
Those are just two of the many letters which I am sure were received by the Government. We are, as we should be, encouraging professors in Canadian universities who wish to learn more and wish to be able to teach their students more about countries in South America, in Africa, in China, in Eastern Europe and elsewhere. If they are to learn more, there must be an exchange of academics. Our professors must visit those countries and their professors must visit Canada.
Let us be realistic. Professors in communist countries are, in all likelihood, members and supporters of those regimes. Otherwise, they could not be professors. We know that when we invite them and when we permit them to come to Canada.
June 19, 1984

We should certainly be able to assure them that, as long as they are here for legitimate academic reasons and are not involved in espionage or any other aspect which is inimical to our security, they will not be spied upon, have their mail opened or their telephones wiretapped. We would expect the same kind of treatment for our professors who visit those countries.
I would urge the Minister, or any Member of the Liberal Party who is in the House, to rise and explain how this proposal, which will affect university professors and their organizations, could be viewed as being impractical. Why did the Government not accept that proposal? I would say that there is a very simple reason. The Minister has forgotten the things he knew before he took his present appointment. The Minister has sloughed off all the principles in which he supposedly believed. He is ignoring the advice and urging he receives from the people he has worked with over the years. He has become a complete captive of his bureaucracy and has caved in to it. That is why he has taken this view.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with a number of clauses in the Bill. But I would first like to refer to a problem with Clause 12, which I think is typical of a great many other areas in the Bill, that is, the very poor English in which it is written. The language could be misinterpreted. If and when this legislation goes before the courts, it is the wording that will decide justice. It is not the way someone else interprets it. It is not the way it is discussed in the House of Commons. It is the way in which it is written in the law that will decide justice. It will decide whether we have justice, or whether we have an unfair type of law.
For example, in Clause 12 a sentence appears which reads as follows:
The Service shall collect, by investigation or otherwise,
The first thing I would like to know is: What does "otherwise" mean? Does it mean the bugging of cars, the bugging of telephones or the bugging of the telephone of a person from another country? What does "otherwise" mean? It is like saying et cetera, et cetera. It can mean everything and anything. That is the first thing which I object to in the Bill. I would like to know what the service can collect by investigation and by what other means. "Investigation" is a pretty big word. It pretty well covers the slate.
The Government added the words "or otherwise". Therefore, it can collect in formation by investigation or it can do so "otherwise". The words are not "and/or"; the words are "or otherwise". Therefore, if the service cannot do it by investigation, it can do it "otherwise", whatever that is.
I have not heard anyone explain that. It is a matter to which I take objection. If this legislation is sound, why are the Members on the other side of the House not taking their proper turn in defending the legislation?

Because we want to vote on it, that is why.

Because you want to vote on it. You want to get it through before people even know what it means. That is what the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) says.
Before the session ends.

He wants to vote on it. He does not care what it means. He does not care how it will treat human souls, not a bit. He wants to vote on it. This Party wants to do more than vote on it. When we vote on it, we want to know what it means. We want to be able to explain to our constituents what the legislation means. But the Government is not giving us that explanation. The back-benchers sit there like a bunch of clones-pardon the expression. They are simply going to accept anything that the Minister puts into the legislation.
I ask Hon. Members on the other side: What does "otherwise" mean? Instead of standing up and giving us a lecture, as the Solicitor General did a few moments ago, why does he not explain the legislation? That is all we are asking. A simple explanation. It is like a teacher who says to a class: "You are doing it wrong. You are doing it wrong". That does not help the youngsters. They will not learn anything. The pedagogue who knows what he is doing will mark it on the board to show why it was wrong in order that the youngsters will not make the same mistake again. That is pedagogy, not dictatorship.
I would like to make a further comment about Clause 12, which reads:
The Service shall collect, by investigation or otherwise, to the extent that it is strictly necessary,
What is strictly necessary, "the investigation" or "otherwise"? to what does it refer? It is simple English. If the youngsters, who are sitting in the Gallery today, were asked to analyse that, they would tell us that it could not be properly analysed. We do not know to what the "it" refers. "The Service shall collect, by investigation or otherwise, to the extent that it is strictly necessary". "It", what in the world is that?
No wonder the committee is befuddled. No wonder an amendment was put forward in an attempt to have that wording changed. The committee proposed that the service's collection of information and intelligence should be limited to what is "strictly necessary for the purpose of protecting the security of Canada". That is what it should say. We are talking about the security of Canada, but the legislation does not indicate that. It says "it". Whatever is that supposed to mean?
The vote on that amendment in committee was: four in favour and five against, with the Chairman not voting with the Government. The Chairman said:
The chairman regrets that the government could not see fit to accept that amendment.
Is that not strange? The committee voted four in favour and five against. The Chairman is a member of the Liberal Party and I believe a lawyer, but I am not sure. I know he is well learned. He said that!

June 19, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
Is it not a simple amendment which attempts to clarify the law? Is that not why we are here, to clarify the law in order to be fair to those people who are charged under the law? All we are asking for is a simple clarification.
That Clause is enlarged by adding words which cannot be defined-"otherwise" and "it". That is supposed to be drafts-menship? Whoever drafted this should enlist the help of a few good school teachers. They could do better.
It was the Senate committee.

It should read, "for purposes which are strictly necessary, and "for purposes of protecting the security of Canada". That is the proper enlargement of that phrase-not "it" and not "otherwise". We are talking about the protection of the security of Canada.
It is too bad, Mr. Speaker, that for some reason we are not hearing from Hon. Members opposite. I do not know whether the new Leader has told the Liberal Members not to talk. Perhaps he has put a zipper on their lips. Perhaps he feels the legislation is so bad he does not want them to talk about it, and now he is going to bring in closure so that even we cannot talk about it. As the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) said, the press just looks at the Bill and does not even bother dealing with the inequities, the poor draftsmanship and what this will mean to the security of human lives later on. That is all we are asking the Hon. Members opposite to do, to think about what this is going to do perhaps to their sons, daughters or grandchildren. Imagine what the courts will do because of the way this legislation is worded and then you might be willing to accept an amendment which is sensible and sound.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was inspired by the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) who has a reputation in this House for telling it as it is. He speaks because he consults. He speaks because he represents his constituents with great distinction and because he is prepared to listen to what people are saying on the streets of this country. I commend that attitude to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and to Hon. Members of the Liberal Party, because what we are dealing with now in this particular clause and the motion which has been put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), is a provision which would put some precision into the definition of the operations of the new security service.
What we have now is a very wide-ranging and vague mandate for this new security service. What we have now under the terms of Clause 12 is authority given to the service to go about this country and collect information on Canadian citizens, community groups, church groups, action committees and political groups as the service deems necessary.
I have never seen a better recipe than what is contained in this legislation, put into statute form, which would provide any
secret service agency with the ability to conduct witch-hunts, politically motivated investigations, and wide ranging irresponsible investigations into the affairs of the people of our country. What our Party has been trying to impress upon the Government is that when one deals with legislation of this sort, which in effect impacts negatively on the civil liberties of Canadians, and for purposes of security allows an agency to go about opening up files on Canadian citizens, to investigate their backgrounds, their social, business and other activities, which gives authority to this group to look at our income tax returns, which allows this service to go into our medical records, then one must say to oneself, "What about Canada which I always understood to be a country where freedoms and privacy are respected?"
So we said to the Solicitor General in committee that we think there should be some more precision in the wording of this Act, that the people of Canada would expect no less in a free and democratic society. We told him that if he is going to bring in legislation which is going to allow an agency of the Government to snoop into our affairs, there should be a very precise definition of those powers. I do not believe that is an unreasonable request to make of any government. I am not trying to be troublesome or controversial. I am simply saying to the Government, "Let us have common sense in this. Let us make sure there is a balance in the wording of this legislation". And that is what happened in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, how delicate the situation was. People did vote on Party lines, so the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver South, was defeated in the committee five votes to four. That was because the Liberals had the majority in the committee. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River, pointed out, the Chairman of the committee-who will admit it himself-is a partisan Liberal who sits on the Liberal benches. He was appointed by the Government and owes his position to government support. But I say to you, he has some common sense and some sensitivity with respect to matters of this import and has demonstrated himself to be a fair and competent chairman, and he has my respect. He was not required to break the tie. He was not required to cast the deciding vote because, I suppose, in that instance, the tradition required that he vote for the government position. However, he made what I consider a telling statement in committee. He said that he regretted that the Government did not see fit to accept this sensible amendment.
The amendment is exactly as was stated by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver South. It gives precision to the provision. It does not say that the agency shall not have the ability to obtain information by these various devices it deems necessary in its own discretion and opinion. We just suggested that there be some tangible criteria established within this Bill and within this clause under which it would be possible for an aggrieved citizen to go to a court of this land and say, "This is not within its mandate because it cannot establish that the investigation was in the interests of the security of Canada". It
June 19, 1984

is a very simple definition of what the parameters should be in this clause.
We have been bringing forward suggestions, and it is an example of the intransigence and the blockheadedness, if you will, of the Government and of the Solicitor General in particular, that he will not accept any reasonable amendment. The Solicitor General is the captive of his bureaucracy, but he is not capable of making a decision on his own without advice from his bureaucracy. It has told him not to put too many constraints on the service, not to give it too many difficulties so that it will have to be accountable. For heaven's sake, that would make it difficult for the service. It would have to work for a living. I am not alone, Mr. Speaker. I will tell you who else thought that this motion was required-
We are with you.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Over here we have quality as opposed to quantity, and I say to the House Leader of the New Democratic Party that I appreciate the fact that that Party is always willing to learn. I am trying to help the NDP-
When we come to vote on your motion, we will rise with you.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I know you will be with us. However, do not make it public, because every time you vote with us it causes me great political embarrassment back home.
What I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, is that the people who are in support of this kind of amendment are responsible citizens of Canada. They include the British Columbia Law Union, the Canadian Bar Association-not exactly a revolutionary crowd-the Attorney General of Saskatchewan and the Attorney General of Ontario. These people are involved in law enforcement and legal matters in their own jurisdictions. The Canadian Bar Association represents the legal profession across the country. Indeed, I believe I can go back to the Senate committee which looked at this matter. It indicated that it would like more precise language with respect to the mandate of this agency. All of these groups and the individuals whom I have mentioned have been supportive of the amendment, which our Party supports and which has been presented by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, you must ask yourself a question: What is so wrong with this proposal? Why is the Government so adamant in its refusal to accept as an amendment an eminently sensible recommendation? Is there not someone over on the government side who can stand up and give a rationale? Let it be just one Member, I do not care who. I would even accept the Solicitor General standing up and telling us why he thinks he cannot accept our proposal. But all we get is silence. It does not augur well for Parliament when Members on the government side refuse to defend their own legislation. Let us assume the agency got out of control; what would happen? We would have a repeat of what happened in early 1970. There would not be one person on the Liberal side with the courage to stand in his or her place and say that the legal processes of Canada are being abused. They are used to silence, to standing
Security Intelligence Service
by like patsies and to doing what they are told. If that is the kind of government we are going to have under the Liberals, you can well imagine how the people of Canada will respond. They will see the cavalier and cynical attitude taken by government Members who do not have the courage of their convictions. They will not stand up and tell us why they refuse to accept the amendment.
They are training for the secret service.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Secret service is right. It should be called the "secret (silent) service". That is the way these people are operating with respect to this legislation. They do not have the courage of their convictions and they do not deserve to be on the Government side.

Mr. Speaker, it was my privilege to serve under the chairmanship of the Hon. Member who just spoke on the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. A more fair, adept and appropriate chairman I do not think anyone could ask for. The Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) talked about why we do not support this amendment, or why the Minister would not listen to the amendments. The facts are of course exactly opposite. Before Bill C-157 was brought in, the McDonald Commission held over 300 hearings, saw 150 witnesses and read 124 written submissions. Then Bill C-157 went before the Senate committee. It heard testimony from over 30 individuals and groups and over 50 submissions. A significant number of changes were made to that Bill. Ultimately it resulted in Bill C-9. Therefore, to suggest that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is not prepared to listen to amendments is just not in accordance with the facts.
The problem we have is that we have another amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). We have been subjected to a farce. For example, at the very last minute we had presented to us in committee something like 300 amendments of the kind being produced here today. The attitude is: If we cannot have it our way, we are not going to play. We are not going to help with legislation and we are not going to have debate.

Unfortunately, as a result of the tactics adopted by the NDP-

There are merits in many of the amendments put forward both by the Government and by Opposition Members. This one is probably a good case in point. On its face it appears to be not a bad amendment. But those of us who sat on the committee know that every one of the amendments put forward here was put forward at committee stage. They were answered by the Solicitor General and all the reasons were given why this amendment or others are not appropriate at this time. Sadly, when we get a decent amendment, one that has been carefully thought out, such as this particular one put forward by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), one feels hamstrung because, by endeavouring to bring the parliamentary process to bear, ond finds that one is participating in a farce orchestrated by the NDP, primarily by the Hon. subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF WESTERN BEAN CROP UNDER AGRICULTURAL STABILIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of great concern to western Canadian coloured bean growers. In the gallery today we are pleased to have the presence of a delegation from the Western Canadian Pulse Growers Association. They are here in the capital to meet with representatives of Agriculture Canada and the Agricultural Stabilization Board.
For the past three years these bean growers have been trying to get their crops recognized as designated crops under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Their request for 1981 was basically refused, and they are still trying to receive a reply to their application for 1982. So far they have only seen and experienced the revolving door. This matter is made more serious by the fact that white bean growers in the Minister's own riding had their white bean crops designated under the Stabilization Act, to the tune of some $22 million for the 1982-83 crops.
June 19, 1984

In a communication which I received from the Minister, he stated "that the need for assistance will be evaluated in light of other government economic priorities at the time". Clearly the western farmers' plight should be an economic priority of the Government. Or is the plight of white bean growers a priority while that of the coloured bean growers is not? I thought we had an entrenched Charter to handle this type of thing. This type of discrimination is clearly not conducive to national unity, nor in accordance with the way Canadians expect to be treated by their elected representatives.
The plight of western Canadian coloured bean growers is critical. They are faced with depressed prices for their commodities due to a lack of demand, caused by over-production in the U.S. along with the inability of Third World markets to import because of the high U.S. dollar.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO EXTENSION TO PRISON INMATES

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: OPPOSITION TO EXTENSION TO PRISON INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have received communications in my office objecting to the introduction of legislation that would give prisoners the right to vote in elections. In my view, extending this right is utterly ridiculous and the proposal should be nipped in the bud immediately.
We continuously give more and more rights to inmates, while doing very little to help victims of crime. Often these victims go through a great deal of suffering and pain, and are sometimes handicapped for the rest of their lives. Meanwhile the criminal does his time in an institution where he, in many cases, he has access to excellent sport facilities and eats better food than some Canadians living on the outside.
And now some are suggesting that the right to vote should be extended to these offenders, to murderers, thieves, rapists, and defrauders, to name just a few. Instead of giving the voting right to inmates, we should be improving the rights of victims. Such legislation has been before the House since February 7, and I urge all Hon. Members to work towards its passage and not to pursue legislation giving prison inmates the right to vote in elections. To extend this right would be adding insult to injury. These people are not confined for a paid holiday. They are confined because they broke Canadian laws, and therefore forfeit the privilege of voting.

Mr. Speaker, I draw to the attention of the House the plight of the subcommittee on acid rain. The subcommittee of which I am, or was, a member, fulfilled its mandate as prescribed by Parliament earlier this month with the tabling of its report. There are presently no provisions to reconstitute this valuable subcommittee. I fear it will fade into a polluted sunset when it is most needed.
Members of every political stripes sitting on the committee agreed that working on the problems of acid rain gave them as much, or more, satisfaction as anything they have done since becoming Members of Parliament. So long as the serious problems of acid rain persist, should the subcommittee not persist in finding solutions to this, Canada's worst environmental blight?
Our report is now in the hands of the Minister of the Environment. Sixteen recommendations appear in the report. Only a subcommittee composed of all Parties represented in this House can monitor the results of those recommendations. Should the subcommittee be dissolved, no single Member will have the clout required to urge the Minister to follow the recommendations. After all the miles travelled, and thousands of hours spent on research, it would be a moral crime to deprive Canada of the follow-through needed to stop acid rain.

subtopic: LIBERAL PARTY LEADER-POSITION ON YOUTH JOB-CREATION MEASURES
LIBERAL PARTY LEADER-POSITION ON YOUTH JOB-CREATION MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was a breath of fresh air to listen to John Turner on Saturday night talk about the relevant employment issues in the country when he spoke about young people being given an opportunity to compete for government sponsored jobs. I know, the Canadian people know, and John Turner knows what the Opposition Members do not know, and what they should know.
I pointed out on three occasions in this Chamber since January that young people, new and re-entrants into the workforce, were placed in the lowest of four categories for referral to job-creation projects started by agreements with provincial Governments. I pointed that out, and asked opposition Members to intercede. Not one of them followed through to bring about a change. It is unfortunate that government backbenchers and John Turner have to do the job of the Official Opposition in the House. John Turner will be the turning point in the fortunes of these young people.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF FOREST INDUSTRY TO ECONOMY
IMPORTANCE OF FOREST INDUSTRY TO ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, across Canada our forest industry is in crisis. More than 300 Canadian communities depend on our number one industry to provide jobs. Municipal, provincial, and federal

June 19, 1984
Governments all look to the forest industry for tax revenue. However, the Liberal Party, like the Liberal Government, is blind to this industry. In the formal nomination speeches last Friday, of the seven candidates for the Liberal leadership, only one made any explicit reference to the forest industry. Who was that? You guessed it, Mr. Speaker. The candidate who mentioned forestry in his speech was the one who came in last with 83 votes, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). We would have hoped that at least John Turner, with his corporate involvement in MacMillan-Bloedel and Canadian Pacific, would have known how important the forest industry is to the Canadian economy.
Hundreds of forestry workers have been laid off by both MacMillan-Bloedel and Pacific Forest Products. Considering this crisis, Mr. Turner should appoint a full-time Minister of Forests to ensure that our number one industry receives proper attention. Apparently the new Liberal leader, like the old one, sees neither federal opportunity nor responsibility in forestry. Mr. Turner cannot see the forest for the balance sheet.

subtopic: LIBERAL PARTY LEADER-STATEMENTS ON PEACE ISSUE
LIBERAL PARTY LEADER-STATEMENTS ON PEACE ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence this morning the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) stated that he was saddened that not one Liberal Member running for the Liberal leadership mentioned anything about peace and security. Such a statement cannot go unchallenged. I would like to remind the Hon. Member for Simcoe South, and all Hon. Members in the Official Opposition, that all seven candidates stressed the importance of pressing for the international peace initiative begun by the Prime Minister.
The future Prime Minister emphasized that he will put his energies towards issues related to international peace and security, with emphasis on defence, arms control, disarmament, and conflict resolution. In Toronto on April 24 the future Prime Minister said:
1 will follow in the footsteps of our last three leaders in the search of peace and international stability. I will seek ways to take advantage of the momentum generated by the initiatives of Prime Minister Trudeau-ways to give it a new thrust.
On the CBC program The Journal in March of 1984 the future Prime Minister said:
Peace is a concern to all of us. The old fears of war have been replaced by an even greater fear-fear for the survival of the human race. The devastation of modern weaponry defies the most fertile of imaginations.

ATLANTIC OFFSHORE DEVELOPMENT-POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to inform the House of the Atlantic Offshore Energy Accord, the bold initiative that our Party has taken which will encourage the timely development of East Coast resources for the benefit of the region and for all of Canada. An important component of our approach is the promotion of a positive and constructive climate of co-operation between the national Government and the provinces.
When Atlantic Premiers sit down with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) to negotiate, they will get a new deal, a fairer deal, and a better deal than that put forward by the Liberals in Ottawa. The agreement in principle between the Leader of the Opposition and Brian Peckford, the Premier of Newfoundland, proposes that a province will be the principal beneficiary of its oil and gas resources. Newfoundland will be a full partner in its own economic development and the management of its reserves.
A joint agency, consisting of three provincial and three federal appointees and a neutral chairperson, would manage the offshore. The province would have the ultimate decision in matters affecting the manner of development, as long as the attainment of self-sufficiency is not delayed. The federal Government will possess paramountcy if energy security is threatened.
Importantly, a province will be entitled to establish and collect resource revenues as if those resources were on land. There will be no discrimination with inshore provinces. Through a series of special offset payments, equalization payments will be protected for a generation.
The proposals of a Progressive Conservative administration outlined here are evidence of the conviction that the energy resources of the Atlantic region must be developed-

subtopic: PROPOSED MOBILE ARCTIC ISLAND ENGINEERING CONCEPT
PROPOSED MOBILE ARCTIC ISLAND ENGINEERING CONCEPT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday both the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Lumley) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) refused to state their support for small-scale oil production in the Arctic by using the mobile Arctic Island concept. Millions of dollars have been spent to prove the viability of this proposal, yet the Minister, who has known about it for several years, still procrastinates and is studying it.
June 19, 1984

Anyone who has examined this scheme would be baffled by the Government's negative reaction. The project would benefit several small Canadian firms that were hard hit by the National Energy Program. It would increase Canada's domestic oil supply, and it would create thousands of jobs, most notably through the construction of a major drydock facility in Nanaimo, B.C.
As I say, the Government's opposition is baffling unless one takes into account the fact that approval of this project would require Liberal Ministers, such as the Minister of Finance, to admit to a major mistake. Of course the mistake is that the National Energy Program includes a regulation and incentive structure that is only beneficial for companies looking for a mammoth oil discovery in the North, a discovery which in all likelihood will not be made.
There is no incentive system to produce tens of millions of barrels from small-scale deposits which have already been found. When there is a choice between a project that means thousands of jobs, increased oil production, and help for Canadian companies, or saving Liberal Cabinet Ministers from humiliation prior to an election, it is obvious how the Government will act.

Mr. Speaker, despite heated warnings, and sound advice from a western Senator on August 6, 1980, the Liberal Government decided to proceed with the development of Northeast Coal. I have opposed this project from the very beginning, and presented over 2,000 petitions to the House of Commons, stating that these new projects will result in an overproduction of coal in terms of markets available to southeastern British Columbia.
I have called for a united front in the communities throughout the riding, urging the coal producers, workers, and municipal representatives to meet on a regular basis to protect the interests of the coal producers and the workers. Despite this, the Government of Canada and the Province of British Columbia signed an agreement in February, 1981, to proceed with the development of Northeast Coal.
I have also called upon the communities to endorse a resolution for the sale of western Canadian coal to central Canada markets. The New Democratic Party and the United Mineworkers of America called for a joint federal-provincial task force to be created. This was rejected by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The Province of Alberta has now recognized the importance of this resolution and has taken steps to ensure that it is fully investigated, which leaves out the producers of southeast British Columbia and the workers involved in the coal mines.
Oral Questions
An executive of Fording Coal has described the situation as an economic crisis, and I plead with the Minister to use his influence with the Minister of Energy in the Province of British Columbia to ensure that the coal producers and the workers of southeast British Columbia have equal opportunity of supplying the coal markets of central Canada, especially since the whole problem was created by the untimely development of the Northeast Coal project by both the federal and provincial Governments.

maintopic: CANADA SPORTS POOL CORPORATION-CALL FOR EXAMINATION OF BOOKS
CANADA SPORTS POOL CORPORATION-CALL FOR EXAMINATION OF BOOKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take advantage of this opportunity to give the new Leader of the Liberal Party a piece of advice. Since he maintained throughout the campaign that he could not tell Canadians or members of his own Party anything about his fiscal policies until he had seen the books of the Government of Canada, and since he claims that he will bring a new breath and a new life to the affairs of government as managed by the Liberal Party, I suggest that his first act within the next 24 hours should be to order that the books of the Sports Pool Corporation be opened to the House of Commons.
The House of Commons knows full well that that operation is riddled with incompetence, patronage, and every arrogant misuse of power for which the Liberal Party is famous. I suggest in all sincerity that the future Prime Minister clearly put his stamp on his Party immediately and open the books of the corporation to let the House of Commons see the contracts and finally find out whether the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mr. Olivier) has been telling the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Otherwise, Canadians will have every reason to believe that the new Leader of the Liberal Party is no better than his predecessors.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: LIBERAL PARTY LEADER-ACCESS TO CABINET DOCUMENTS

That in relation to Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto, one sitting day shall be allotted to the consideration of each of the report stage and the third reading of the said Bill; and
That fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for government business on those days, any proceedings before the House shall be interrupted, if required, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question necessary in order to dispose of the stage of the Bill then under consideration shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I must confess, and I know it is no secret, that the Government always acts with great regret when any time allocation resolution must be introduced. Under a properly working House of Commons, one would hope that a debate would be proceeded with seriously and in good faith by all sides of the House and, having exhausted all of the reasonable arguments and exchanges which ought to take place in parliamentary debate, that Hon. Members opposite would be prepared at a certain point to see the question put, to express their views through the procedure of voting, and see legislation proceed. Regrettably, virtually all serious legislation of this Government and this Parliament has needed the assistance of some form of time allocation at some stage or other in order for that legislation to be carried forward. It has regrettably become a necessary role of the Government at a certain point in the proceeding of every major piece of legislation to introduce time allocation. Therefore, with regret, I rise to introduce time allocation at this point in the consideration of this very important piece of legislation.
Let it not be said, as the Opposition has been attempting to do, that this legislation, the ideas and concepts, and the question of national security, have not had adequate debate or adequate public consideration. Nothing could be further from the truth. This is an issue which has been on the front burner before the Canadian people in many ways, I can say, for the past 17 years.
A royal commission on security known as the Mackenzie Commission was established in 1966 and its report was published in June of 1969. At that time there were 175 hearings and 250 witnesses who all recommended that a separate civilian security service be established in Canada. Mr. Tommy Douglas, a distinguished Member of this House at the time, reported in this House, and I quote:
Without any reflection whatsoever on the very excellent service the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have performed, there is a great difference between law enforcement and the carrying out of the duties of a security service... Therefore, I think the recommendation of the royal commission for the setting up of a civilian non-police agency has a great deal of merit.
There was then the McDonald Commission which was established in 1977. That commission held over 300 hearings and heard nearly 150 witnesses.

In summary, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the New Democratic Party is not interested in responsibly stating its position and seeing Parliament function. It is simply interested in delaying the passage of this Bill and preventing Parliament from carrying out its responsibilities.
We are very close to the end of the session and the end of a Parliament. I would like to end my brief remarks with a recent quote of Professor Peter Russell, research director of the McDonald Commission. He commented as follows:
I cannot think in living memory of legislation coming as close to a Royal Commission's whole set of recommendations as C-9 now does. Let's get on with the job.

That is exactly what this Government is trying to do. For the first time in this country's history, it is seeking to enact legislation that would define the framework, mandate and powers of a Security Intelligence Service and make each of its activities subject to judicial control and a system of external monitoring. This would be a major step, but the New Democratic Party members have, through their actions, not only discredited their Party, they have also made it difficult to pursue the very debate they were demanding.

This Government, in the tradition of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), will shoulder its responsibility and, with the assistance of this House, complete the final chapter of this long book and bring in legislation that represents a great step forward in this important area of public concern.

Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) indicates that he has run out of patience with the process. Well, isn't that too bad! Let me tell you what we have run out of. We have run out of patience with a Government that, on second reading, says that when the Bill goes to Committee it will consider the representations brought to it and, where appropriate, make amendments. That is what this Government said, but it had no intention of keeping that commitment. It has put everyone through a fraudulent process on Bill C-9 which has gone on for some months. The Minister said 25 witnesses appeared at committee and there were 50 briefs filed. True. The one amendment of any substance passed in committee was one which got past Government Members and allows the review committee to see the Cabinet documents which directed the security service. What is the Solicitor General doing now? He is bringing in an
amendment to wipe that amendment out! That is what we are impatient with. We are more than impatient; we are fed up to the teeth.
The Minister talks about the Mackenzie Commission. Lord love a duck! Half the reporters in this town were in knee pants or in the cradle when that Commission came in. The so-called terrible things which created the need for the McDonald Commission were done 13 and 14 years ago. I asked the Minister questions in committee about the RCMP. I said:
The fact is, Mr. Minister, that for many months now-for many years in fact-since the revelations in the House of Commons in 1977 and the action which was taken consequently, the security service has been working as a part of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The commissioner has been reporting to the Solicitor General effectively, competently and in a manner in which I am sure you would agree meets with your approval. You testify that this has been done in a manner which meets the appropriate sensibilities of the Canadian public. Is that not so?
What did the Solicitor General reply? He sat there and meekly agreed. He said:
Yes, that is so.
So much for his argument that the security service has to be removed from the RCMP. As for the argument that this is some brand-new security service being invented by the Bill, that is the most errant nonsense. It is exactly the same people, same typewriters, paper, cupboards, floor and rugs. The same everything. All this Bill does is set out an appropriate mandate and more rules within which that security service is to be constrained.
It is very interesting that the first act of this Government after the great convention that was going to reform the Liberal Party with the great new leader, John Turner, is to move closure on a security Bill which Alan Borovoy, the distinguished and eminent leader of civil rights in this country, says is the greatest threat to civil liberties since Confederation. But it is not surprising. Mr. Turner talks about a new deal. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, this is the old deal writ large. Mr. Turner was part of the Government that used closure in 1968 to impose the rules under which this closure is taking place. So much for civil liberties.
As for this pack of fellow travellers on the Government side who, with unseemly haste, bounced over to Mr. Turner when the Liberal establishment told them to many weeks ago, the question that should be asked the Canadian public is: Would you buy a used government from John Turner?
Under other circumstances and on other occasions the Solicitor General is a good personal friend of mine, but what he is saying today cannot go unchallenged. The reason we in the House are still fighting this Bill is that the Government has not accepted a single suggestion made by all of the competent people who came in front of the committee. Not one. That process has been made fraudulent by a Government that was not going to listen or accept suggestions. Clause 2(a), (b), (c), and (d) are the definitions of what constitutes a threat to the security of Canada. Those are the key sections which trigger all of the activities of the security service. The language is loose and does not adequately constrain the activities of a security force acting in secret. But this Government will not
June 19, 1984

accept a single amendment. The Government does not want a parliamentary review committee.
Interesting, isn't it, that our neighbour, the United States, has a Senate review committee for security matters as well as one in the House of Representatives. But this Government, which just spent all last weekend talking about reform, does not want Members of Parliament to have anything to do with reviewing security in this country. That is the Government that does not want the review committee to see even the Cabinet documents that direct the security service because that would be a breach of Cabinet solidarity. Well, one of the American witnesses said that your review committee has to be a watchdog committee and it better not be a sleeping dog committee. Well, if you cannot see what the Cabinet is directing the security service to do, the committee is a sleeping dog committee.
These are substantive and important amendments. It is no good that the Government or some nameless person in a editorial office somewhere is talking about the Mackenzie Commission, the McDonald Commission, Bill C-157 and the Senate committee, saying that there has been debate. Why can these people who are supposed to be educated in the journalism schools of this country not understand that what rules us is the wording of the legislation here in the House of Commons, not in the Senate, the Mackenzie Commission or the McDonald Commission? What is wrong with a fundamental and elementary understanding of our system? That fact does not seem to pervade the editorial boards of this country, and it certainly has not pervaded the cranium of the Solicitor General.
As for the pack of sheep on the Government side, with the exception of the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and one former Solicitor General, the members of the so-called reformed Party have sat there in dumb obedience week after week after week. Then they wonder why we are impatient. The whole process has been traduced by a government which put a Bill into committee and never intended to make one change to it.
It is all very well for the Solicitor General to talk about the 25 witnesses whocame in front of him. How do you think those witnesses feel knowing what is going on here? I talked to some of them. They asked what it was all about and why they bothered. Trust and reform are incredibly easy words to use. When you have a majority at your back for a limited period of time and the arrogance of appearing always to be in power, trust is dissipated like a will-o'-the-wisp at the first notion that someone may raise something which would mean you cannot have your own way absolutely. In 1688 we traded the Divine Right of Kings for the Divine Right of a Prime Minister with a majority at his back for a period of years. This is a brutally powerful system. When it is coupled with the attitude which has been exhibited on this Bill by the Government, the Solicitor General and the new leader, Mr. John Turner, there are no checks and balances in the system whatsoever.

Let there be no doubt about why the Opposition is arguing about this Bill. It is because the Bill is not as good as it could be. It is a flawed Bill. We know there must be a security service, but eminent, intelligent and capable people came before us and made suggestions which would make this Bill better and more trusted by the Canadian people. The Government accepted none of it. This is not a day to be very proud of in the House. Every Member of the Government should be ashamed, as I am ashamed, of what is happening here.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the motion of closure before the House I would seriously suggest to members of the Chamber that this represents one of the darkest days for democracy in the history of this country. I remind members of this Chamber and those Canadians who are observing our proceedings that it is the same Government that brought forward the proclamation of the War Measures Act in 1970 that now brings forward legislation which constitutes nothing less than a massive assault on the fundamental civil liberties and privacy of all Canadians and anyone visiting our country. In the guise of protecting our national security the Government would take a sledge-hammer to our civil liberties. In the pretext of fighting totalitarianism and totalitarian governments characterized by an atmosphere of oppression and the suppression of dissent, the Government would itself adopt those totalitarian tools.
It has been argued that the status quo is not acceptable. I agree. One need look no further than the litany of horror stories documented by the McDonald Commission which reported in 1981. However, let there be no misunderstanding. Far from being an improvement on the status quo, this Bill represents a very serious step backward. Given the alternative between the status quo, flawed though it may be, and the provisions of this Bill, many Canadians would certainly say that we should not move forward with this flawed legislation.
The debate on some of the provisions which are of greatest concern has been stifled consistently. The Bill was introduced in January and the Government cut off debate at second reading. After having begun a discussion at the clause by clause stage in committee, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Gourde), the Minister's number one flunky on the committee, brought forward a motion of closure to shut down debate. I filibustered that motion of closure for three days and I make no apology for having done so. The essence of that debate was that by moving in that heavy-handed manner, the Government was denying the committee the right to debate, in a full and informed manner, the provisions of this Bill. The Government denied the committee the right to hold public hearings across the country on legislation which so fundamentally affects the rights, liberties and privacy of Canadians.
If there had been public hearings, perhaps there would have been a little more attention paid by the members of the press. I accuse them of blatant disregard of one of the most important pieces of legislation to come before the House. The gallery was

June 19, 1984
Time Allocation
empty this morning and yesterday and is virtually empty today. They move around in their discussions, debates and great analyses of the flim-flam of leadership and completely ignore one of the most important pieces of legislation to come before the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-9
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-9
speechtext:
That is a shameful denial of their obligations to the people of the country for which they stand condemned. I suggest that it is indeed members of the press who may be victims of their own negligence down the line.
The Government denied public hearing, cut off debate at second reading and choked off debate in committee. The chairman of the committee was forced to resign after having taken action to shut down debate in committee, which is unprecedented in the history of this country. We come before the House for debate at report stage and third reading and the Government once again brings in the guillotine. The Government shuts the debate down using closure. So much for democracy! So much for the rights of Canadians to a full and informed debate on this Bill.
We in this Party said that we would do what we could to block the Bill if the Government did not accept amendments which would narrow the powers of the new security service and prevent it from having the right to target Canadians who have broken no law whatsoever. The McDonald Commission would have denied that power to the security service. That power is not granted to any security service in any western country in the world. That power is unprecedented in the United States. It is the power to target Canadians suspected to be subversives or spies. That power should not have been granted. We in this Party said we would not tolerate that power.
We said that there must be a role for Parliament, as did the McDonald Commission. We said there must be effective parliamentary oversight to prevent this new security service from becoming a political weapon in the hands of the government of the day. Yes, we said we would block this Bill if the Government did not move in that direction. We said we would not stand idly by as the Government brought forward a bill which would brutally suppress civil liberties and expand the powers of the service. The expanded powers include the right to open first-class mail, the right to access confidential medical records, the right to break into one's home and steal from it, and the right to access all government records. Nothing is sacred in this country.
With regard to foreign intelligence, the Government proposes new powers which are again unprecedented in any western country in the world. The Government proposes to have the power to spy on anyone who visits this country. This is all in the name of protecting the national security of Canadians.
We in the New Democratic Party make no apologies for standing up for the civil liberties of Canadians. I can only express my profound regret that we did not have more support from my colleagues in the Conservative Party in this fight against this repressive Bill. They stood by in committee as this
Bill was being debated. They certainly have not put up the kind of fight which they put up against the National Energy Program or the Crow Bill. This bill is certainly one of the most important Bills to come before this Parliament. This closure motion effectively denies the right of Members to debate this Bill in an orderly and comprehensive way.
The Bill has been condemned by witness after witness who appeared before the committee. The Reverend Clarke MacDonald, Moderator of the United Church of Canada, indicated that church and community representatives have detailed the flaws of this Bill and suggested alternative ways of serving the legitimate security needs of Canadians. He states: "We urge you to withdraw the Bill in its present form". These are the views of church groups, academics, labour groups and civil liberties organizations. To whom is the Government and its future Prime Minister, John Turner, prepared to listen as it proceeds to ram this legislation through the House of Commons? This is a dark day for democracy in this country.
I would like to conclude my remarks with a quote from Mr. Justice Powell of the United States Supreme Court, who said:
The price of lawful public dissent must not be a dread of subjugation to an unchecked surveillance power. Nor must the fear of unauthorized official eavesdropping deter vigorous citizen dissent in discussion of government action in private conversation. For private dissent, no less than open public discourse, is essential to our free society.
This Bill must be stopped in the interest of democracy, liberty and freedom in this country.

None of the witnesses who came before us and no honest, right-thinking person would deny the necessity for having a security service in Canada. We have been singularly fortunate that we have essentially been spared the problem of terrorist activities such as those that have taken place in so many countries around the world. However, we are not totally immune and have had our own incidents, and we need this security service. It should be in civilian hands. We need this
June 19, 1984

service in order to have proper accountability so that our civil liberties might be protected.
As a former member of the rules committee, a high priority for us was to enhance the role of the Private Member. The way this can be done is through the committee system. It is in the committee that the ordinary Member of Parliament has an opportunity to participate in debate and to make necessary changes. This is typical of an NDP member. I am expressing a point of view and the Hon. Member is endeavouring to shout me down. I basically disagree with the position taken by the Progressive Conservative Party which indicated that it would like to see this security service returned to the RCMP despite the decision of the McDonald and Mackenzie Commissions, and the decisions made by the Senate and the Government, for that matter.
What approach did the Conservatives take? I thought that the Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) asked a series of very pertinent questions at the committee stage. I basically disagree with the judgment of the Progressive Conservative Party on this particular Bill. I do not believe the service should be returned to the RCMP. No one has more respect for that particular agency than I. I had the privilege of working with the RCMP when I was Minister of Employment and Immigration. We had to deal with security matters and had to rely in large measure on the judgments and decisions of the RCMP. I was satisfied that we received excellent briefings and that the reports which I received had been carefully thought out before I was asked to make a decision.
In order to complement that particular protection of civil liberties of Canadians or of others coming to the country, I saw fit to appoint a board. It was made up of three members, a former civil servant, a former Cabinet Minister and a former judge of the Supreme Court in Quebec. They were to study the
Time Allocation
evidence that had been presented to me to determine what weight I should give to this material. I had no other way to check other than relying on the RCMP and the judgment of these three senior Canadians whose judgment I respected.
That is what we are looking for in the security service. We are seeking a "delicate balance", as I believe it was put by the Senate committee. We must have an indication that the information that comes before us has received all the necessary screening. I believe the report from the Senate committee was one of the better reports from the Senate that I have had the privilege to read. That Senate committee and the McDonald Commission indicate that a civilian agency is the proper medium for this particular service in Canada.
Hon. Members opposite say that they did not really have an opportunity to study this matter at committee. The fact of the matter is that the Minister has indicated that he was at approximately 24 committee meetings. In each instance the Minister indicated why the Government could not accept a particular amendment. Those reasons made eminently good sense, which Hon. Members opposite knew. In some instances they could not accept those reasons and they appropriately brought forward amendments when they could not accept that reasoning. I know that in many instances they accepted the Minister's reasons. However, likely in an attempt to delay the Bill, they saw fit to move a whole series of amendments. I am specifically referring to the New Democratic Party. We discussed many of these amendments at committee stage. Again, it was a complete waste of members' time. What is the point in having committees if every amendment that is presented at the committee stage is presented again at the report stage?
I hear Opposition Members talking with approbation about the American experience. American witnesses appeared before the committee. We had a particularly good witness from the security section of the American Government. She told us that they tried to introduce a Bill which provided for everything necessary to protect all rights and prevent any interference. That Bill collapsed under its own weight. There were so many qualifying phrases in the Bill in an attempt to protect civil liberties that the Americans ultimately had no Bill at all. Therefore, that country has a presidential edict. The Attorney General of the United States indicates what is to be done.
We do have accountability in our Bill. I think the individuals who will be called upon to look into the actions of the other security service will recognize their responsibilities. They will be well respected Canadians, I am certain. They will require the approval of the Leaders of the Parties in the House of Commons, so there is significant accountability in this Bill.
I for one am happy that, after some five years, we will have another look at this Bill. Others will do that because I will not be here. They will look at whether it has worked. They will look to see if there have been any infringements of or intrusions into the civil liberties of Canadians. I find it very difficult to understand that kind of thing happening. If I were their leader, I would be very unhappy to be, I suppose, catalogued for the rest of a short career as the leader of the Liberal Party who imposed closure on a Bill which restricted the rights, liberties and freedoms of Canadians. If that man is not Mr. Yesterday, I do not know who is.
Earlier a Member talked about the committee system and how this Government tried to improve it. This legislation was first before a committee in the other place, before many commissions, and was examined in long hearings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. It is precisely because of the way the Liberals have used that committee system that we on this side are so upset. The Government has received representations right across the country from very
august groups, universities, church groups and civil liberties groups. The Government has paid absolutely no attention to those representations.
This set of circumstances reminds me very much of the committee hearings on the National Energy Program. Every witness- and I say every witness-who appeared before the committee concerned with the National Energy Program opposed the legislation and found fault with it. But what did this Government do? It did not accept one recommendation of the committee. If you want to know the history of the National Energy Program, Mr. Speaker, which turned into an economic disaster, I would ask you to read the projections made by the witnesses in those committee hearings as well as the reports which outlined in detail the effect of that legislation. This same thing is happening with Bill C-9. The Government heard representations in the committee hearings. The Government listened to briefs. But the Government has not acted. Why do we have a committee system if the Government intends to impose legislation on Parliament? Why waste the time of so many people? If people are not listened to, it is frustrating to those both inside and outside Parliament. Also people who have taken the time and made the effort to present their expertise before a committee will think that the democratic process is poor because they realize they are not going to be listened to. That is why we on this side of the House are so opposed to this kind of procedure.
A Member opposite said the Conservative Party opposed this legislation because control of the new service was not within the RCMP. That is true, but that does not go far enough in our view. That is one of our proposals. Basically the real opposition we have to this Bill concerns the definition found in Clause 2. Clause 2 gives this super-snooper outfit the power to permit an agent or agents to enter people's homes and destroy property. In fact, innocent people can have their whole way of life upset by this legislation. This is because the definition section is too wide.
A previous speaker said that the Government has tried to create a balance. The Minister many times in committee admitted that Clause 2 was perhaps too wide and was open to abuse by a secret service force. He said: "I cannot draft the legislation. I cannot find the right balance. We find it impossible. The best draftsman have tried to do what we want but it could not be done." That is because the Minister is trying to give the secret service super-snoopers wide enough scope that they can solve every single problem or every single threat, no matter how small.
We tried to impress upon the Minister time and time again in committee that instead of giving the super-snoopers a Lincoln or a Chevrolet with which to do their work, make it difficult for them. If this agency over the next four or five years finds that it cannot do its work properly, there is provision for the law to be brought back to Parliament to be rewritten. It would be far better for the secret service to come
June 19, 1984

back to Parliament and say that the Bill is not wide enough, that it does not give them enough power to do their work. We should be shown specific instances, which has not been done to this day, and 1 am sure Parliament would respond and say: "Fine, we will widen your mandate and give you power to solve this real threat about which you now tell us". It is far better for the security service to come back to Parliament than the average Canadian citizen who has had his rights run into the ground and who has suffered at the hands of some overzealous secret police. You know how difficult it is, Mr. Speaker, for any individual to do that. It would take years. I say this Bill puts the onus on the citizen to protect his rights. I am sure it will be echoed in this House, it will certainly be echoed in the country, that there is an obligation on the Government to ensure that the Canadian citizen is protected, that his privacy is protected. Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a couple of observations concerning the procedure today. I remind the House that the subject matter or the intent of this particular Bill was dealt with by two royal commissions in the past two decades. Substantially they recommended what the Bill provides. The committee has been studying it for about two months. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) spent many hours before the committee. Some 25 or 26 individuals and organizations made representations to the committee. I understand that there were more than 50 speeches at second reading. It was the subject of a very valuable Senate report. Some of the very worth-while recommendations of the Senate committee were incorporated into this Bill.
The subject matter under discussion today is closure. It is interesting to listen to Hon. Members talk about closure. They say that somehow the rights of Canadians are being denied by closure. One wonders just how the time of the House of Commons is used throughout the year. We could look at a situation where an entire year was spent in this Chamber dealing with very few Bills. Very few Bills ever see the light of day out the other end.
If I were to suggest that we bring in a parliamentary rule change providing that every motion put would come to an automatic end at the end of the day on which it was put, I would be accused of putting Parliament to rest or taking away all its rights. That would be absolutely outrageous to Hon. Members, but it is the exact change which has been implemented in most legislatures under the British parliamentary system. The motion is put and it comes to an end in one sitting day. That would be absolutely outrageous to us as parliamentarians in Canada. That is the system which is the effect in our
Time Allocation
Mother of Parliaments. The reason for it is that legislatures under the British parliamentary system, except the Canadian Parliament, eventually decided that they would go along with changes in parliamentary procedure not made by Members of Parliament. In effect, in Britain today there is an outside committee which is not connected with Members of Parliament. It brings in recommendations for rule changes in that Parliament.
Unless similar action is taken in terms of our Canadian Parliament, I am afraid that we will not keep up with the times in trying to deal with the many issues facing the country.
I am referring to the many issues with which Parliament never deals because there is no chance and the mechanisms are not in place.
I could outline what has happened to committee structures in legislatures throughout the British parliamentary system. I could outline what happens during Question Period and every other part of a day's sitting. I could outline what happens when motions are brought before those chambers. We would see that their procedures differ vastly from what is in effect in the Canadian Parliament. When we question the people who brought in these changes in other legislatures, they indicate that we are back in the dark ages and they wonder how we can function. Somehow there is always an attitude in our Parliament that unless we keep things the same, we lose a part of our democracy in this Chamber.
The only point I wanted to make today was that our parliamentary system is quite different from that of other Parliaments under the British parliamentary system. To say that closure is an outrageous act by government to shut off debate, to another Parliament would in itself be an outrageous statement.
