At least I give him credit for looking there for some precedent. However, he forgot to mention the fact that the United Kingdom is a country which does not have a separate provincial jurisdiction. It deals with legislation which is covered by our provincial legislatures as well as by our federal jurisdiction in Canada. Its workload is quite different, its scope is quite different and its rules are quite different. It is modelled upon their own experience. We in Canada have a system which is adapting and in fact reflects regional disparities. At least some of us in the House think that individual Members of Parliament should have a role to play with respect to the important issues facing Canada.
I should like to talk about the kind of approach we should take to this legislation. I should like to quote, because the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is wont to do so, the McDonald Commission. Section 28 on page 15 of its second report, Volume I, dated August, 1981 is headed: "The need for trust". It reads:
The most important word in the Commission governing this Inquiry is "trust". No police force protecting the peace can be effective unless it has the trust of the people it seeks to protect; no security intelligence agency can be effective without the trust of citizens. Moreover, neither can be effective without the trust of government.
That is what we are talking about. We are talking about trust. We are talking about a Government Party which has just gone through a convention in which the word "reform" was used liberally, if I may put it that way. Its members indicated that there would be parliamentary reform and that their new Leader would ensure Parliament was relevant. What was the first thing they did after the election of a new Leader? They brought in John Turner's chief operative on the floor-I saw him on television in black and white-and he came into Parliament and gave notice of closure. If that is their idea of parliamentary reform, God protect the people of Canada.
Let me put the facts before you, Mr. Speaker. They are simply this. We were involved, by virtue of a ruling by Your Honour, in a procedural debate on the admissibility of motions to amend at report stage until the day before yesterday. Finally these matters were resolved. Only yesterday we made our final procedural argument. I venture to say that at report stage, forced as we are with a great number of suggested amendments, we have had something in the vicinity of five or six hours' debate on this Bill.
This Bill does not involve some kind of contract for snow clearing in Sarnia. It is not a minor Bill. This Bill will have a very serious impact on the civil liberties of Canadians. It will create an agency with enormous powers. To use the words of the McDonald Commission, this agency will not be able to function properly unless it has the trust of the people of Canada. It will not operate unless the citizens of Canada have trust in the Government of this country.
When talking about curtailing civil liberties, is it consistent with the concept that we have of a government moving the weight of its majority in this House in a dying Parliament, in the dying days when this Government has no mandate, when
its new Leader is talking about an immediate election, that one of its final acts is to curtail debate without any consideration of reasonable amendments? It says it is not going to listen to the representations, that it will not listen to those who came before the committee, will not listen to the advice of the provincial Attorneys General and will not listen to the advice of representatives of church groups, public interest groups and civil liberties groups.
Worst of all, what the Government is saying by this motion is that it cares not a whit what Members of Parliament say with regard to this legislation. The Government does not want to hear any more, does not want further discussion, even though it knows that its mandate has expired. It is exhausted. It is going to push this Bill through whether the people of Canada like it or not. That is what is at issue.
I am not so completely partisan that I am not impressed by my colleagues. I realize that no Party has a corner on people of goodwill and good spirit, that there are people of that type in every party in Canada. I listened with care to what was going on with the new Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, Mr. John turner. He has had experience in this House. He left the Government of Canada for his own reasons and now has come back. I heard him talk about the new approach, the new spirit of civility that he wants to bring to the Parliament of Canada. The first act that takes place after he has been elected is the heavy cloud of closure which is now being presented to the House of Commons. This is a very foreboding development.
If we cannot discuss issues, if we cannot have a perspective in terms of the issues before us in this debate, if we cannot, as the McDonald Commission said, instil a feeling of trust with respect to the fact that there are to be some reasonable rules governing the control of this agency, if we are to enter this experience in terms of our own security, having an intelligence service which will not be under the discipline of the RCMP, if we do not have a fine and honourable tradition to guide it in its operations, its deliberations and its accountability, our country will be in a sorry state indeed.
I say with all the emotion I am capable of that I resent the cynicism with which this motion has been brought forward. I resent the attempt at this time in the life of our Parliament to throttle free discussion of a Bill which involves the rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens. It brings into being a service, Mr. Speaker, that will have access not only to your tax returns and mine, but to those of all Canadians across this country. It will have the ability to go into medical records, to put intrusive devices in our homes in order to gain information which can be a valuable tool in the hands of an unscrupulous government. When closure is being brought forward on this legislation, those who watch these proceedings or read them will be left wondering. They must ask themselves, why do they stay? They must echo the words of Oliver Cromwell: "In the name of God, go!" I say to the Government of Canada that that sentiment is appropriate with this dying Government.
June 19, 1984

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess I see myself as still being relatively new in this House in the sense that I was first elected in 1979. I have just served five years as a Member of Parliament. After having lived through the constitutional process, having lived through times in which time allocation and closure was imposed on this House, I can understand why early framers who looked at the American Constitution with its congressional form have said that it is the perfect form of government. The individual elected there is held accountable on a non-partisan basis to his or her constituents. I am convinced that unless we can radically reform this place to the point where there are genuine free votes which will impose an individual responsibility on each of us, on every piece of legislation, to look at that legislation, to vote as our constituents and our conscience dictate, we will continue to have the parliamentary form of government where a cabinet, in conjunction with a very well educated and powerful bureaucracy, will make decisions that it can force through this House because if back-benchers, however well
Time Allocation
intentioned they may be, vote against the government, they will bring on a general election.
I am convinced that as a result of all the complexity of government, the volume of government as well as the legislation that is necessary, the system has broken down. Either we have radical changes within our responsible parliamentary forum or we move to a congressional forum where the executive would be isolated off to the side and charged with administering the laws. Then the House with its Party system, where there would be cross-representation depending on the issue, would be much more responsible to the people.
I have just read some poll data on this Bill. Over 80 per cent of the Canadian people have indicated they would like to have the security service remain with the RCMP. Yet the Cabinet and the bureaucracy, for very good reasons that they generated in their own minds which are logical and rational to themselves, are going to foist their view on the people. That is not satisfactory and we must return to a better system.
Twenty-five witnesses appeared before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and gave well-meaning and valuable evidence. In a sense, these witnesses were the experts. When members of the Canadian Bar Association speak, we should listen to them. When members of the Canadian Jewish Council speak on a Bill that deals with individual liberties and freedoms, surely the people who hear their words should give them enormous weight. There is no doubt that if you were a judge, Mr. Speaker, who heard the evidence that came before the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, you would not have hesitated at all in accepting the recommendations for amendments. Yet this just has not happened. Therefore, our system has fallen down.
If an individual who worked for this new civilian intelligence service had reasonable grounds to suspect that you, Mr. Speaker, were a threat to the security of Canada, then your mail could be opened, your medical records could be seized, your legal records could be seized, your tax files could be searched, your home, office or car could be bugged and searched overtly or covertly, your telephones could be tapped and your doctor's or psychiatrist's offices could be searched. All that remains confidential is your five-year or ten-year census records. Everything else can be stripped and investigated. For one year you could have intrusive devices placed on your person and your telephones could be tapped, and after that year it could go on for a further year and yet another year. That flies in the face of those fundamental freedoms that our ancestors came to this country to achieve.
Our ancestors did not cross the ocean on boats, stand at the corner of a quarter section of land containing only rough prairie and trees, give their lives cutting trees, breaking land and living in sod huts simply to pass the time of day. They did all of that because they came from jurisdictions in which they felt oppressed. Often times they felt oppressed because of the economic situation of a country or because of the laws of a

June 19, 1984
Time Allocation
country. In most cases they felt oppressed by their country's government of the day.
I would say to the Government of this country that with this legislation we are creating a real possibility and perhaps even a probability that at some future time this new civilian security agency will become oppressive to our own people. Clause 2(d) defines threats to the security of Canada and deals with subversion. Subversion means actions taken by our own citizens.
None of us has any trouble at all with paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of Clause 2 which deal with the actions of KGB agents and people who come to Canada to hijack airplanes and blow things up on behalf of other countries. Clause 2(d) deals with our own Canadian citizens and therefore should be drafted in an extremely narrow fashion. If such a narrow definition does not work in the future, then the agency could return to a future Parliament which would gladly decide, based upon actual cases, to expand that definition so that the proper delicate balance is achieved.
The present wording of Clause 2(d) gives such a wide mandate to the Bill that many of our people will have to suffer dramatically before the definition will be narrowed. That means that those people who are affected will then be required to hire a solicitor, if they happen to find out that they are being investigated. These people may not be able to get jobs and will never find out why they could not get jobs. They may lose their jobs and never know the real reason why. They may not be able to get passports or be bonded and never know the reason. All this because this clause has been cast too widely. That is why I say we must begin with a narrow definition and let future generations widen it based upon experience.
I wish Government Members would take another look at Clause 2(d) because it is never too late to do so. Without expanding the size of the Minister's head, I would say that I believe the Minister wants to be reasonable and, in many respects, is a reasonable man. As I listened to the Minister's speech, when he got right down to it he pointed out that the reason for the imposition of time allocation is that we are nearing the end of a session. When dealing with a statute that will have influence on future generations, saying that we are nearing the end of a session is simply not a good enough reason for imposing time allocation. A future Parliament could deal with this legislation.
If we had the time, we could improve this legislation. I found that when given the opportunity at committee, Government Members were prepared to sit down and discuss this legislation. Indeed, they themselves proposed some amendments. If we could just discuss the legislation with them further and hear more witnesses, we could get it right.
I would like to be critical of members of the NDP as well because at the beginning of the process they were so radical that they polarized the Government to the point that reasonableness and common sense could not prevail. That is not what I was elected to accomplish. My people sent me here to do a job, to look at legislation and to rise and speak on their behalf. I show you a questionnaire, Mr. Speaker, which asks: "Are
you satisfied with the RCMP performance on matters of national security intelligence?" Of the respondents to that questionnaire, 71 per cent said yes and only 8 per cent said no. Surely we should listen to what the answer to that questionnaire is telling us.
I know that my friend, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), has an absolutely incredible and revolutionary idea. He believes that elected representatives should do what the people want. That is not the way the Liberal Government has operated. However, that is his view and that is my view as well. It is a view to which I wish we would all adhere.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Gourde (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-9
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to speak to the motion on time allocation for the debate on Bill C-9.
This afternoon we have heard a lot from the Opposition, and the gist of it seems to be that these Hon. Members who represent the Canadian people have not had a chance to consider all the whys and wherefores of this Bill.
Mr. Speaker, I have been Parliamentary Secretary since March and have attended all the meetings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which dealt with this Bill. I must say there were times when we were almost ashamed to admit we were Members of Parliament and were sitting opposite certain Members of the New Democratic Party who were using every trick in the book-and I am referring to the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson)-and I am sure they would have found a few new ones if they had had more time, to set up a regular filibuster. In fact, that is more or less what the Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) said, and I would refer you to Hansard of June 12, 1984, at page 4568, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some sadness at report stage of this Bill because we are again faced with a situation in which NDP members are helping the Government achieve one of its goals while loudly protesting what the Government is doing. NDP members are actually helping the Government because they are going to force the Government to put time allocation on report stage and third reading stage-
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that in Canada, security is an issue that has been discussed for many years.
Commissioners Mackenzie, Pratt and Coldwell reported to the Government in October 1968, and the Commission's report was published in June of the following year. In the course of their inquiry, they heard about 250 witnesses, including Ministers and former Ministers of the Crown, public servants and retired public servants, private citizens and representatives of public sector organizations. They examined numerous files and documents, received briefs and papers and consulted public information sources. Their report was well received by a very large audience.
June 19, 1984

The work of the McDonald Commission, created in July 1977, consisted in the most thorough examination of security intelligence issues and procedures ever carried out in Canada's history, or in the history of any nation, for that matter.
Commissioners McDonald, Rickerd and Gilbert were assisted by an exceptionally competent staff of seven full-time investigators, thirty lawyers and sixty research officers. In the course of an inquiry that lasted four years, the Commission held 169 public hearings and 144 hearings behind closed doors. The combined transcripts of these hearings filled 174 volumes. As many as 149 witnesses were heard. More than 805 exhibits were received. The Commission investigated 292 allegations and examined 124 papers on national security policies, procedures and legislation.
In addition to hearings held in Ottawa, the Commissioners travelled throughout the country to receive briefs from the Canadian public, and I am surprised there are still Hon. Members who say today that Canadians have never had a chance to give their views on the subject. Especially since, in addition to the trips made by the McDonald Commission and our committee meetings, the Chairman published notices in forty newspapers across Canada, so that individual Canadians or groups would have an opportunity to testify before our Committee or submit written representations. In fact a number of groups and a number of individuals were able to testify. I shall get back to this later on.
The Commissioners of the McDonald Commission also met with Ministers, Members of Parliament and senior federal and provincial officials. Their research covered more than 500 books, articles and reports on the subject. They produced three reports, the second about 1,200 pages long and containing 285 recommendations. Therefore, I am indeed surprised to hear Hon. Members saying that the issue of security in Canada has not been examined. Strange as it may seem, the Opposition Parties often quote the McDonald Report, but only when it suits them.
While the McDonald Report speaks for itself, and I think that the Government, and we shall see later on . .. I read somewhere the following opinion given by Professor Peter Russell with respect to Bill C-9: "It is a pretty good Bill. I cannot think in living memory of legislation coming as close to a Royal Commission's whole set of recommendations as C-9 now does". Professor Russell concluded with: "Let's get on with the job" . . . and a subtle recommendation for approval or enactment of Bill C-9.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, last year Bill C-157 was tabled, and at the time it gave rise to some serious questions by groups and individuals. Bill C-157 was referred to a Special Committee of the Senate, and I might refer the House to a statement by Mr. W. A. Wilson ... If the Hon. Member for Burnaby insists, I am quite willing to table the document! In an article published on June 2, 1984, and I cannot quite read the name of the newspaper, Mr. Wilson said that the report of the
Time Allocation
Senate Committee chaired by Senator Michael Pitfield was one of the best reports ever produced here in the Senate and that the Senate had every reason to be proud of producing such a document.
The Senate Committee heard more than thirty individuals and groups, and received more than fifty representations or letters. Last January, realizing that Bill C-157 was raising serious questions, the Government, through the Solicitor General, tabled an amended version of Bill C-157, now known as Bill C-9. The new Bill C-9 contained forty amendments made by the Government. Subsequently, at the committee stage, the Government added seven more amendments. When we proceeded with clause-by-clause consideration, the Government accepted several amendments which, although minor, helped to improve considerably the original version of the Bill.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is clear that today, we have a motion for time allocation because Opposition Members, and the New Democratic Party led the way in this respect, have given us no other alternative but to ask the House to limit debate. At the second reading stage, we had six days of debate and fifty-seven speeches. The Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs met for two months. In those months we had forty-three meetings and eighty-five hours of debate. We heard twenty-five individuals and groups, we received fifty written representations, and the Solicitor General attended the proceedings of the Committee for fifty-nine hours at twenty-four different meetings. If, after all that, no consensus could be reached in Committee or in the House, I think that even if we continued debate for many hours and many days, we would never get anything more substantial from the New Democratic Party, the NDP, also known as the Non-Decision Party, a party that has a habit of talking instead of making decisions. We had a taste of that in committee! The Hon. Member for Burnaby talked for hours on end to try and hold up committee proceedings.
In the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, we have no choice- these will be my last words-but to move the motion for time allocation, and that is why I support the motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary has attacked the NDP as leading the opposition to this Bill. On behalf of the NDP, I proudly stand here to add to that opposition. It is a proud tradition. In this House, NDP Members have stood against the tidal wave of public opinion to oppose the taking away of the property of Japanese Canadians. We stood against the War Measures Act and we stand against this Bill. I believe that history will prove us right as it has proven us right in the past.
The Parliamentary Secretary is missing the point. The point is not that security in Canada has not been debated. Of course it has been debated. It has been debated for a long time. Canadians may get tired of the debate, but it is a tough debate and it is a tough decision. Yes, we had the McDonald Commission, but that is not the point. We are dealing with this Bill and we should focus on it. This Bill is a flawed Bill. It must be

June 19, 1984
Time Allocation
corrected because this subject is too important. This is one of the most important subjects which the Elouse has tackled in this Parliament since 1980.
I can recall the debate on the Alaska pipeline. Closure was moved on that Bill. I can recall the debate on the Constitution and the debate on the National Energy Program. This Bill ranks with those kinds of fundamental debates and fundamental decisions which will affect the future of Canada. Frankly, I find it unbelievable that this Government should now bring in that Bill, which is a seriously flawed product of a lame duck regime.
I have heard Hon. Members bringing John Turner into the debate this afternoon and in a way, criticizing him, for this Bill. I would exclude that criticism. We are dealing with the Trudeau Government, and we are dealing with a lame duck government, which has no right to bring in this seriously flawed legislation at the end of a session, because this legislation is going to have such an incredible effect on the country. I say it is a Trudeau Bill because it bears all the earmarks of the Trudeau-Pitfield elitist form of bureaucracy. It creates a small security service which will not be accountable to Parliament or to anyone. I predict it will get out of control. The problem with Revenue Canada will be nothing compared to what is going to happen here. The political masters will not be able to control this service. This represents the kind of elitist centralized small bureaucratic thinking which was the great flaw of the Trudeau-Pitfield years. We are seeing that in spades in this Bill.
It is unbelievable that Liberal Members should support this kind of flawed legislation at the dying end of a session. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that they should call an election on this legislation and that we leave the Bill right where it is. Let them leave the Bill now and go out to seek a mandate. If they get one, let them come back and then we can start off from where we are right now. We will get agreement from the other Party. I suggest that to the Solicitor General and I challenge the Liberals to do that. But they will not do it. They would prefer to hurry this Bill through Parliament.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), who is to be congratulated for his great work on this Bill, and the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), who spoke today, gave two of the best speeches I have heard since I came to the House of Commons. They were hard hitting speeches which took to task the national press for its coverage of this Bill. That is a hard thing to do for a Member of Parliament, but it was the right thing to do, because the Canadian people are asleep right now and the press is asleep in letting this kind of Bill go through. There is an exception, Mr. Speaker, and that is The Vancouver Sun who published an editorial. The Toronto Star, for example, said the Government should push the Bill through, "You heard 25 witnesses or so. Push the Bill through". But it forgot to say that most of those witnesses were against the Bill and that the Bill was seriously flawed. I will quote from the editorial in The Vancouver sun. It reads:
But the opposition parties must fight tooth and nail to prevent the government from ramming through its security and intelligence legislation-
Well, we are fighting tooth and nail. The editorial continues:
It is not just civil liberties groups that have condemned the legislation. Doctors and lawyers, labour and religious organizations, provincial attomeys-general and, yes, even some Liberal MPs have serious misgivings about it.
The language of the bill is simply too broad and loose to assure Canadians that their fundamental rights and liberties would not be infringed by the new civilian security agency.
It is not just outside sources like The Vancouver Sun which say that. Roy McMurtry, the Attorney General of Ontario, is quoted as saying:
It is critical in developing laws to protect our freedoms that we do not by these very laws destroy the very freedoms that they are meant to secure.
This law will destroy those freedoms. I suggest that Hon. Members opposite should seriously consider whether they should vote for this Bill. They should not be muttons or sheep, as they have been called. I suggest that those Hon. Members look at Issue No. 16 of the committee report. The Hon. Member for Burnaby asked Mr. Stewart, who lead a group from Vancouver, this:
What effect do you think that would have on the nature of dissent and certainly on the activities of the groups you represent?
He was referring to closure on the Bill and bringing this Bill through right away. Mr. Stewart answered:
I think it would have a couple. It would make some people quite cautious about what they did. You see, when you leave a tinge of suspicion in people's minds ... We all know the police never investigate anyone without cause; that is drilled into us at school and is certainly confirmed in every day experience for a lot of people. If that general public view is maintained and we see that the Bill as it is presently written makes its way through the House, I think it will have a real sensory effect on a lot of activity.
In other words, it will stop dissent, legal dissent, in this country. Mr. Stewart continued:
That is one thing that will happen. It is going to make a lot of people very angry. It is going to make things much worse than they presently are, I believe. If people believe normal activities of dissidents, of protest in this country, are being closed down, I believe some people will be more likely to use alternative methods.
And we will see more of the Squamish Five, and that nonsense rather than less, if we pass this kind of a police state type of Bill. Mr. Stewart continued, and I will quote it in French for the Parliamentary Secretary:
Le resultat, comme le donne a entendre notre memoire, c'est la fin du regime democratique au pays. Cela aurait pour effet que la police chargee d'assurer notre securite deviendrait, a la fin du compte, des gardiens de prison.
I will repeat it in English. He said:
What that does in the end as our brief suggests, is close down democracy in this country. That would be the net effect; that these police who are here to look after our security would, in the end, become our jailers.
I think Mr. Stewart put it very well. The Hon. Member for Burnaby said in his speech that this Bill is unprecedented, that it gives new powers to the police to open first class mail. Do Liberal Members of Parliament want that? Do their constituents want that? It gives access to medical records. Is that what those Hon. Members want? Do Canadians want that? Do they want to give access to their medical records? It gives access to income tax returns. Do Hon. Members in this House and the
June 19, 1984

people watching want to see this happen? It allows people to target Canadians who have broken no law at all. The definition clause, Mr. Speaker, will make it easy to go after legitimate groups who voice their dissent.
I believe the Government, in sneaking this legislation through, thinks that the people do not care. I was at a pot luck supper in Vancouver last weekend. A woman stood up and said that we need to support Svend Robinson on this Bill, and some people wrote on the tablecloth about stopping the Bill. I went to the Maritimes and people asked me questions there about this Bill. They asked, "Are they taking away our liberties?"
I would like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying this: This is a flawed Bill, for all the reasons which other Hon. Members have given. The Government is pushing this Bill through and accepting no amendments. Let the Government accept some amendments to the Bill. Many of us in this House, Mr. Speaker, have spent our lives fighting for civil liberties, for law in this country, and now we see a Bill that in fact attacks what is the nature of Canada itself. There is an ink blot, Mr. Speaker, on the Charter of Rights. It is a small blot, an act of some crazy person. But this Bill, if it passes, will do something worse. I feel that in the end it will kill the spirit and the letter of that Charter of Rights. The Liberal Members, the people of this country and the press, would be wise to take another look at this Bill before hurrying it through.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin my remarks on Bill C-9, which establishes the Canadian Security Intelligence Services, by referring to two matters which I believe are vital to this debate. First and foremost, Mr. Speaker, is the survival of the Canadian parliamentary democracy and the vital effect it has on our society, both in political terms and in real terms for the Canadian people. Second, I want to speak about the status of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as Canada's national police force, and how it is affected by Bill C-9 and this process to which Bill C-9 has been subjected.
Let me say first, with respect to parliamentary democracy, that the purpose of having elected representatives and the whole idea being a parliamentary democracy is to invoke an evolutionary process in order to establish the laws by which Canadians are governed. That evolutionary process is designed to prevent and preclude the development of a revolutionary process. It is interesting to note that the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), referred to what may be a revolt on the part of the Canadian people with respect to a legislative measure such as that contained in Bill C-9. We are denying the parliamentary democracy which was established for Canadians over 100 years ago by taking the steps in this House of Commons which are being taken by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and his colleagues in the Government and in the Liberal Party. We are denying the opportunity for that evolutionary process to go through whereby we establish to everyone's satisfaction that a legislative measure brought to Parliament has the support of the Canadian people. That is the end test.
Time Allocation
I agreed with the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, for once in our political lives, when he said, "If the Government is so sure of its position on this matter, let it be tested by the people". Let us go before the people and ask them whether they want Bill C-9 passed. Let them decide whether they want Bill C-9 passed. Let them decide whether they want a Canadian Security Intelligence Service in the form which is proposed in this Bill. But that is not what the Government wants, Mr. Speaker. That is not why it is rushing this Bill through the House of Commons, to get it stamped with the approval of Parliament so it can be a fait accompli before the Canadian people even get to realize and recognize what is part and parcel of the provisions of Bill C-9. The Government wants to put this dramatic and drastic change in our national police force behind it before government Members have to face the Canadian people. Unfortunately, they know that the public's memory is short. If the Bill can be enacted and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service created and put into operation, it may be forgotten. There will be complaints across Canada from a great many people but there will be no widespread movement against the action taken by the Government. The public will not blame the Government of Canada.
The Liberal Party has just gone through a dramatic national convention at which all the candidates, particularly the successful candidate, spoke of the need to reform the institutions of Parliament and Government. What a mockery! They talk about reform and then come into the House of Commons and clamp closure on such an important legislative measure. I cannot believe this was done without the consent and concurrence of the future Prime Minister, Mr. Turner. I cannot believe that the Solicitor General would introduce a drastic measure without consulting with the future Prime Minister. Let us make it very clear. We are casting the blame on the future Prime Minister, Mr. Turner, for this Bill. He will be the J. R. Ewing of Canadian politics. He will be the backroom schemer who directed that these actions take place and then, when the deed is done, he will come into the House and deny any knowledge or participation in that deed. But he is not going to fool anyone because it is now on record. We know that the actions of the Solicitor General must have the consent and concurrence of the future Prime Minister or we will not see the Solicitor General sitting where he now sits. We are not going to let Mr. Turner forget this measure. We are not going to let him pretend it was done by someone else at some other time. speakeroldname: Mr. J. R. Ellis (Prince Edward-Hastings) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-242, an Act to stabilize the representation in the House of Commons, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my remarks by referring briefly to the Bill itself. I would like to read into the record the two short amendments which are the subject of this Bill. There are only a couple of clauses in the Bill. Clause 2(1) reads:
This amendment would dispense with the necessity of a readjustment of federal electoral districts based upon the 1981 census. The most recent readjustment, based on the census of 1971, did not finally come into effect until the election of 1979. The adoption of a revised representation formula in the year 1974, after an initial readjustment had taken place, required the whole process to be repeated a second time. The amendment would spare the public from further confusion and expense on this account during the 1980s.
Clause 2(2) reads:
This amendment would maintain the size of the House of Commons at approximately its present strength. The relative representation of the various provinces is determined by a formula found in Rules 1 through 6 of section 51 in which one province, Quebec, serves as the reference point. Quebec's representation now stands at 75, but is to increase by four with each successive readjustment of electoral districts, producing a corresponding increase for other provinces through application of the formula, which takes into account relative populations among other factors.
By virtue of this arbitrary increment, it is estimated that the number of members will rise from 282 to over 300 at the next redistribution. However, if, as proposed by the Bill, the figure for Quebec were held constant at 75, the figures for the other provinces would also remain steady under the formula, unless their population grew at a rate significantly higher than Quebec's.
The amendment would leave intact the formula itself, which was arrived at after extended negotiations among members of all parties in Parliament. At the
Representation Act, 1984
same time, it would avert the expansion of the House of Commons to unwieldy proportions by the year 2001.
In preparing to discuss this Bill this afternoon I took the time to go back and look at my speech on a similar Bill, Bill C-276, which I introduced in this House in Private Members' Hour on July 23, 1982. I distilled the 20-minute speech I made at that time to a very few points. The point was made in debate that large ridings with twice the population of the average riding received only half the representation. I agrued then, as I would argue now, that large ridings, usually urban ridings obviously, because of the concentration of population and the growth in population following a census, received equally good representation from their Members as those ridings in Prince Edward Island, for example, where the total population of a constituency is perhaps 25,000 or 35,000 people.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) and his neighbour on the other side of the House, the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) sometimes complain that they have difficulty in attending to all the mail and phone calls they get. I have a great deal of sympathy for that position. I suggest, however, that increasing the number of Members of Parliament in the House of Commons is not the answer. There are a great many ways that the workload can be made easier for them. I will deal with some of them in a little while.
We only have to go south of the border to see that our counterparts there in the House of Representatives have an average of 400,000 people in each of their constituencies, while we have, on average, less than 100,000. I suggest to you that our constituents are not four times better served in Canada. I would make no comparison between the two. I am confident that our colleagues south of the border do their very best to serve their constituents as we do. The number of people in a constituency is not any reason at all to enlarge the House of Commons.
I also took some time to look at the speech given by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), on January 13, 1981 when he introduced a Bill not dissimilar to mine in intent, although there was some lack of similarity in the wording. Bill C-223 was finally referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections but unfortunately, despite the excellent arguments made by my colleague from Red Deer at that time, the Bill died there. I do not intend to go into detail on the arguments that were made by my colleague at that time. Not unreasonably, they dealt primarily with the way the Bill would affect western Canada. However good his arguments were, the committee, with a majority from the Government Party, allowed the Bill to die and no action was taken.
I could make the partisan argument which my friends on the government side of the House may well want to consider, that is, that leaving the membership of the House as it is how would be better for them than it would be for Members on this side of the House. If you were to follow the redistribution process and add, as is required now, four more seats to the

June 19, 1984
Representation Act, 1984
Province of Quebec, you would indeed add over 30 seats to other provinces, primarily Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. Given the preponderence of the members of this political Party in those provinces, it would seem to me that any cautious Liberal Government would not want the membership of the House to increase since it would obviously stand to lose in an election. We could use that argument, but I do not think it is a particularly valid argument. I happen to think that in the next general election there may well be a major shift in the representation of our Party from Quebec and certainly a large increase in Ontario. If the Government Party wants to look at it that way, it may well want to support this Bill.
I intend to deal with what I perceive to be the need or, more correctly, the lack of need for the enlargement of the House of Commons. In legislation the House of Commons primarily reacts to the need of the population of Canada. In those instances where the Government has very rashly gone against the wishes of the electorate in general-instituting the metric system and doing away with capital punishment are two examples of this-there have been repeated requests by the population in all provinces to undo those measures. Those are two examples of which I can think where there was a general outcry from the public to take action. Where does anyone hear a general outcry by the public now to increase the number of Members of the House of Commons, to increase the spending that goes with it, to increase the bureaucracy and the office space and to increase the services and amenities? Where is the general outcry for that? I suggest that it is really not there.
Having said that, I want to interject one note. I have been a member of the Management and Members' Services Committee for some years. I know that you have sat on that committee from time to time, Mr. Speaker. However, I have sat there longer than any other Member, barring one, since its inception. I want to say that with a new administration in the House of Commons brought in by the previous Speaker, the increases in the House of Commons itself, as opposed to the increases in general government spending, have been very much in line. As a matter of fact, those increases have been kept to 5 per cent or less over the past few years at a time when other Departments have gone to 15 per cent and as high as 20 per cent increases. Even so, at the time when my colleague, the Hon. Member for Red Deer, was debating his Bill, the cost of the House of Commons stood at approximately $100 million. In 1984, the cost of the House of Commons has risen to $146 million. Surely there is no desire on anyone's part to increase that cost.
As you will be aware, we have introduced for the benefit of Members of Parliament a system that goes by the name of OASIS. That stands for Office Automation System and Information Services. That system, which in part could be brought on stream later this month, will be the finest electronic system in any legislature in the world when it is completed. I say that with a great deal of pride, having been part of the body that has worked on that system over the past few years.
Indeed, we have been consulted by members of other legislative bodies. Most recently there was a small group from the United Kingdom here to look at what we were doing. That system will allow present Members of Parliament to serve their constituency far better and easier than they have in the past, yet it will continue to provide Members with the background information that is necessary for them to serve in the House of Commons, perhaps to a greater degree than they presently are.
It seems to me that there is within the system the promise of the ability for all Members of Parliament to serve double and indeed triple the number of people whom they already serve. If this is the case, where is the justification for enlarging the House of Commons? There is no justification. There is no justification for the disruption caused by the changes in boundaries. We have all gone through them. While I do not say this to denigrate urban areas, we know that particularly in rural areas Members can drive down a country road and know every resident along that road. When the Government arbitrarily redistributes the boundary lines and sets out new areas so that people can participate in the next election, citizens become terribly upset. They have been used to dealing with a constituency. They are used to dealing with the people in the area. To have that changed is an unnecessary disruption.
Let me use my own constituency now and my former constituency prior to the redistribution as an example. Over the years, the people in Hastings County have obviously dealt with the City of Belleville as their county seat. They are used to listening to the radio from Belleville and watching television from that area. They are used to using the telephone book and newspapers emanating from Belleville. When the Government arbitrarily changed that and chopped Hastings into two ridings, they found themselves torn apart.
While my colleague, the Member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Vankoughnet), does a good job of serving those people whom I previously served, nevertheless they do not relate to the town of Napanee. They do not read newspapers from the town of Napanee. They do not find the town of Napanee in the telephone book. There is a distinct confusion when this happens.
There is no justification for the disruption. There is no justification for the confusion, and certainly there is no justification for the expense that would follow a redistribution which would increase the number of Members of this House to perhaps 310 members. Just the physical problem alone of putting 35 Members within this Chamber would be tough enough. Despite all that confusion, disruption and expense, there is simply no justification for increasing the size of the House of Commons.
I ask my colleagues within the House today, rather than talking the Bill out, to allow it to go to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Perhaps we will still have an opportunity to deal with it in some depth before the end of the session.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-
June 19, 1984

Hastings (Mr. Ellis) for bringing this subject to our attention at this time. It is a timely subject because we are just on the eve of the redistribution order going out which will make into law the recommendations of the redistribution commissions across Canada.
I can sympathize with his remarks about rural constituencies. When I was first elected in 1965,1 had a small, compact riding of approximately 45,000 square miles. As a result of two redistributions, it is now 155,000 square miles. I can understand the pressures that rural Members come under in trying to serve ever-increasing geographical areas as well as ever-increasing numbers of people scattered over a wider geographical base. There is no question that it makes life more difficult for those Members and that it also reduces the quality of the representation that people in rural areas get because their Members are spread over such a wide distance.
Having said that, I think I should return to the terms of the Bill and point out to the Hon. Member and the House that, according to the Constitution of Canada, we are obliged to have a redistribution of parliamentary seats after each census. I was the Parliamentary Secretary to two Presidents of the Privy Council in the 1970s who had the responsibility of bringing forward the current legislation based on what we call the amalgam method.
I recall very well the original Bill for redistribution as put forward by the then President of the Privy Council, the current Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). That Bill provided that there would be a redistribution in which there would be a decrease in the House of Commons of one seat from 265 to 264. Hon. Members will recall the outcry, the outrage and the viciousness of the attacks on the Government not only from the four Opposition Parties in those days but from the back-benchers on the government side at the horrendous changes the redistribution Bill would have made to the House of Commons. What it would do in effect is to take away seats from five or six provinces and redistribute them to Ontario and, I believe, to British Columbia. There was a vicious debate that went on over a period of time until the Government got the message and, at the final moment, intercepted with a piece of legislation that interrupted the process. It was clear from that debate and the arguments in the House of Commons and in committee that the House was not prepared to accept a redistribution that would involve the loss of seats to smaller provinces.
As a result of that commitment, which the Government was forced to accept, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections was re-established to look into the matter, and the Government, after the election of 1974, came down with a series of proposals which were put before that committee.
One of the problems is that the Constitution of Canada provides for a form of representation in the House of Commons based on representation by population. We have never done that in the absolute. We have always tended in that direction but we have never attempted to apply that principle
Representation Act, 1984
across the board. We have always recognized that there are very large provinces, very small provinces, and some in the middle. We have always recognized that provinces require a certain level of representation in the House of Commons. There have been a number of formulae in various Acts which have protected the position of small provinces. It was really not until the great demographic changes of our country in the 1950s and 1960s, which led up to the redistribution of the 1970s, that we realized that the old system would no longer work. Therefore, a drastic overhaul was called for.
In the case of the proposition that representation was a major point of the exercise, three other principles also were developed to protect it.
The first was that no province could have fewer Members of Parliament than it had Senators. This principle protected, for example, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. This principle was added in 1915. The second principle was that no province could lose more than 15 per cent of its representation in a redistribution. This was added in 1952. The third principle was that no province could have fewer Members in the House of Commons than a province with a smaller population.
The problem was how to balance all of these conflicting problems. Furthermore, how could you balance these conflicting problems in light of what happened from 1972 to 1974 when it was clear that the House would no longer accept the principle that provinces could lose seats? Even with these three principles, the provinces had to be protected.
The difficulty was finding a new system. When the Privileges and Elections Committee met in 1974, it had five propositions before it which were designed to give the committee a variety of options. The committee, after investigating, chose the one which the Government proposed, the amalgam method. Why? Because that seemed to satisfy the requirements. As a result, the committee accepted it with a certain amount of enthusiasm. When the committee examined what could be done with the other four recommendations which the Government had presented, it decided that the amalgam method made the most sense. Second, the committee cast its net as broadly as it could among those few experts in Canada who knew anything about redistribution, and it was unable to come up with any other interpretation that would be satisfactory. The consequence was that, with some minor amendments, we ended up with the amalgam system and it went into effect in the redistribution which took place in the election of 1979.
I can certainly agree with the Hon. Member for Prince Edward Hastings that every sitting Member at that time who went through the redistribution found it an extraordinarily painful process. The problem we face today is that this is the second redistribution under that formula. As the Hon. Member for Prince Edward Hastings noted, the size of the House will increase substantially.
Shame.

The question we now have to decide is whether that redistribution should take place,

June 19, 1984
Representation Act, 1984
whether it will provide better representation for Canadians, whether it will be neutral or whether it will produce less representation for Canadians. Like the Hon. Member for Prince Edward Hastings, my own personal prejudice, quite frankly, is toward a smaller House. I would prefer a smaller House.
Hear, hear!

I was here, like many other Members, when the House consisted of 264 Members. When we had the elections in 1979 and 1980, I was rather overwhelmed with the impact that another 12 Members could make in the House of Commons. But nonetheless I believe the question has to be looked at basically from the view of the smaller provinces, and whether or not their position in Confederation would be better or worse. Second, what will be the quality of representation available to the rural areas. If you do not increase the number of seats, then clearly any redistribution that takes place will quickly move seats from the rural areas into the cities. We all know why. The cities are growing more rapidly than the rural areas. Third, we know that population is moving from smaller provinces to the larger provinces. Fourth, if we do not provide additional seats, these tendencies will be hastened with a smaller House and will be made far more difficult.
I was of the opinion that the proposals of the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, who led the charge against the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act of 1972, would, in effect, have an adverse impact on his home province of Saskatchewan, on Manitoba, and on the Maritimes. It struck me that those provinces were better off with a system in a smaller House where their Members would have more clout than in a bigger House where their Members would make up a smaller proportion of the whole. I argued that point with Members from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and the Maritimes. But so overpoweringly difficult was the concept that provinces would lose seats, that some provinces would come down to their Senate floor, and that some provinces would have enormous problems of compression when it came to the redistribution of seats that, by and large, they opted for the easy way out, which was to expand the membership. Having done that, and having agreed to that proposition, we ended up with the question: if you added 12 Members, what would be the status the next time? Could you just live with the increase of 12 Members? When you examined the demographics of the situation, you came immediately to the proposition that you could not, that you would end up with exactly the same proposition in the next redistribution. Therefore, the amalgam method was designed to provide a controlled increase of the House over three redistributions where it was thought it would level off and hold.
We are debating whether or not this should go forth. I believe that we have to look back to what our reactions were in the 1972 to 1974 period. It is my view that we cannot ignore the judgment we made at that point. Those of us who represented rural ridings know what happened even with the
increase in seats. My constituency in the Province of Ontario, which received seven additional seats, I believe, tripled in geographical size, and in terms of population increased from about 52,000 to about 78,000, an increase of over 50 per cent. The representation of those people in that geographical area is a very difficult job for whoever happens to be the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River.
This was not an isolated case. If we take a look at rural Canada and at rural Ontario, we find that the rural ridings expanded pretty well all over, except those which had a significant urban population moving into the edge of it, for example, Nepean-Carleton at one point.
The dilemma is how we provide representation which will be acceptable. As a result of the premises which I have outlined that no province should lose seats, that no province should be in a position of going below its Senate numbers and that no province should have fewer Members in the House than a province with a smaller population, if we accept those principles we are in a conundrum. We would be in a conundrum if we stopped it at the population of the House of Commons today, at 282.
I doubt the redistribution commissioners would be any more successful in satisfying the House now than they were in 1974 when their last propositions came forward. It seems to me that that is the nub of the problem. The nub of the problem is how we represent all parts of Canada on an equal base. How do we represent all parts of Canada on a relatively equal population base or on a relatively equivalent regional base? In other words, how do we square the circle?
When we studied the present system in committee, we realized that it was certainly not perfect. It has great difficulties. It operates in some ways very irrationally, according to the formula we have laid down, but only because the conditions we have built into the formula are somewhat contradictory and somewhat irrational. Therefore, I regret that I cannot support that proposition of the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) because it does not deal with the conundrum facing us at this time. I know that he and the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) have been very aggressive in arguing the point that we should stop. However, it seems to me that where they have been deficient is in not being able to tell us how to resolve the very real regional, provincial and local conundrums into which we keep running.
Ideally it would have been practical to put into place the original proposition of the then President of the Privy Council, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), but it was unacceptable. If the Government had come before the House with a similar Bill today, it too would have been unacceptable. It would have been acceptable to certain provinces in the West. Certainly it would have been acceptable to many provinces in the East, but probably it would have been unacceptable to Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia as well. We have a very real problem in balancing the considerations of locality, provinciality and regionalism.
June 19, 1984

I should like to go one step further and talk about the Bill presented by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings. There is a bit of a technical problem with the proposition he has raised. In dealing with some of the details of this matter, it would be helpful for Hon. Members to understand just exactly what are some of our problems. Let me start first by looking at the explanatory notes to the Bill. They indicate:
The relative representation of the various provinces is determined by a formula found in Rules 1 to 6 of Section 51 in which one province, Quebec, serves as a reference point.
That is partly right and partly wrong. It is true that there is a base number of seats for Quebec. This is stated in Rule 1 under Subsection 51(1) of the Constitution Act. The number of seats allocated to Quebec is to rise at each subsequent redistribution by four. Under Rule 2, the electoral quotient for Quebec is divided into the population of each large province to determine the membership of the large province in the House of Commons. A large province is defined as any province other than Quebec having a population of more than 2.5 million. Following the 1971 census, only Ontario was categorized as a large province. Following the 1981 census, British Columbia was also included in this category.
The technical problem with the Bill is that the number of Members for small provinces, that is those with less than 1.5 million people, and for intermediate provinces, that is between 1.5 million and 2.5 million people, is calculated independently from the electoral quotient for Quebec. There is no relationship between their quotient and that for Quebec.
For small provinces, an electoral quotient is obtained by dividing their total population at the penultimate decennial census by the number of Members assigned to those provinces in the readjustment following the completion of that census. In other words, the practice is completely different, taking into account this census and the last census, as opposed to how we calculated for the large province where it is only done on the basis of population for that particular census.
Having done that, the quotient is then divided into the population of each province at the most recent census to determine its representation in the House of Commons. The Senate floor rule then comes into play. It prevents any province from having fewer seats than the number of Senators who sit for that province in the Senate. In the redistribution which led to the Representation Order proclaimed on June 11, 1976, the computation resulted only in Prince Edward Island being entitled to one seat and New Brunswick to nine. However, the Senate floor rule raised Prince Edward Island to four and New Brunswick to 10.
If Hon. Members thought that was difficult, they should look at the computation for what is called the intermediate provinces. It is more complicated. Again it is not determined by the electoral quotient for the Province of Quebec. It is calculated independently. In the last redistribution we had only two provinces in that category-British Columbia and Alberta. Under the present redistribution, British Columbia has moved into the large province size and Alberta is the only province which sits in the intermediate sector. I think Hon.
Representation Act, 1984
Members understand the difficulty with the proposal of the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings.

Mr. Speaker, having been a Member of Parliament through two redistributions- and perhaps I will be one through the third redistribution-I understand the concerns of the Hon. Member who made the proposal today. While he has raised and described the difficulties, he has not really answered any of the problems. He suggested at one point that what we have now was brought forward by the Government. That is true only to the extent that anything that passes Parliament is brought forward by the Government. The fact is that the present system which led to the increase in the number of Members of Parliament was agreed to by the majority of the House of Commons and, if I remember correctly, by a majority from every Party. The reason it was agreed to was because many Members of Parliament realized the tremendous difficulties which would be created if we did not increase the size of the House.
When I was elected I represented 125,000 people because in the years before the 1962 election my part of Winnipeg, like so many other areas and cities across Canada, had experienced a very rapid expansion. I had more people in my constituency than lived in the Province of Prince Edward Island. When there were federal-provincial meetings, I would ask why I could not be present because I represented more people than did the Premier of Prince Edward Island.
Let us look at what would happen if we do not increase the number of Members of Parliament. The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) has gone through a description of how the number of seats is allocated to each province. In the Province of Manitoba, which I represent, we went from 14 seats when I was elected to 13 seats. We could do the calculations very easily. In about 25 years, Manitoba would be down to ten seats. We would stay at ten seats only because that is the number of Senators for Manitoba. Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would be in the same situation. The largest provinces would have more members and the smaller provinces would have fewer members.
That is not the whole story, or even the worst part of it. Of 14 constituencies in Manitoba, the constituency of Churchill covers two-thirds of the geographic area of that province. CLose to 60 per cent of the people of Manitoba live in the metropolitan area of Winnipeg. The same situation exists in British Columbia where the Cities of Vancouver and New Westminster have a very large percentage of the population. There is the same situation with Calgary and Edmonton in Alberta, Toronto and Hamilton in Ontario and Montreal in the Province of Quebec.
What is happening and will continue to happen if you limit the number of Members of Parliament to a fixed number will be predictable. The population will continue to grow in the urban areas. Not so many years ago, more than 50 per cent of the Canadian population lived in rural and isolated areas. I do not have the exact figures, but I believe in the United States

June 19, 1984
Representation Act, 1984
about 7 per cent of the population now lives on farms. I presume we are moving in that direction in Canada.
What will happen in the smaller provinces in particular, and in the larger provinces as well, is that the population in the urban areas will grow and in the rural and isolated areas it will be reduced or remain constant. Therefore, at the time of each redistribution the number of Members from urban areas will increase and the number from rural areas will decrease.
In my own Province of Manitoba, at some point in the future 650,000 or 700,000 of the one million population may live in the area of metropolitan Winnipeg. If the present constituency of Churchill remains as at present, covering two-thirds of the area of Manitoba, and if we drop to ten Members, one from Churchill and nine for the rest of the province, there will be six or seven Members from urban Winnipeg and two or three for the rural population of Manitoba. Province to province, you will have the same situation.
This is the exact reverse of what the Member who introduced the motion wants to do. Those representing rural constituencies would represent very large areas. With telephones, modern means of communication and better roads, it is much easier than it was 30 or 40 years ago. Far be it for me to claim to be an expert on the work of a rural Member of Parliament. However, I believe it would be very difficult for a rural Member to represent an area 300 to 400 miles from west to east and from north to south.
I agree there are many difficulties with the system we now have, which was agreed to by most Members of all Parties. While there are many difficulties, while we have not achieved the principle of representation by population, which is our theoretical objective, we have recognized that there are special problems with rural and isolated areas. A rural Member or a northern Member will represent less people than a Member representing an urban area. While we have not solved all of the problems, we do have a system which is as fair as possible.
I recognize all the objections to the system. I understand how people feel when they read that in the future we may have 300 Members of Parliament. However, the alternative of fixing the number, given that we want some concept of representation by population and want to ensure that rural and isolated areas have adequate representation, the present system is probably as good as can be devised.
I would be happy if somebody made suggestions to improve the system. I would look at any ideas. However, the simplistic solution of fixing the number of Members that we have at present would create tremendous problems, something the Member who introduced the motion wants to avoid.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us this afternoon presented by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward Hastings (Mr. Ellis) proposes to maintain the size of the House of Commons at approximately its present strength by amending Rule 1 of the representation rules set out in Section 21 of the Constitution Act, formerly known as the British North American Act, so that the number of Members
from Quebec would not automatically rise by four in each redistribution of seats.
I have been thinking about this for some time. I agree in great part with the Member. Before getting into my main speech and the information I have gathered, it seems that over the years we have done a great deal of talking about representation by population. With all respect to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), I suggest that we represent people as opposed to areas.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell), who was here a few moments ago, represents 25,000 people. From 1974 to 1979, I represented 125,000 in the riding of St. Catharines. If there had been representation by population, there should have been five of us in that city. I have not been able to come to grips with the whole idea of area versus people. Unlike people, areas do not have rights, and in that sense it is the people in the areas that we represent.
My dilemma is that basically I agree that we should limit this House to whatever number of seats we decide upon collectively. What will happen to this House of Commons over the years? The grievances that we have had will not be rectified in any particular way and we will keep going down the same path. Representation by population will ultimately fall by the wayside.
We often talk about rural areas. The Hon. Member has said that the rural area constitutes two-thirds of the Province of Manitoba. We could all understand the difficulty of getting around in an area like that if we had access only to horses and buggies. I could even understand it if there were only automobiles in which to get around. However, these days we have aircraft at our disposal. The Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky) is present today. I know that his riding is very large in area.
Three hundred and fifty miles from the north to the south, and 250 miles across, and I have no airplanes at my disposal.

That is why we are having some of these problems. However, airplanes and helicopters tend to minimize problems which we once thought were insurmountable.
At one point or other, the House will truly have to come to grips with the whole concept of representation by population. I would like to put myself on the side of those people who say that we should be representing people as opposed to representing areas or land masses. Having said that, I am not sure that the Bill as it has been put forward by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings will necessarily accomplish what the Hon. Member sets out to accomplish. Perhaps I could put the matter into my perspective and share with other Hon. Members some of my dilemmas.
Even though the Bill which is before us proposes to leave the number of Members from Quebec at a static level, the representation from other provinces would still increase at the time of the redistribution which would follow the 1991 census.
June 19, 1984

Only the representation from Quebec would stay the same while the representation from the other provinces would change. The number of seats allocated to Quebec directly influences only the number of seats allocated to the so-called larger provinces as outlined in the redistribution rules. The effect of this Bill would be to leave unchanged the rules for allocating seats to the small and intermediate provinces. As I understand it, there will be only one intermediate province after the next redistribution and that will be Alberta.
I do not wish to dwell on the fault inherent in this Bill. I do wish that I had a perfect solution to offer. I wish I could say: "Look, your Bill is wrong and this is what is right and this is what we should be doing." I am still struggling with the concept. Logic would tend to put me on the side of those who say that they are representing people as opposed to geographic areas.
If I may, for the benefit of all of us, I would like to offer some comments on the background of electoral redistribution in Canada. It is important to note that it is not a simple matter. Other Members have already said that. There are probably as many solutions to the problem as there are Members of Parliament. Redistribution is an especially complicated matter because of the federal nature of our country, and also because of some of its unique geographical and ethnic characteristics. I shall try to deal with both of those reasons.
It is widely held that Members of the House of Commons are elected on the basis of representation by population. I believe that is the myth that we hold out. The old cry for "rep by pop" arose in Canada West, the area which is now the Province of Ontario, prior to confederation. The residents of that part of the United Province of Canada complained bitterly about the fact that Canada East and Canada West had equal representation in the Parliament of that day, even though the population of Canada West had come to exceed that of Canada East. In 1840 when Upper and Lower Canada were united, the opposite was the case. However, the situation had become reversed and this grievance was one of many which had to be settled in the years of discussion which led to confederation in 1867.
When the Constitution Act was passed, it provided for the apportionment of seats in the House of Commons after each census according to certain rules and limitations. The distribution of seats among the four founding provinces was outlined in the original Section 51 of the Constitution Act. Quebec was assigned 65 seats, a convenient arrangement since that was the same number of constituencies that existed within Canada East before confederation. In 1867, the other three provinces were allocated Members of the House of Commons according to the relationship of their populations to the population of Quebec. Section 52 of the Constitution Act provided and continues to provide the following:
The number of Members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the Parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this Act is not thereby disturbed.
From the beginning, the distribution of seats among provinces was automatic. The ratio between seats from the various
Representation Act, 1984
provinces and the total number of Members in the House of Commons could be changed only by constitutional amendment. On several occasions since 1867, amendments to the Constitution Act were necessary. The most recent such amendment occurred about nine years ago in 1975 when the representation of the Northwest Territories was increased from one seat to two. The necessity for a constitutional amendment was entrenched in the Canadian Constitution by virtue of the provisions of paragraph 42(1) (a) of the Constitution Act, 1982, which requires that an amendment to the Constitution of Canada in relation to the principle of proportionate representation of the provinces in the House of Commons prescribed by the Constitution of Canada may only be made in accordance with the general amending procedure set out in Subsection 38(1) of the Constitution Act of 1982.
It is clear that the principle of representation by population was established early in our history as a united country. Within provinces, the size of constituencies often varied dramatically. Witness the words of the previous speaker, a Member who comes from Winnipeg, who said that one out of the ten ridings in Manitoba covers a geographic area equal to two-thirds the size of the entire province. This reflected the existence of huge, sparsely settled areas throughout the nation and the fact that there were limits on the size of a constituency which a Member of Parliament could reasonably represent. In addition, it became a fairly well established custom, even in the late 19th century, that urban seats would, as a rule, be larger than those in rural areas. Note that we are speaking of the 19th century, 100 years ago. Surely we have progressed enough now that we must somehow be able to make decisions based not solely upon geography.
The rule of representation by population was applied much more accurately among provinces than among the electoral districts within the provinces. Even so, there were departures from the principle of representation by population not long after confederation.
When Manitoba entered confederation in 1870 it was granted four Members, even though the population of the province entitled it to representation by only one Member. In 1871, British Columbia, which is now one of the larger provinces, was given six Members when there were only enough inhabitants in that province to justify two Members. In 1873, Prince Edward Island became the seventh province and, though entitled to only five Members, received six Members. When the great expanse of land which now includes Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Territories was first given representation in the House of Commons in 1886, the strict rules of representation by population were again departed from.

We should not compare the British system to the one we have.
The Government brags about how many hours of debate there have been. The House has heard that from the two or three Liberal speakers who finally rose to speak today on closure.
