Why does the Government not accept some of the recommendations which have been made? If recommendations are not made by Liberals, they are no good. That is a terrible situation to have in a country such as ours. However, that is what happens every time the Government does not want to accept recommendations.
The Government brags about the hearings which were held on this legislation. Recommendations were made by 25 organizations. Did the Government accept any of those recommendations? Is there an amendment based on one of those recommendations? Those organizations did not come to Ottawa simply to talk, they wanted action. Most of the organizations were opposed to a civilian organization. But, that does not make any difference; the Government knows better. The Liberals do not go by democracy any more. They go by totalitarianism-the Government knows better and it knows what is good for the people. The Government will tell the people what is good for them. That is what the Government has been saying for a number of years.
Almost half of the nation objected to the national energy policy, but it did not make any difference. Closure was moved,
the legislation was passed and an industry was destroyed. It ruined hundreds of people in western Canada. Recommendations were made to the Crow legislation but that did not make any difference, the Government knew better. It introduced the legislation and gave the whole shebang to the CPR. No wonder Mr. Turner decided to run for the Party. How could he lose with the whole organization backing him? The Government could not be against the CPR. Now we have the future Prime Minister who is a director of the CPR.
Another matter which bothers me is that there has been no debate on why the RCMP was not chosen. What did the Government say? It said that the MacKenzie Commission in 1969 recommended a civilian service. The Mackenzie Commission did not study a civilian organization. What did the commission have to compare with since there was no civilian organization? If it was so wonderful in 1969, why did the Government not adopt it? It has been 15 years since that recommendation and the Government has not done a thing about it. Do not tell me about the Mackenzie Commission; this Government rejected that 15 years ago.
We could talk about the McDonald Commission which was set up to investigate the RCMP. That commission did not investigate a civilian organization. In no way did it have the authority to start telling people what kind of an intelligence service we should have in this country. Now we have this Bill.
Was the RCMP too hard on the communists? Is that why the Government does not want the RCMP? Has the RCMP refused the patronage which the Government wanted to give to it? Sure, the RCMP would do that. Maybe that is why the Government does not want it. It wants a civilian organization which will provide a few more jobs for a few more Liberal hacks.
In Britain, legislation goes to the Senate. If it is not right, it goes back. What happens here? It goes to a Liberal-dominated Senate which would pass anything and everything. The Canadian Senate even passed the holiday Bill. It was passed in this House by 13 Members. It went through all stages in one afternoon. In Britain, they would throw it back to the House of Commons. They have a system over there. This Government should not compare itself with the Mother Parliament.
In Canada, 71 per cent of the people do not want a civilian organization. They do not want civilians who are appointed by this Government to open their first-class mail. Neither do I. That does not matter because this Liberal Government knows better. It is made up of totalitarians. When these Liberals became Members they suddenly obtained a mass of wisdom they did not have before. Therefore, these Members can now tell the people of Canada what is good for them. The Government tells the people of Canada that this Bill is good for them, but the people do not want it. Mr. Speaker, I believe that, considering the importance of this legislation and the motion for time allocation now before the House, it would perhaps be useful to put things into perspective and try and find some serious justification for adopting a Bill that, I agree, is controversial. I have been sitting on the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and have been a member of the Committee since 1968.1 have tried to analyse the facts, to find some convincing reasons for supporting a Bill that, I repeat, is controversial.
I have found three reasons, Mr. Speaker, and I shall mention them briefly.
In the last fifteen years, two commissions have recommended creating a separate, civilian security intelligence agency.
In 1969, the MacKenzie Commission stated, and I quote:
Aside from a number of similarities in the investigation methods used, the differences between the responsibilities of a police corps and those of a security service would seem to be very distinct. The primary concern of a police corps is to enforce the law, to investigate offences, to collect evidence and to bring offenders before the courts. Security services are mainly engaged in preventive action and the collection of information ... Briefly, we believe that there is a distinct difference between the professional security officer and the professional police officer, and that this difference should be reflected in how they are recruited-
Mr. Speaker, I could also quote the McDonald Commission and the Senate Committee. In other words, I feel that anything is preferable to the status quo. It was the status quo that allowed the RCMP, that respected force, to take inappropriate action in Quebec, and I can certainly not find here any justification for the attitude of my hon. friends opposite, who in spite of all its shortcomings and imperfections, prefer the present situation to the proposed system. I am giving this Bill my approval in principle in order to eliminate the status quo and look to the future, even if I would have preferred to see a number of clauses amended.

speechtext:
1.	Does the Department of Fisheries and Oceans have specific responsibilities in connection with the surveillance of coastal waters and, if so, what are they?
2.	Does the Royal Canadian Mounted Police patrol coastal waters?
3.	Does the Canadian Coast Guard make routine surveillance patrols in coastal waters?
4.	To which ministry do the RCMP and Coast Guard report for co-ordination of their activities?
5.	Is the Department of National Defence responsible for the co-ordination of any search and rescue operations and which ministry has the responsibility for determining the need for and extent of such operations?
6.	Does the Department of the Environment maintain any continuing activity in coastal waters and, if so, what activity?
7.	Do the Departments of Energy, Mines and Resources and of Indian Affairs and Northern Development maintain aerial surveillance over coastal waters and, if so, is any information obtained passed to one or more co-ordination centres?
8.	Which ministry, or ministries has or have the authority to issue instructions to private shipping in coastal waters?

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed as follows:
1.	Under the Government Organization Act, 1979 the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans' duties, powers and functions include all matters not by law assigned to any other department, board or agency of the Government of Canada relating to:
(i)	sea coast and inland fisheries,
(ii)	fishing and recreational harbours,
(iii)	hydrography and marine sciences, and
(iv)	the co-ordination of the policies and programs of the Government of Canada respecting oceans, and such other matters over which the Parliament has jurisdiction relating to oceans as are by law assigned to the Minister.
In order to fulfil the Minister's responsibilities, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans operates a fleet of fisheries patrol, hydrographic and marine science craft on both coasts. The fisheries patrol vessels conduct patrols for the purpose of monitoring foreign and domestic fishing activity to ensure the conservation and protection of fish stocks under the Fisheries Act and the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act.
2.	The Royal Canadian Mounted Police has several motor vessels located on both the East and West coasts. These vessels are a means of transportation and used for the enforcement of several federal statutes, such as the Fisheries Act, the Canada Shipping Act, the small vessel regulations, the Narcotic Control Act, the Excise Act and others. In addition to these duties,
Order Paper Questions
the RCMP vessels are also used in an assistance capacity, in search and rescue operations, and mercy escorts (transportation of sick/injured persons) whenever the situation arises.
3.	The Canadian Coast Guard (CCG) conducts surveillance patrols of coastal waters by ship for the purpose of marine search and rescue, the maintenance of aids to navigation, and pollution prevention. Canadian Coast Guard icebreakers carry out missions in these areas as secondary tasks. Pollution prevention patrols are also carried out by a Coast Guard fixed wing aircraft over the Canadian portion of the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence River, and the Gulf as far as Sept-Iles. The Department of National Defence assist the Coast Guard in pollution surveillance as a secondary task during the course of their normal air reconnaissance missions.
4.	In their individual capacities, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and Canada Coast Guard report to separate ministries. The RCMP reports to the Solicitor General of Canada and the CCG reports directly to the Minister of Transport. Should the RCMP and CCG work jointly on a venture, i.e. search and rescue, they do so still under the auspices and direction of their individual Ministers.
5.	The Minister of National Defence is responsible for the co-ordination of SAR operations and for determining the necessity and extent of these operations. The Department of National Defence is responsible for co-ordinating all air and marine search activity in Canada and adjacent areas for which Canada has accepted responsibility under international agreements and for providing dedicated air resources to respond to both air and marine distress incidents.
6.	In so far as the Department of Environment is concerned, the following activities are carried out by each service in coastal waters:
Atmospheric Environment Service-issues marine and aviation weather forecasts to the 200-mile limit; operates ice reconnaissance, oil slick trajectory, and voluntary weather observing programs.
Canadian Wildlife Service-carries out inventory surveys and research of marine birds and implements regulations under Migratory Birds Convention Act.
Environmental Protection Service-responsible for protection of marine environmental quality through (i) environmental assessment; (ii) protection from specific environmental threats (discharges from mines, pulpmills, municipalities, etc.); (iii) administration of Ocean Dumping Control Act and part of the Fisheries Act; (iv) response to environmental emergencies (e.g. oil spills); (v) general coastal zone management.
Parks Canada-controls certain surface water activities such as recreational boating around Pacific Rim Park and evaluates potential for establishment of other national marine parks.
7.	No.
8.	In so far as the Department of the Environment is concerned, the Environmental Protection Service does issue instructions pursuant to the Ocean Dumping Control Act and

June 19, 1984
Order Paper Questions
the Fisheries Act in relation to environmental protection considerations.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has the authority to direct the activities of foreign fishing vessels in terms of virtually all their operations within the 200-mile economic zone. The Department has no legal power to direct the activities of domestic fishing vessels except as they relate directly to fishing.
The Ministry of the Solicitor General does not have primary statutory responsibility in respect of shipping in coastal waters. However, the RCMP assists several federal departments in carrying out their statutory enforcement obligations in coastal waters. In this connection, the force is empowered to issue instructions to private shipping in coastal waters.
The Department of Transport is responsible for the safety of shipping and prevention of pollution from ships in Canadian waters. The Canadian Coast Guard has the authority to issue instructions to private shipping in coastal waters related to vessel traffic services, ship routing, conditions of shipping, or conditions of the ships themselves requiring intervention by the regulatory authority. The Department is also responsible for issuing notices to mariners and notices to shipping to warn mariners of any dangerous or unsafe conditions such as pending storms, the presence of ice or outages of aids to navigation.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this group of motions is a very important grouping. It deals with Clauses 17 to 20 inclusive of the Bill. These clauses establish the terms pursuant to which the proposed civilian security service may, as it was euphemistically called, share information with other government Departments, with foreign security intelligence services, or with foreign agencies.
The provision in Clause 18 is the provision which makes it an offence to disclose the identity of any person who is or was a confidential source of information or a person who is or was an employee engaged in covert operational activities.
Clause 19 is the provision which permits disclosure of information obtained by the service to a whole series of individuals, including literally any person in the Public Service of Canada where the director in his or her opinion believes that that disclosure would be helpful.
Clause 20 is the final clause in this package which grants the full array of immunities which are possessed by peace officers to the members of the proposed civilian security

June 19, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
service. It establishes a mechanism whereby possible illegality will be reported.
The purpose of these amendments is to strengthen what are at the moment clearly very seriously and fundamentally flawed clauses.
Dealing first with the provisions of Clause 17, this clause permits the service to pass on information which it has obtained, using all of the most intrusive techniques set out in this Bill. It permits the service to pass on this information literally to any security service anywhere in the world. I think it is appalling that Canada should be prepared to share information on Canadians and on refugees from other countries with foreign security agencies which, by the admission of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) himself, are not even acknowledged in their own countries. What kind of regressive, military dictatorships are we dealing with, Mr. Speaker, that would not even acknowledge their own intelligence agencies and with whom we are quite prepared to share all the information they seek?
The Canadian Council of Churches appeared before our committee and expressed its very grave concern about this provision, particularly in terms of the potential implications for political refugees from Third World countries. The Council had recommended that the Bill specifically prohibit arrangements with nations and organizations that have been found to permit gross systematic and consistent violations of fundamental human rights. That is one of the provisions which I have proposed in this package of amendments in the motions now before the House.
I have only ten minutes so I will be brief on Clause 18. This clause sets out the criminal sanction for any individual who discloses information that could reveal the identity of an individual who is or was an employee of the service. This provision goes far, far beyond comparable legislation in the United States, the Intelligence Identities Protection Act. I would note that that Act applies only to operatives engaged in foreign intelligence. We know the provisions of Bill C-9 would not in fact enhance the operations of the service outside Canada. This Bill would make it a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, for an individual to disclose that he or she was or is an operative of the service. It is only because of this kind of disclosure that historically in 1976-1977 many of the most serious abuses and criminal wrongdoings were revealed. But under the provisions of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, any individual who makes such a disclosure or any person in the press who repeats such disclosure could go to jail for five years. The provision was drafted far too broadly.
Clause 19 permits the service to use the information it has obtained through the use of intrusive techniques, bugging phones, breaking into homes, accessing income tax records and medical records. There is a whole array of powers. To whom can the service give this information? Incredibly, they can give that information virtually to anyone under the provisions of Clause 19 where it is stated that in the opinion of the director, the disclosure of the information to any Minister of the Crown or any person in the Public Service of Canada is essential in
the public interest. Not only is there a massive intrusion on the privacy of Canadians initially but, having intruded on that privacy, the director of the service can then pass on any of that information literally to any public servant anywhere in the country. One of our motions would ensure that that kind of massive violation of the privacy of Canadians would not be tolerated.
The final motions in this package which are tabled deal with proposed Clause 20. Clause 20 is the clause which was inserted in the Bill to provide the full array of protections accorded to peace officers to the agents of the new civilian security service. This is completely unacceptable, Mr. Speaker. It would permit agents of the new service effectively to take unto themselves the decision as to which laws can or cannot be broken in pursuit of the sweeping mandate under this legislation.
We know all too well the unfortunate history of the RCMP security service which involves breaking and entering, theft, fraud, kidnapping, forgery, and breaches of a whole series of laws. This would provide carte blanche to the service to decide whether or not, in pursuit of their objectives, their civilian security objectives, they should be permitted to break laws.
I proposed an amendment which would have clearly prohibited the service from at least breaking the Criminal Code. But Members on the Government side voted even that proposal down. There is nothing that would prevent the security service from breaking the Criminal Code in the pursuit of its activities.
The McDonald Commission documented a whole series of violations of the law. The response of this Government is, "Well, it may have been illegal then, but we will change the law and we make it legal now." What does that do to the rule of law in this country?
Finally the motions which I have before the House would ensure that not only the Attorney General of Canada but also the provincial attorneys general will be informed of any suspected breach of the criminal law. As it stands now, it is only the federal attorney general who is informed of such possible breaches of the law. We know all too well the history of this Government in refusing to take action, in refusing to uphold the rule of law in Canada, in insisting there is one law for the RCMP and another law for all other Canadians. We want to ensure, through this motion, that the provincial attorneys general as well will be given the authorization to proceed to prosecute if, indeed, there is evidence of a breach of the law.
In conclusion, with respect to the sweeping nature of the powers to hand on information to other police agencies, with respect to the overly broad nature of the offence of disclosure of identity, with respect to the abuses which can occur in disclosing information obtained and with respect to the law enforcement powers accorded under this Bill, powers which are not accorded to comparable agents in other jurisdictions, these motions, I submit, must be adopted by the House in order to protect the fundamental civil liberties of Canadians.
June 19, 1984

Mr. Speaker, the clauses we are considering now, Clauses 17, 18, 19 and 20, have caused a great deal of alarm not only in the riding of Spadina that 1 represent but in many other parts of the country. People are shocked to think that the Government is about to insist on establishing a secret police that will not be fully answerable to Parliament, because the information which will come to Parliament will all be screened by the director of the secret police, and that could enter into any kind of secret agreement with any agency of any foreign power which the Minister in charge and the Secretary of State for External Affairs choose to designate.
We have people in Canada who have come from all countries of the world with all kinds of governments. Some of them came on the run for their lives and have relatives or friends back home. I have spoken with many refugees, particularly from Latin American countries but also from eastern European and Asian countries. They are very uneasy, even under present conditions, about what might be done to people back home if certain agents of their home country obtain information about lawful words they may be uttering here or about legitimate and lawful actions which they may be taking here in criticism of dictatorial administrations back home. There are many people from countries such as those in Latin America who dare not speak out in Canada out of fear of the persecution which might be visited on their families and friends back home.
These proposals by the Government would make that situation far worse since it would then become potentially the duty of Canada's secret police to hand information to goodness knows whom in whatever country, perhaps based upon activities of naturalized Canadian citizens acting in Canada completely within the law. It is shocking that Canada would be asked to undertake to be the cat's-paw, the stooge for foreign dictatorships. That is clearly what the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) intends to provide when he refuses any kind of limitation on this clause concerning the human rights practices of governments to which this life and death information might be given.
There are millions of Canadians who are members of labour unions in Canada. Perhaps they are mostly Canadian born. I am not necessarily speaking of immigrants, but they are members of labour unions affiliated, for example through the Canadian Labour Congress, with groups such as the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions and with other labour bodies such as the International Labour Organization. There again they have grave concerns about what may be done by way of transferring information through Canada's proposed secret police to the secret police of any other country.
We have heard more than once the expression of concern of the Moderator of the United Church and others of the Canadian Council of Churches who have obligations as brothers and sisters within the Christian faith. The same applies to people of other faiths such as the Jewish faith and Asian faiths. Those
Security Intelligence Service
concerns are legitimate ones of people who practise those religions in Canada.
I should like to refer to a telegram from the Canadian Council of Churches dated June 6. It reads as follows:
Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, should not be passed by the present Parliament until (a) it makes clear and rigorous provisions for the accountability of the service,-
This is what we are concerned with in one of the amendments. Any lawbreaking should be fully accounted for, not covered over as provided by the Government's position. The telegram continues:
-(b) defines national security and describes more precisely those activities which are illegal under the Act, (c) provides for the continuation of a free and vigorous participatory society in which work for justice on behalf of the poor, the marginalized and refugees may be carried on without fear of surveillance and prosecution.
It was signed by the Reverend Dr. Donald W. Anderson, General Secretary of the Canadian Council of Churches. Also I have a telegram from the Committee for the Defence of Human Rights in Colombia. We may think of the problems in Colombia as being a small matter, but there are Canadians who are concerned about human rights there. The telegram reads:
As a committee which condemns the human rights abuses of the Colombian Government, we find the proposed Bill C-9 alarming and threatening. Even though our work is entirely legal this Bill could be used to secretly monitor our activities. It could be used to misinform, or inform out of context, the Colombian Government of our activities. In short, this is a dangerous and complex Bill which must not be passed.
It is signed by the Committee for the Defence of Human Rights in Colombia. I have another telegram which reads:
I am strongly opposed to Bill C-9. As someone who grew up in a Latin American dictatorship, watching Canada become more repressive frightens you.
It is signed by R. Mesa. Also I have a very practical proposal from another constituent, which reads:
Any Canadian who doesn't actively oppose Bill C-9 should be sentenced to a few years in many Latin American countries, to learn what a dangerous thing repressive power is.

Mr. Speaker, I accept your advice and wish to explain that I read them for the purpose of showing how this Bill or the proposal in it threatens the perceived safety of residents of Canada who consider that they are acting lawfully. They feel threatened because Clause 17 of the Bill proposes to give information to unnamed foreign powers under, perhaps, secret arrangements.
There is one further point I wish to make. I believe it is not sound in law to try to bind the conscience of any public servant. If it should happen, as it has throughout history, that a public servant engaged in police work feels that he has been led or pressured to violate his conscience in what he has done, and if he wishes to correct that situation morally and spiritual-

ly by speaking up, it ought not to be a matter for punishment if what he says is true. This Bill proposes to punish people for telling the truth about what they consider to be the misdeeds of the service. That is shameful. This provision ought to be withdrawn.
Finally, we should think of what will be done to all professional and government record keeping in the country if every time a person makes an entry he considers that it might be looked at by Canada's new secret police. It will destroy generations of professional tradition in objective and conscientious record keeping. The damage will not be undone for many years thereafter even when this unjust law has been repealed.

Mr. Speaker, I had thought that perhaps I might have to speak on a motion proposed by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) but I am very pleased to see that that motion is not being moved at this time. Therefore, I will confine my remarks to the motions which are before the House at this time.
These motions deal with Clauses 21, 22 and 24 of the proposed legislation, Bill C-9. These provisions really lie at the heart of this Bill because they deal with the powers which can be accorded to the new service. Clause 21 is the clause which permits the service to obtain warrants for unprecedented interventions into the private lives of Canadians. This would include warrants for mail opening, warrants for obtaining access to confidential income tax records, warrants for obtaining access to medical records, warrants for breaking into homes and warrants for stealing documents. The list goes on and on.
I would emphasize that the powers proposed in this provision of the legislation are unprecedented and are powers which do not exist at the present time. The Pitfield Committee, in reviewing these particular provisions, urged for the use of a number of safeguards before a judicial warrant could in fact be issued. One of the most important of such safeguards is one which would in effect provide a balancing test to ensure that a judge, in granting a warrant, would in fact weigh the possible threat to the privacy of Canadians against the worth of the information which would be obtained in the pursuit of national security. The amendment in question would require that where the judge is of the opinion that the intelligence to be gained through the issuance of a warrant outweighs the harm to

June 19, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
privacy that will result, provided that the judge is satisfied with the other conditions, the warrant could in fact be issued.
As well, I would note that the intrusive powers referred to in this Bill go far beyond those which were recommended by the McDonald Commission, because they could indeed be used against so-called domestic subversives. On that basis, I would strongly urge that these sweeping intrusive powers not be granted to the new agency. I could go on at some length to speak about the fact that these powers are unprecedented, but at this point I will take my seat and allow the debate to take its course.

Mr. Speaker, this grouping of amendments relating to clauses in the Bill concerns me very greatly. I have been engaged in labour union activities, church activities, peace movement activities and civil liberties activities. I have been active as a member of a residents' association. I have been aware of the activities of the RCMP which, in many cases, has infiltrated these groups and treated us as though, somehow or other, we were enemies of the state. That is very destructive and very harmful. The police have no business doing that.
For example, I know of the case of a theological student who joined a civil liberties group at McGill University for the purpose of opposing the padlock law, a law which some years later was struck down by the Supreme Court of Canada as being beyond the powers of the provincial Government of Quebec. Yet this student was harassed in the sense that the police visited his academic superiors to try to hinder his graduation and subsequent ordination. What does the Government envisage happening in Canada in the next few years that has never happened before that will require it to be allowed to snoop on the private medical records of patients against their will and the longstanding tradition of confidentiality?
Will we become another Bronx? It was not long ago that I was talking to two German deputies from Schleswig Holstein at a NATO parliamentary conference in Copenhagen. These two members of the Bundestag visited Houston, Texas, and New York City. The one who visited New York City spent two nights in a patrol car in the Bronx. He was horrified because it
reminded him of bombed out industrial Germany when he was a child. However, it was not only the physical condition that affected him, it was that no one gave a damn.
Is that what the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Government perceives the situation to be in the inner core of Canadian cities? Is that why it is so concerned about the possibility of widespread subversion and civil unrest, that it wants to be able to pry into medical records, taxation records and to continue to snoop by electronic means and the opening of private mail that the law does not permit it to do today?
What does the Government know that we do not know? Perhaps a member of the Government will tell us why it considers this matter of espionage and subversion to be so high on our national agenda that it is prepared to shove every other piece of legislation aside in order to proceed with it. I hope this is a bad dream and a figment of the Government's imagination. There must be a reason why it is willing to subvert our whole process of law in a way that has never been done before in this nation. Perhaps a Government member will enlighten us as to exactly what is taking place that our national priorities, and what is acceptable and unacceptable in law must be changed or will change.
The matter of prying into medical records was the subject of a rather interesting letter from the Canadian Medical Association on May 4, 1984. Mr. Freamo, Secretary General of the Canadian Medical Association, wrote a letter to the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in which he said:
My attention has been drawn to criticism of the Canadian Medical Association expressed by committee members during yesterday afternoon's hearing. The criticism appears to have been based on the perceived "non-interest" in Bill C-9 on the part of the Association and in this context I would like to outline for you the CMA's actions to date.
In September of 1983, the CM A was made aware of problems that could ensue if sections of Bill C-157
That was the parent Bill to this one. It continues:
-were to become law. Concern had been expressed by Dr. Phillip Berger in a letter to Ms. Lorraine Gotlib, QC and it was through the Canadian Bar Association (CBA), to whom the letter had been forwarded, that the CMA was made aware of Dr. Berger's concerns.
The joint committee of the CMA/CBA reviewed Bill C-157 and agreed that the concerns and reservations expressed by Dr. Berger were valid. The joint committee reported to its respective executive bodies. Subsequently the CMA communicated its views to the chairman of the Senate committee charged with reviewing Bill C-157.
In mid-April the joint CMA/CBA committee reviewed Bill C-9 and concluded that the concerns previously expressed had not been allayed by the new version of the bill.
Of particular concern to the CMA are the following sections: Section 16- Collection of information concerning foreign states and persons; Section 19- Authorized disclosure of information; Part II Judicial Control, Sections 21-28.
Section 16 does not appear to build in any safeguards in respect to the Service obtaining from physicians information about individuals not protected under the section. The physician may well be in the 'protected' category and as such not have his or her actions investigated; an attempt to do this is outlined in Section 16(2). This section does nothing to protect the patient from having his or her records examined and/or drawing the physician into providing information about a patient over and above what may be recorded in the record.
I do not intend to read any more of that letter. However, I want to again point out to the Government and the public that
June 19, 1984

this agency is going much further in regard to investigative powers than Canadian law has hitherto provided. Why is it necessary?
In the report filed by the Solicitor General for the period covering the last year, we see that some 44 per cent of the electronic snooping carried out in Canada was for reasons of national security. That in itself was a shock. However, when we see the Government paying undue attention to new and unheard of legal powers in Canada, we must be more than just a little disturbed.
Many of my constituents experienced the dark McCarthy era in the United States. We know what can happen even under a regime of law that has traditionally been much more protective of individual liberties than has our own. We have seen the abuses that have taken place once a certain climate of opinion is created. We saw how many people across Canada, including all of the people in the Government, were prepared on the very shallowest of evidence to obliterate or suspend civil liberties across Canada; because a few kids were running around in a couple of cars with guns. We know how easy it is for mass hysteria to be whipped up, just as it was against the Japanese Canadians during the early period of the Second World War.
It is important when we are dealing with these kinds of excesses and new powers that we remember we have to design law not only for normal times, but design the law in such a way that it will safeguard our basic rights at a time when national and public opinion may be, to say the least, abnormal and excited to the point where steps may be taken that would not normally be pursued.

Mr. Speaker, I want to proceed to a very sober consideration of this important grouping of motions to delete. The motions in question would delete a number of clauses. I will certainly not take the time of the House to refer to all of them in the 10 minutes available to me.
Why not?

Because there are members of the public who have copies of the Bill available. I am sure they will follow with interest the debates in the House with copies of the Bill in their hands. They know that Liberal Members of the House have taken no interest whatsoever in the Bill to this point. Certainly we would welcome the participation of those Members in this debate for the first time.
Clause 23 gives a new power to enter any place, to remove anything which has been placed in a dwelling house, office or any other location. I would note briefly that this is a power which is being accorded to the service for the first time. As well, under the provisions of Clause 26 of the proposed Bill, none of the procedural safeguards which exist under the provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to interceptions of telephone communications under the code, none or at least minimal safeguards apply under this Bill. For example, the rules of evidence with respect to derivative evidence are not applicable. None of the safeguards that this Parliament insisted upon under the provisions of this Bill. We say that is wrong.
As well, under the provisions of the Bill that deal with the powers and functions of the proposed Security Intelligence Review Committee, I would note that this committee can engage in very sweeping powers, but the powers are circumscribed by one very essential element. That element is the oath of secrecy which is included in Clause 37. Under the provisions of Clause 37, the members of the Security Intelligence Review Committee are required to swear that they will not disclose or make known to any person any information acquired by them by reason of the duties that they are performing under the Act. Effectively what this does is to deny any power of meaningful oversight when coupled with the provision of this Bill that would deny them access to Cabinet documents as well.
In addition, the powers and functions of this review committee are set out at proposed Clause 38 of the Bill. These powers as set out in that clause fall short of those which are required for full and effective scrutiny and oversight. For example, there is no power under the provisions of the Bill as it is now worded for the service to review the relationships that exist between the security service and all other bodies and agencies engaged in security or intelligence functions in Canada. Despite the clear recommendation of the McDonald Commission and number of other witnesses that any review committee should have jurisdiction over all of the players in the intelligence community, this Bill would not grant that jurisdiction to the proposed Security Intelligence Review Committee.
As well, the committee has no explicit power to review the criteria which are set out for security assessments under subclause 13 of the Bill, security assessments which are obviously critical when it comes to the awarding of contracts, the hiring of individuals for government jobs or promotions. The criteria for those assessments are currently set out in an outdated Cabinet document, Cabinet Directive No. 35, which dates back over 20 years to 1963. There is no requirement whatsoever that the new review committee review the criteria of these security assessments to ensure that there is not an excessive number of such assessments and that such assessments are being carried out pursuant to carefully drafted criteria.
I would note as well there is no provision in the Bill that grants the review committee the power to review the terms of conditions of employment which are established by the director pursuant to Clause 8 of this Bill. I made reference to this on an earlier amendment, the possibility of unfair or unreasonable terms and conditions of employment being established by the director and with the denial of any form of collective bargaining rights to members of the service. They have no alternative whatsoever, no recourse at all. Clause 38 should permit the members of the service to have the terms and conditions of their employment reviewed by the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
Under the provisions of Clause 47 of the proposed Bill, where there is a complaint about the activities or conduct of the new civilian security service, the review committee has to tell the director ahead of time: "Excuse me, Mr. Director, there has been a complaint made about you. We are coming in to investigate." What does that do to the powers of independent investigation, this so-called independent watchdog that is supposed to be scrutinizing the new service? When they want to investigate a potential wrongdoing, before they get to first base they are denied any access to Cabinet documents and they have to inform the director that they are coming in to investigate. It makes a mockery of any suggestion of effective or independent oversight.
Clause 50 is another clause which would be deleted under the motions which have been grouped for the purpose of this debate. It was important that the Speaker not dispense with the reading of those motions so that the people of this country will know clearly that at least one Party in this House is

prepared, unfortunately without the assistance of the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), to fight the fight against this repressive legislation, a fight which in the past the Secretary of State was prepared to wage against similar repressive provisions in the Immigration Act.
Under Clause 50 of this Bill, the review committee has sweeping powers to summon individuals before it, to receive and accept evidence and other information, whether on oath, on affidavit or otherwise, as the committee sees fit. That means that in the case of an individual such as Victor Regola-do, the El Salvadoran refugee who, despite being found to be a bona fide political refugee in this country was ordered out of Canada, ordered deported by virtue of a signature by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and his colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts), the review committee could rely upon hearsay evidence submitted to them in the form of a letter from a secret police service in one of these repressive military dictatorships suggesting that the individual in question is a threat to security. There was a time when the Secretary of State would have stood in his place and denounced these repressive measures. Sadly, that time appears to have been passed. This provision makes a mockery of the rules of natural justice which should apply when dealing with the fundamental liberties of Canadians and indeed the fundamental civil liberties of visitors to this country.
In conclusion, I urge the Members of this House to support the motions before us. They deal with clauses which pose very serious concerns to Canadians. They deal with clauses which should be deleted in the interest of protecting and enhancing the civil liberties of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, this perversion in the Government's Bill of the idea of a review committee is one of the two or three most serious faults in it. We have been told that the Government's legislation follows much of the McDonald Commission's recommendations. On certain points it does. We have been told that it follows the Pitfield recommendations. On certain points it does. One point on which the McDonald Commission was explicit was that this review committee should be set up to have real powers of review and should be subject to Parliament. There is something now being proposed, given the same name, that in its essential nature was changed by the Solicitor General's Bill.
This review committee has no right to access to Cabinet documents. I have heard Members opposite state publicly and to the media that this committee will have access to all information. That is false. I think that Members opposite, including some of the senior front-benchers who have made that statement, must know that what they are saying is false and intended to mislead the public. The committee will not have access to all information. It will be denied access to any Cabinet document which the director or the Cabinet or both together may choose to deny it.
The committee will not have the unfettered right to inquire into the actions of the secret service. It will need to give notice
Security Intelligence Service
so that matters can be covered up, re-arranged and fudged over before the committee looks at them. The committee will be limited by an oath of secrecy so that it may learn things only under circumstances which prevent it from acting on the knowledge it receives. It may find itself in a position of servere conflict of conscience.
Parliament is essentially denied its control over that committee. I was very sorry to hear the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) say earlier this evening that the appointment of senior people to the committee will require the approval of the opposition Parties. That is false. I suppose the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton knew what it was false when he said it. However, he is not present so that he may blush. According to the legislation, those appointments do not require the approval of opposition Parties. The recommendation of the McDonald Commission was that those appointments should require that approval.
I do not know the intentions of the Hon. Member, but I regret the fact that he is not here to correct any unintentionally misleading remark he may have made. It was certainly misleading when he said that such approval is required. That is entirely false and I am sorry that a front-bencher for the Liberal Party would make that kind of remark. We have been told how this matter has been discussed over and over in caucus so as to create the best possible Bill. I am sure the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton was party to those discussions. He must know that on the very point about which he spoke, what he said was not true.
This Bill does not require that the members of the review committee be approved by the leaders of the opposition Parties. It only requires that the Prime Minister shall consult with the leaders of the opposition Parties. In other words, the Prime Minister may say: "I am going to appoint Mr. So-and-So and Mr. So-and-So, what do you think?" The leaders of the opposition Parties may say: "No, they are not fit," and the Prime Minister may reply: "Tough luck, boys, I am appointing them." That is consultation. It is consultation that is not subject to any requirement that the Leader of the Official Opposition or the leader of any other Party having 12 Members of the House should give approval.
It is very interesting that while the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is using every dirty trick in the book to drive this legislation through the House, his front-bench colleagues find it appropriate to mislead the public by saying that appointments to this vital review committee require the input of the leaders of the opposition Parties. They know that that is false. They should be ashamed of their attempt to mislead the public in such a fashion. They are not misleading the opposition Parties. This is a point about which both opposition Parties have already made a very clear complaint. However, it is a point about which it appears the government Party is willing to try to mislead the media or, through the media, to mislead the public. It is very unfortunate that government Members have stooped so low.
These clauses of the Bill ought to be deleted. Better still, they should be withdrawn by the Government for reformula-

June 19, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
tion so that they will be in accordance with the recommendations of the McDonald Commission. The recommendations of the McDonald Commission have the support of everyone in the country who has spoken to this matter, except the Solicitor General and his Party. They form the tiny minority in this country which disagrees with the McDonald Commission on this point, along with perhaps a few Party colleagues in the Senate.
The people who have spoken on this matter want that review committee to fall under the authority of the whole of Parliament, and not only the authority of the Government in consultation with the rest of Parliament. They want Parliament to have the powers of investigation that were recommended by the McDonald Commission. I urge the Government to withdraw these clauses. If that does not happen, I urge members of the Government to join with the opposition in voting them down.

CROWN CORPORATIONS-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION COMPANY LIMITED-PROPOSED SALE OF COMPANY. (B) CASH ASSETS OF COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I raised a particular question in December my main concern arose from the prospect that members of the management of NTCL may be involved in a consortium to purchase NTCL. This would give them a decided advantage over all other interest groups as they have had over four years to prepare for the sale of the company. It is for this reason that I raised that question.
In July, 1983, as a member of the Indian and Northern Affairs Committee, I began investigating the operations of NTCL. I placed my many concerns on the Order Paper. I have not received answer to those questions, even though the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave me the assurances that then would be responded to before the company was privatized.
My concerns regarded safety practices; the quality of the steel which was used to build the barges for bulk fuel hauling, general mismanagement, as evidenced by the Thruster bargers and the refitting of the M.V. Broderick and the M.V. Banks-land, and the desire for public hearings in communities which are serviced by NTCL in order that the people in the North could provide their input as to the conditions of sale.
I would like to put three concerns before the House. They are the assessment of the land, the accounting of revenues and the legislative requirements of the sale. As this company is
June 19, 1984

intended to be privatized, it is important that there be an accurate assessment of the value.
The share value of the company is $25 million. There are shares of $250,000. The assessed assets are $60 million. That means that there is a share value of $240 per share. Some say that the assessed value is as high as $250 million. That would mean that the share value is $1,000 per share. If the assessed value is $100 million, the share value would be $400 per share. These are examples of assessed values. It is important for perceived buyers to know what the company is worth.
I would like to examine the Fort McMurray problem, which involves some 49 acres, most of which was seconded during wartime for this company. It was received at a very low book value, which is now the value it is assessed at in the company's assets. In Fort McMurray, the assessed value of its property, undeveloped, zoned industrial with no development plan at the present time is $5.5 million. As soon as a development plan is put forward and this property is zoned commercial the value will increase to $8.5 million. We know that NTCL has put forward a development plan, even though the chairman indicated that that was not taking place.
Now there is the arrival of First Boston of Canada. They are supposed to perform an assessment of the value of the company. It is important for that company to know what NTCL's assets are and what the potentials are if those assets are developed. We need a fair, accurate and real assessment. Therefore, I hope that the report of First Boston will be tabled in the House so that we all will know that it is an accurate assessment of the value.
We know that there is an architectural development plan for a shopping complex, complete with office towers, in progress. In fact, the present land has been re-zoned from industrial to commercial. Therefore, its assessed value will increase.
Another concern I have relates to the ARD-31. This ship was given to NTCF by treaty from the United States Government. NTCL is required by that treaty to report all revenues and profits to the United States Government. We are very concerned that this is not the case. We heard in the standing committee the state of the declared revenues from 1979 to 1980. There were no profits. In 1981, there was a profit of $4,000. In 1982, there was a profit of $233,000. In 1983, there was a loss of $321,000. It is impossible for NTCL to have revenues of $233,000 in 1982 if one company had leasing fees in that year of over $1 million. NTCL serves many other companies.
My concern is that for some reason there has been an improper reporting to the United States Government of the actual revenues and profits that the ARD-31 is earning in the North. I have been listening to the questions of a Congresswoman in the United States regarding the reporting of this income. The President of NTCL was asked to provide answers to those questions and he refused to do so. That indicates that there is some suspicion of what is taking place.
I have a copy of a letter which is addressed to the Congresswoman, the Hon. Patricia Schroeder, wherein it reads:

The Air Force contract administrator, Captain Mohn, attempted to obtain the requested information; however, Mr. L.R. Montpetit, President of NTCL, declined to provide the information.
Grimshaw Trucking, a wholly-owned subsidiary of NTCL, a Crown corporation, had been bidding for contracts this year at 1980 rates. Is it fair that a company which is a Crown corporation should be under-bidding the private corporations in that area, many of which are showing losses? They can in no way compete with these 1980 rates. Why would that company be doing this now, at a time when it is supposedly going to be privatized? The only reason I can see for that is they want to bring the value down so that those people who are interested in buying the company, perhaps even the managers themselves, will have a better opportunity to do so.
If one looks at the company, one will find that it has liquid assets almost equal to half the value of the company. It is almost possible to buy the company out with its own cash and the sale of some of its subsidiaries. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I want answers to these questions before this Government privatizes that company. I believe that anyone who would buy that company would want the same kinds of answers. I want to make sure that the taxpayers of this nation get fair value for what they have put into this company and that the citizens of the north who depend on it for service continue to receive that service.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Eva Cote (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION COMPANY LIMITED-PROPOSED SALE OF COMPANY. (B) CASH ASSETS OF COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to answer the question raised by the Hon. Member for Wetas-kiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) concerning the sale of Northern Transportation Company Limited.
The Hon. Member's concern seems to be that the Government of Canada is proceeding too quickly with the sale of this company to the private sector. However, it stands to reason the Government would want to expedite the sale. The Hon. Member should realize that once the decision has been made to sell the company, there is no reason to delay the sale. Any delay would create confusion that would cause concern among both employees and prospective buyers. We want to avoid this as much as possible. We would like to dispose of the company in circumstances conducive to getting us the best price. We would like Northern Transportation Company Limited to continue its important function as a reliable and efficient supplier for Northern communities and businesses.
As for the questions raised by the Hon. Member, I can assure him that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) is aware of these questions and that they will be answered. There is no connection between the decision to sell the company and questions that have been raised about details of the company's operations. Our decision to sell Northern Transportation Company Limited was made after an exhaustive analysis of the implications for native peoples and Northern development, not out of opportunistic, short-term considerations.

June 19, 1984
Adjournment Debate
The Hon. Member has expressed concern about the company's assets. He ought to know that the company runs a seasonal operation which therefore needs more working capital than most other operations. He should also realize that the end of the year happens to be the time when the company's cash flow is at its maximum. It is therefore inaccurate to infer a connection between the financial situation of the company and the shutdown of the Athabasca operation. The decision to shut down the Athabasca operation was made after substantial financial losses were ascertained and after a thorough analysis of the situation, which confirmed there were acceptable alternatives to this traditional service.
As far as the Churchill operation is concerned, Northern Transportation Company Limited has not slowed down this operation at all, whatever the Hon. Member's questions may seem to suggest. Traffic depends on customers and not on Northern Transportation Company Limited.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ENERGY-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND ENERGY COSTS- GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) IMPACT OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not federal Government policy to directly subsidize electricity rates in any province, including Prince Edward Island. We have encouraged Prince Edward Island to negotiate long-term, firm power purchases with New Brunswick power and Hydro-Quebec. Such an arrangement represents the best opportunity for Prince Edward Island to bring its electricity rates down to the national average over the long term.
It is, and has been, federal Government policy to subsidize energy costs generally in P.E.I. in a variety of ways. In 1976 Canada provided assistance to P.E.I. through construction of an underwater electrical transmission cable linking the Island's distribution system to that of New Brunswick. The $36 million cost of this cable was supported by a 50 per cent federal Government grant and a 25 per cent loan.
Prince Edward Island's particular energy circumstances were recognized in the National Energy Program of October 1980. A number of measures special to Prince Edward Island were announced. The enhanced conservation portion of the Canada Oil Substitution Program provided special grants for residential investments reducing oil heating costs on the Island. The Altantic Energy Conservation Investment Program was established, providing grants to firms for investments that increase energy efficiency. In addition, Prince Edward Island benefited from national conservation and renewable energy programs. To date $19.16 million has been expended in Prince Edward Island under the following programs: Canada Oil Substitution Program, $2.85 million; Canadian Home Insulation Program, $10.01 million; Atlantic Energy Conservation Investment Program, $.35 million; Conservation and Renewable Energy Demonstration Program, $3.25 million; Forest Industry Renewable Energy, $1.9 million; National Energy Audit Program, $.8 million.
In 1982 Energy, Mines and Resources agreed to undertake a special study, Prince Edward Island energy alternatives. The First phase of this study, which was completed in December, 1983, concluded that the most economic means of reducing energy costs on the Island lay primarily in conservation and the use of wood or biomass. Both alternatives involve a significant degree of provincial content generating economic benefits to the Island.
The federal Government is in the process of concluding an energy sub-agreement with Prince Edward Island which would expend several million dollars on initiatives which would concentrate on utilizing underdeveloped biomass and agricultural waste resources as alternative fuel sources, help to offset high energy costs, reduce the province's relatively heavy dependence on oil and provide a significant economic stimulus to the province itself.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-MILITARY ACCIDENTS-RELEASE OF INQUIRY TRANSCRIPTS. (B) NAMES OF INQUEST WITNESSES
NATIONAL DEFENCE-MILITARY ACCIDENTS-RELEASE OF INQUIRY TRANSCRIPTS. (B) NAMES OF INQUEST WITNESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to follow up on a question that I asked of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) some time ago. When I rose in the House on that day I was concerned that a promise the Minister had made on the nationally televised CBC, The Journal, was not being kept up to that point.
I was referring to the fact that the Minister had appeared on The Journal with respect to a case, which came to his attention through my raising it in the House, of the accidental deaths of two militia privates in Saskatchewan in August of last year. It is a long story which I will not go through, but through a series of questions in the House we came to a point where we broke some new ground in terms of the release of information to parents of militiamen killed in accidents while on duty.
The Minister indicated to me that no longer would people have to go through the access to information route to get copies of the transcripts of the inquiries that the militia conducts when such incidents occur. I had to go through that process on behalf of my constituents in order to set some precedents, and after that the Minister said that from now on parents or designated next of kin would not have to go through that process. All that they would have to do is indicate that they wanted a copy of the transcript and they would get it. That is the commitment that he made on national television that evening.
Some weeks later, however, I phoned the mothers of two militiamen who had been killed and they still had not received the transcripts, even though the Minister said on television some weeks before that all they had to do was call the next morning and he would see to it that everything was looked after and would turn out just fine. Yet we found out some weeks later that although those people had phoned the next morning they had not heard back from anybody and had not received a copy of the transcript. I rose at that time to push and hopefully embarrass the Minister into doing something about living up to that commitment.
I did make one accusation that day that I want to correct. At that time I indicated that the coroner who will preside over the coroner's inquest which is to be held this Friday in fact, into the Krosney-Laurendeau accident had been unable to get a copy of the Board of Inquiry transcript from the Canadian Armed Forces. That was the situation to the best of my information when I said that to the Minister in the House on that day. I learned later that day, from talking to people who were concerned, that the coroner had on the previous weekend been supplied with a copy of the transcript. Just for the record, and out of respect for the facts, I wanted to make that correction on the record.
However, a number of other concerns still stand. I would like to know, and I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary who is here to answer for the Minister will be able to tell me,

June 19, 1984
Adjournment Debate
whether or not the two designated next of kin who were the object of my discussion with the Minister the last time I rose in the House have now received a transcript. The Minister indicated to me in a letter that he would be in communication with those parents and would be providing them with the transcript. I would like to know if that has happened.
I would also like to know, Mr. Speaker, why in the case of Krosney there only seems to have been reform from the top down so far. I have to give the Minister some credit for having responded to the pressure we put on him through the media, through questions in the House and through petitions, etc. It took some doing, but nevertheless there has been some response. We see this reform from the top down but we still see no reform at the bottom, so to speak, at the regional and local level within the militia. The parents of Private Krosney and Private Laurendeau have still not heard from the militia. They have not received a letter of explanation, apology, or regret that all of this hassle had to be gone through, on top of their grief.
I wonder whether the reason for that is because in the final analysis, in spite of the fact we now have the transcript, and we were even able to get the recommendations which were initially hidden from us through the use of the access to information exemption, the fundamental question of whether or not Private Krosney on that day was trained to drive the vehicle he was driving was not addressed in the recommendations. In the evidence there is plenty of indication that he was not trained. In fact, there was a bald admission that he had no previous training driving a jeep with a gun on the top and a trailer behind it. If that is not addressed in the recommendations, maybe that is why there is still that kind of silence. I do not know, Mr. Speaker. I hope the Minister will have some answers for me.
May I just say that I do not want my comments in any way to be construed as an attack on the militia or the cadets or anything like that. I am a supporter of them. I rose in the House the other day to ask for increased funding for the army cadet leader course at Vernon. There are many other issues on which I will have occasion to rise in support of some of the work the militia and the cadets are doing. But they have to clean up their act with respect to how they relate to accidents and how they relate to next of kin. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will have something positive to report.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-MILITARY ACCIDENTS-RELEASE OF INQUIRY TRANSCRIPTS. (B) NAMES OF INQUEST WITNESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the I Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) for his j continued interest and his continued support and concern for the militia. 1 understand the Minister has written the Hon. Member a letter in response to his May 23 question in the
House. I believe in the three minutes allotted to me that it is worth recording the salient points which the letter contained.
When a member of the Canadian Forces dies in the course of his military duty, Canadian Forces authorities, by regulation, are required to conduct an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death. This investigation usually takes the form of a board of inquiry which, I might add, is not a substitute for the provincial coroner's investigation, report or inquest.
In addition to determining reasons for and cause of death the Canadian Forces investigation may be used in support of an application for a pension for dependants, it may identify problems regarding material, it may alert authorities to critical requirements pertaining to operations and training. The investigation is a record as defined by the Access to Information Act and, as such, one may gain access to it in accord with and subject to the provisions of that Act.
The Minister has directed that the designated next of kin of a deceased member of the Canadian Forces need not follow the prescribed procedures in the Access to Information Act. Such a request, be it written or oral, is to be treated as if it were an access request under the Access to Information Act. It will be reviewed and subject to the exemptions provided in the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act, the investigation will be provided to the requester.
Addressing now that part of the Hon. Member's question which dealt with the provision of information to the Coroner of the Province of Saskatchewan in respect of the deaths of Privates Krosney and Laurendeau, I am able to inform you that on 27 April 1984 the Minister personally corresponded with Dr. McMillan. He also directed Canadian Forces authorities to extend fullest co-operation with the Coroner in the discharge of his duties. To that end, a copy of the minutes of the proceedings of the board of inquiry convened to investigate the deaths of Privates Krosney and Laurendeau was provided to the Coroner. The minutes provided were complete and include the names of personnel who gave evidence with the exception that the findings and recommendations portions had been removed. The minutes were provided to him for his personal use in the performance of his duties and, as a consequence, they were not to be made public or form part of teh evidence submitted at the inquest.
I am pleased to advise the Hon. Member that the Minister has personally written both to Mrs. Anne McKinnon and Mrs. Caroline Davies forwarding each a copy of the Board of Inquiry they requested. This should have given them the information the Member requested concerning the licence to drive. The only information not contained is that which is exempted from disclosure under the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act.
June 19, 1984
